title: Inheritance resolver for SchemaModel (declared → inherited)
description: Second pass over the declared SchemaModel that walks each type's supertype chain and populates inheritedOwns, inheritedPlays, inheritedRelates with provenance.
design:
## Purpose

This bead owns the second pass over a declared `SchemaModel`: computing inherited owns/plays/relates capabilities with provenance and surfacing role override relationships. It is separate from `one-2xg.38.1.2` (type definitions only) and `one-2xg.38.1.3` (parser into declared facts only).

## Scope

Given a declared `SchemaModel`, produce a resolved model or companion resolved view where:

- Entity inherited owns and inherited plays are populated from the entity supertype chain.
- Relation inherited owns and inherited relates are populated from the relation supertype chain.
- Every inherited capability retains `declaredAt` pointing to the ancestor that introduced it.
- Direct declarations remain distinct from inherited declarations so proposal authoring and explanation can say exactly where a capability came from.
- Role overrides are detected when a relation subtype declares `relates childRole as parentRole`; the resolved model surfaces the override pair explicitly.
- A subtype declaration that shadows or overrides a supertype role wins in the inherited view for that subtype.

Out of scope:

- Parsing TypeQL text. `one-2xg.38.1.3` owns parser behavior.
- Changing Lingo tool output or existing consumers. `one-2xg.38.2` owns consumer migration.
- Core ontology slice computation. `one-2xg.38.4.12` consumes the resolved model after this bead lands.

## Implementation Notes

Recommended shape:

```swift
enum SchemaModelInheritanceResolver {
  static func resolve(_ declared: SchemaModel) throws -> SchemaModel
}
```

The resolver should be deterministic and pure: no database calls, no TypeQL parsing, no UI dependencies. It should build lookup tables by type label, walk supertype chains, detect cycles defensively, and produce stable ordering for inherited capabilities.

Role override handling is the load-bearing behavior. The three-level relation inheritance fixture should include a role override at level 2 and prove that level 3 sees the correct effective role declarations with provenance.
acceptance_criteria:
- Three-level relation inheritance fixture returns correct inherited capabilities at every level
- Role override fixture surfaces override pairs explicitly
- Provenance correctly identifies the declaring ancestor for every inherited capability
close_reason: Added pure SchemaModel inheritance resolver with provenance-preserving inherited owns/plays/relates, role override shadowing, cycle/missing-supertype errors, and focused Swift Testing coverage.

title: Build TypeDB 3 schema parser producing declared SchemaModel
description: Parse schema() text into the declared portion of SchemaModel. Cover all annotation forms, role specialization (relates X as Y), function blocks (params, return spec, body).
design:
## Purpose

This bead owns the TypeQL parser work that turns full `database.schema()` text into the declared portion of `SchemaModel`. It is separate from `one-2xg.38.1.2`, which defines only the Swift model types, and from `one-2xg.38.1.4`, which computes inherited capabilities.

The parser must consume `database.schema()`, not `database.typeSchema()`, because `one-2xg.38.1.1` verified that installed `fun` declarations appear in `schema()` and are omitted from `typeSchema()`.

## Scope

Implement parsing from TypeQL schema text into declared SchemaModel facts:

- Entity declarations: label, supertype, annotations, declared owns, declared plays.
- Relation declarations: label, supertype, annotations, declared relates, declared owns.
- Attribute declarations: label, supertype, value type, annotations.
- Role specialization: `relates childRole as parentRole`.
- Capability annotations: `@card`, `@key`, `@unique`, `@subkey`, `@cascade`, `@distinct`, and unknown future annotations.
- Type/value annotations: `@abstract`, `@independent`, `@doc`, `@regex`, `@range`, `@values`, and unknown future annotations.
- Function declarations: name, parameters, return spec, raw body, annotations if present, and best-effort referenced type labels.

Out of scope:

- Inheritance resolution. The parser populates declared arrays only; `one-2xg.38.1.4` owns inherited arrays and role override resolution.
- Replacing current `ParsedSchema` consumers. `one-2xg.38.2` owns migration of Lingo tools, verifier, validator, diff, explorer, and UI consumers.
- Golden fixture framework beyond whatever focused parser tests this bead needs; `one-2xg.38.1.5` owns the reusable harness.

## Implementation Notes

The existing `TypeQLParser` and `ParsedSchema` code are useful reference points, but the new parser must target the approved `SchemaModel` types instead of extending `ParsedSchema` further. Prefer a new parser entry point over changing every old consumer in this bead.

Recommended shape:

```swift
enum SchemaModelParser {
  static func parse(_ typeql: String, source: SchemaSource) throws -> SchemaModel
}
```

The returned `SchemaModel` should have only declared capabilities populated. Inherited arrays should be empty until the resolver pass runs.

Function body parsing stays shallow: preserve raw body text and derive referenced type labels by comparing tokens against labels declared in the parsed model.
acceptance_criteria:
- Parses every annotation form: @card, @key, @unique, @subkey, @abstract, @independent, @cascade, @doc, @regex, @range, @values
- Parses relates X as Y role specialization
- Parses fun blocks structurally (params, return, body)
- Function records include set of referenced type labels
close_reason: Added SchemaModelParser for declared-only database.schema() parsing, including annotations, role overrides, functions, and referenced type labels, with focused Swift Testing coverage.

title: Design SchemaModel type system
description: Define the Swift types: SchemaModel, EntityType, RelationType, AttributeType, RoleType, FunctionDeclaration, Owns, Plays, Relates, Cardinality, Annotation. Include provenance fields for declared-vs-inherited views.
design:
## Motivation

Lingo is moving from a conversational elicitation assistant into a schema synthesis system. The remaining synthesis-loop work cannot safely generate, judge, migrate, or explain TypeDB changes from raw TypeQL strings or the current partial `ParsedSchema` projection. The system needs one explicit schema object model that represents what the live database schema says, including functions, declared capabilities, inherited capabilities, role overrides, annotations, and provenance.

The concrete failure this model is meant to prevent is the current class of Lingo schema-inspection dead ends: the agent is told to use schema inspection instead of `run_read_query`, but the inspection surface does not expose enough facts to answer questions such as “are any relations subclasses?” or to reason about inherited roles and ownership. A complete `SchemaModel` makes that guidance true: schema questions and schema proposal checks should be answerable from one canonical model instead of ad hoc parsing, forbidden read queries, or lossy summaries.

## Scope Of This Bead

This bead implements only the SchemaModel type system and a small readability test proving the model can be hand-written clearly. It must not implement TypeQL parsing, database access, inheritance resolution, SchemaModel serialization for Lingo tools, or migration of existing ParsedSchema consumers.

Those responsibilities are captured separately:

- `one-2xg.38.1.3` — parser from `database.schema()` TypeQL text into the declared SchemaModel.
- `one-2xg.38.1.4` — inheritance resolver from declared SchemaModel to inherited capabilities and role overrides.
- `one-2xg.38.1.5` — fixture/golden test harness and round-trip coverage.
- `one-2xg.38.2` — migration of Lingo, validator, diff, explorer, and tool output from ParsedSchema to SchemaModel.

## How The Model Will Be Used

`SchemaModel` is the canonical in-app reasoning contract for TypeDB schema state. It will be consumed by:

- The TypeDB schema parser task (`one-2xg.38.1.3`), which populates the declared model from `database.schema()` text.
- The inheritance resolver task (`one-2xg.38.1.4`), which computes inherited capabilities and role overrides as a separate pass.
- The fixture/golden test harness (`one-2xg.38.1.5`), which proves the model is readable, round-trippable, and cheap to extend with new fixtures.
- The future `getSchemaModel` or upgraded `getParsedSchema` Lingo tool (`one-2xg.38.2`), which serializes this model across the LLM boundary.
- `LingoProposalVerifier`, `SchemaContractValidator`, schema diffing, the Lingo inspector/explorer, and the synthesis-loop Generator/Judge, which need one shared view of schema facts.

TypeQL text remains the durable import/export and review artifact. `SchemaModel` is the app’s reasoning surface. JSON tool output is only a transport view over `SchemaModel`, not a separate source of truth.

## Source Surface

Use `database.schema()` as the source when building `SchemaModel`. Live verification in `one-2xg.38.1.1` showed that `database.schema()` includes installed `fun` declarations, while `database.typeSchema()` omits functions. `typeSchema()` can remain useful for type-only export/review paths, but it is not sufficient for the full reasoning model.

The parser should populate only declared facts. Inherited facts are deliberately computed by a separate resolver pass so parsing, inheritance, and explanation remain independently testable.

## Design Constraints

1. Round-trippable to TypeQL text.
2. Every capability carries `declaredAt` provenance.
3. Inherited views are computed by a resolver pass, not embedded in the parser.
4. The model must be easy to hand-write in tests. If a small fixture’s expected `SchemaModel` literal feels heavy, the design is wrong.
5. The model should be explicit enough for agents and UI to answer schema questions without reparsing TypeQL or querying schema facts as data.

## Proposed Type Shape

Core decision: `SchemaModel` is an immutable value model parsed from `database.schema()` text.

```swift
public struct SchemaModel: Sendable, Hashable {
  public let source: SchemaSource
  public let entities: [SchemaEntity]
  public let relations: [SchemaRelation]
  public let attributes: [SchemaAttribute]
  public let functions: [SchemaFunction]
}
```

Use separate structs for entity/relation/attribute because their legal declarations differ enough that one generic `SchemaType` would either be too loose or full of irrelevant optionals.

```swift
public struct SchemaEntity: Sendable, Hashable, Identifiable {
  public let label: TypeLabel
  public let supertype: TypeLabel?
  public let annotations: [SchemaAnnotation]
  public let declaredOwns: [OwnsCapability]
  public let declaredPlays: [PlaysCapability]
  public let inheritedOwns: [OwnsCapability]
  public let inheritedPlays: [PlaysCapability]
}

public struct SchemaRelation: Sendable, Hashable, Identifiable {
  public let label: TypeLabel
  public let supertype: TypeLabel?
  public let annotations: [SchemaAnnotation]
  public let declaredRelates: [RelatesCapability]
  public let inheritedRelates: [RelatesCapability]
  public let declaredOwns: [OwnsCapability]
  public let inheritedOwns: [OwnsCapability]
}

public struct SchemaAttribute: Sendable, Hashable, Identifiable {
  public let label: TypeLabel
  public let supertype: TypeLabel?
  public let valueType: TypeQLValueType?
  public let annotations: [SchemaAnnotation]
}
```

## Roles

Roles are represented as relation-scoped capability labels in V1, not global top-level model objects. TypeDB roles are addressed as `relation:role`, but in schema text they are declared through `relates` on a relation and consumed through `plays` on player types. Modeling them through those two edges keeps the common reasoning path direct.

```swift
public struct RoleLabel: Sendable, Hashable {
  public let relation: TypeLabel
  public let role: String
}
```

If a global role inventory is needed later, derive it from `SchemaRelation.declaredRelates + inheritedRelates`.

## Capabilities And Provenance

Every capability carries `declaredAt`. Inherited capability arrays contain the same capability records, but with `declaredAt` pointing to the ancestor that introduced them. This makes explanation cheap: “employee plays employment:employee because worker declared it.”

```swift
public struct OwnsCapability: Sendable, Hashable {
  public let attribute: TypeLabel
  public let cardinality: Cardinality
  public let annotations: [SchemaAnnotation]
  public let declaredAt: TypeLabel
}

public struct PlaysCapability: Sendable, Hashable {
  public let role: RoleLabel
  public let annotations: [SchemaAnnotation]
  public let declaredAt: TypeLabel
}

public struct RelatesCapability: Sendable, Hashable {
  public let role: String
  public let overriddenRole: String?
  public let cardinality: Cardinality
  public let annotations: [SchemaAnnotation]
  public let declaredAt: TypeLabel
}
```

## Functions

Functions are parsed enough for reasoning, diffing, and dependency detection, but V1 does not attempt a full function-body AST.

```swift
public struct SchemaFunction: Sendable, Hashable {
  public let name: String
  public let parameters: [FunctionParameter]
  public let returnSpec: FunctionReturn
  public let body: String
  public let referencedTypes: Set<TypeLabel>
  public let annotations: [SchemaAnnotation]
}
```

`referencedTypes` is best-effort from parsed schema labels appearing in params, return specs, and body text. The raw body remains canonical for round-trip and diff.

## Annotations

Annotations use structured known cases plus an escape hatch so future TypeDB annotations are not dropped.

```swift
public enum SchemaAnnotation: Sendable, Hashable {
  case key
  case unique
  case subkey([TypeLabel])
  case card(Cardinality)
  case abstract
  case independent
  case cascade
  case distinct
  case doc(String)
  case regex(String)
  case range(String)
  case values([String])
  case unknown(name: String, arguments: [String])
}
```

## Approval Status

Ken approved these design points in conversation on 2026-05-03:

1. Separate `SchemaEntity` / `SchemaRelation` / `SchemaAttribute` structs instead of one generic type.
2. Roles as relation-scoped capability labels in V1, not top-level model objects.
3. `declaredAt` on every capability, with inherited arrays populated by a resolver pass.
4. Functions as structured signature + raw body + referenced type labels, not a full body AST.
5. `database.schema()` as the source for `SchemaModel` when functions are needed.
acceptance_criteria:
- All types have docs and Sendable/Hashable conformance where appropriate
- Provenance is a first-class field on every capability record
- Fixture-driven design review: a hand-written SchemaModel literal for a small fixture is readable
notes: Ken approved the five SchemaModel design points in conversation on 2026-05-03. Implementation may proceed for the type-system slice only; parser/resolver remain separate beads.

title: Ontologist posture: elicitation, teaching, gist-mirroring
description: Make Lingo behave like a senior ontologist guiding a domain expert. The user knows their domain; they do not know gist, TypeDB, or modeling. The agent leads.
design:
Today's LingoSystemPrompt is overwhelmingly tool-discipline rules (~40 of ~70 directives are 'do/don't call X' or render-shape constraints). It mentions 'understand the user's intent' once, with no scaffolding. There are no instructions to ask before proposing, no vocabulary mirroring, no gist teaching.

Three posture rules to encode:
1. Elicitation-first: ask before proposing. Capture domain, goal, examples, edge cases, vocabulary gaps.
2. Vocabulary mirroring: when the user uses a domain word, restate it in gist terms before introducing TypeQL.
3. Gist teaching: explain gist primitives in plain language tied to the user's domain.

EngineeringHierarchyRequestPart already exists in LingoTranscriptItem.swift but is unused — wire it as the first-class elicitation surface. Agent populates it before any propose_schema_change call.

Optional but high-leverage: an explain_gist_concept tool that pulls definition + canonical use + an example from search_ontology_memory, framed for a non-modeler.

Posture is hard to test mechanically. Use recorded fixture sessions with a rubric (did the agent elicit? did it mirror? did it teach?). Some questions are LLM-judge-able; some need a human pass.
acceptance_criteria:
- A novice user describing a concept gets an elicitation turn first, before any TypeQL proposal
- Agent visibly mirrors domain vocabulary back in gist terms in conversation
- Agent explains gist primitives it uses, in plain language tied to the user's domain
- EngineeringHierarchyRequestPart is rendered as a chat widget and populated before propose_schema_change
- Posture rubric (elicit / mirror / teach) passes on at least three recorded fixture sessions

title: Replace ParsedSchema with SchemaModel across Lingo
description: Migrate every consumer of ParsedSchema to the new SchemaModel and expose the model across the LLM tool boundary as Lingo's single canonical schema contract.
design:
Today ParsedSchema is the de facto reasoning model and is re-parsed at every call site (LingoProposalVerifier, SchemaContractValidator, getParsedSchema, EngineeringHierarchyProposalPart, LingoExplorerRow, the inspector, the diff). After Feature 1 lands, all of these become consumers of one SchemaModel.

Two new boundaries:
1. `OntologyTypeDBClient.schemaModel(database:) async throws -> SchemaModel` — single live introspection method. Backed by `schema()` + new parser. Existing `typeSchema()` stays available for round-trip/export.
2. New LLM tool `getSchemaModel` (or upgraded `getParsedSchema`) returning a stable, versioned JSON serialization of SchemaModel. Types grouped by kind, each with declared + inherited capabilities, functions with structured signatures, provenance everywhere.

The `run_read_query` schema-inspection guard exists today because the agent kept generating broken match queries trying to reach facts `getParsedSchema` couldn't expose. Once the model is complete, the guard's reason for existing is gone — narrow it or delete it.
acceptance_criteria:
- No production code path parses TypeQL via TypeQLParser directly; all schema reasoning consumes SchemaModel
- LingoProposalVerifier and SchemaContractValidator consume SchemaModel
- EngineeringHierarchyProposalPart, LingoExplorerRow, inspector, and diff consume SchemaModel
- Lingo answers "are any relations in knowledge subclasses?" from one tool call without using run_read_query
- The run_read_query schema-inspection guard is either deleted or reduced to a minimal note
notes: Downstream consumer: the synthesis-loop Schema Generator (one-2xg.38.4.13) and Judge (one-2xg.38.4.14) consume the model-shaped tool surface introduced here (38.4.13 takes a SchemaModel-derived slice from 38.4.12; 38.4.14 re-parses post-apply schema using the parser this Feature exposes).

title: TypeDB 3 schema object model with full fidelity
description: Build the Swift model and parser that represents a TypeDB 3 schema completely, including inheritance resolution with provenance.
design:
Top-level `SchemaModel` container with two members: `types` (entity, relation, attribute, role) and `functions`. Every type carries declared capabilities (owns, plays, relates) and inherited capabilities computed by a second pass. Every capability record carries provenance: which type declared it.

Capability records:
- `Owns`: attribute label + cardinality + annotations (@card, @key, @unique, @subkey)
- `Plays`: role label (relation:role) + provenance
- `Relates`: role label + role specialization (relates X as Y) + cardinality + annotations

Type-level annotations: @abstract, @independent, @cascade, @doc.
Attribute-specific annotations: @regex, @range, @values plus value type.
Function records: name, parameters (name+type), return spec (tuple|stream + types), body text, set of referenced type labels for dependency tracking.

Parser consumes `schema()` (not `type_schema()`) so functions are included. Inheritance resolver is a separate pass — keep parsing and resolution decoupled so each is independently testable.

Test harness is the load-bearing risk: the model design has to be powerful enough that golden-file tests over fixture schemas are quick to write and maintain. If the harness feels heavy, the model design is wrong.
acceptance_criteria:
- Given a fixture schema with three levels of relation inheritance and a role override at level 2, the model returns correct declared-vs-inherited answers for every type at every level
- Round-trip property holds: parse → model → serialize → parse → equal, on every fixture
- Function blocks parsed structurally (params, return, body); referenced type labels extracted
- Every annotation form (@card, @key, @unique, @subkey, @abstract, @independent, @cascade, @doc, @regex, @range, @values) covered by at least one fixture
- Inheritance resolver handles role overrides correctly (subtype declaration shadows supertype)
notes:
Consumer: one-2xg.38.4.12 (core ontology slice computation) consumes SchemaModel as its substrate. Slice computation needs declared+inherited capabilities with provenance — that's why Feature 38.1's Task 38.1.4 (inheritance resolver) is the specific gate for 38.4.12, not just the bare SchemaModel parse.
## TypeDB schema surface observation (one-2xg.38.1.1)

Verified against live TypeDB CE 3.10.3 via TypeDBSwift/C driver. `database.schema()` returns the full define surface, including `fun` declarations. `database.typeSchema()` returns only entity/relation/attribute type definitions and omits functions, so the current `getParsedSchema` path that reads `typeSchema()` cannot report functions. TypeDBSwift/C driver exposes no `database_rule_schema` / `ruleSchema()` API; rules are legacy/non-surface in TypeDB 3. Captured fixtures live under `OneApps/Ontology/Resources/Fixtures/schema-surface/` and are covered by `TypeDBSchemaSurfaceTests`.
close_reason: Completed the full-fidelity SchemaModel foundation: schema surface verification, approved model types, declared parser, inheritance resolver, golden fixtures, round-trip harness, and focused Ontology test coverage.

title: Lingo as a world-class ontologist
description: Make Lingo the agent that guides domain experts — who understand their domain but not gist, TypeDB, or modeling — to evolve well-modeled, gist-aligned ontologies. The agent leads; the user supplies domain truth.
design:
## Problem

Domain experts know their domain but do not know ontology modeling, formal type systems, or schema query languages. Building or evolving a TypeDB 3 ontology that captures their domain — and that they trust — currently requires either an ontologist as intermediary or the user themselves learning a discipline orthogonal to their work. This epic builds the conversational system that removes that intermediary while preserving the rigor an ontologist provides.

## Conceptual framing: schema synthesis as program synthesis

Schema evolution is treated as a program-synthesis problem. The schema is the program; competency questions (CQs) — natural-language questions the user wants the ontology to be able to answer — are the executable specification; the system runs an iterative loop until the program satisfies the spec.

Each CQ binds two forms: the natural-language question as the user posed it, and the executable TypeQL query that answers it once the schema supports it. That pairing is the bidirectional commitment between the conversation and the schema. A CQ is not "answered" until its query compiles and runs.

CQ coverage replaces the structural-completeness termination criterion used by retrieval-driven schema-generation systems (such as RIGOR's table-walking traversal of source-relational schemas), because in a conversational setting the spec itself is being authored as the conversation proceeds. The user keeps adding CQs as the model develops; convergence is reached when no CQs remain unanswered and no new CQs are being introduced.

## System boundaries

In scope:
- A single user, in conversation, evolving an ontology starting from an empty base or an existing GIST-grounded schema
- Both creation (greenfield) and evolution (brownfield) treated as one loop; greenfield is the limiting case where every change is additive against an empty schema
- Native TypeQL throughout; no parallel OWL or SHACL representation maintained at runtime
- Programmatic guidance via competency questions, GIST alignment, and reuse of patterns from existing ontologies

Out of scope (deferred):
- Concurrent multi-user merge resolution
- Bulk import from external schema formats (Excel, SysML, OWL ingestion)
- Ontology versioning and release automation (handled by adjacent infrastructure)

## Conceptual roles

The system separates concerns by role:

- **Conversational interlocutor** — the only role the user interacts with directly. Owns elicitation, vocabulary mirroring, and teaching of upper-ontology primitives.
- **Anchor proposer** — maps user-surfaced concepts to candidate positions in the upper ontology (GIST). Resolves ambiguity by surfacing it back through the interlocutor.
- **Pattern recall** — retrieves prior modeling patterns from existing ontologies so synthesis builds on precedent rather than inventing from scratch.
- **Schema synthesizer** — proposes a candidate schema delta plus the executable form of every CQ the delta claims to newly answer.
- **Adjudicator** — judges proposed deltas against multiple oracles before they reach the user. Combines deterministic native validation (the type system enforces structural correctness for free) with semantic review (catches modeling pitfalls type systems cannot see). Returns accept, reject-with-feedback, or escalate-to-clarification.
- **Migration synthesizer** — when a delta is non-additive, synthesizes the data transformations needed so existing instances remain queryable under the new schema. Engages only when needed.
- **Committer** — the transactional boundary. Makes a validated, user-confirmed change durable and recorded.

## Architectural qualities

- **Convergence is observable.** Progress is measured by CQ status. A session converges when no CQs are unanswered, no new CQs are introduced, and no deltas are proposed within a quiet window.
- **Generation is separated from judgment.** Synthesis without an adjudicating step either commits broken schemas or pushes validation onto the user. Separation of generator from judge is a precondition for tractable synthesis (Gen-LLM / Judge-LLM in RIGOR).
- **The type system is the free oracle.** Structural correctness (type cycles, role-player violations, ownership conflicts) is enforced by the database itself when a delta is applied to a shadow instance. Application code does not duplicate this.
- **Shadow-then-commit.** Validation runs against a disposable copy. The live ontology is mutated only after the user explicitly confirms.
- **History is non-negotiable.** Every accepted delta is recorded with the conversation that motivated it, the CQs it claimed to satisfy, the validation trail, and any data migration. Replay, rollback, and explanation are first-class consequences.
- **Durable across interruption.** Long modeling sessions span hours or days. Atomic checkpointing — only after a delta is committed — ensures a crash never leaves a partially-applied state.

## Co-evolving artifacts

Three artifacts evolve together and are stored alongside each other in the user's working ontology:

1. **The core ontology** — the user's TypeQL types and functions.
2. **The CQ Registry** — the structured record of what the user wants to be able to ask, in both natural-language and executable form, with status and lineage to the conversation turns that produced each entry.
3. **The Delta Log** — the append-only record of every accepted schema change with motivation, validation history, satisfied CQs, and any associated data migration.

Co-locating these artifacts means the ontology, its specification, and its history are queryable as one graph.

## Core patterns and algorithms

- **Iterative generate-and-test with bounded retries.** From program synthesis: synthesizer produces, adjudicator evaluates, feedback returns to the synthesizer for retry. Bounded so a stuck loop escalates to the user rather than burning context.
- **Multi-agent role decomposition.** Distinct conceptual roles map to distinct agents with focused prompts and constrained tool surfaces. Roles do not share prompts; the conversational interlocutor never gains schema-write capability.
- **RAG over prior ontologies.** New schema work consults what has been modeled before. Prevents reinvention; keeps naming and pattern conventions consistent across ontologies.
- **Value-correspondence synthesis for refactoring.** Non-additive schema changes (renames, splits, merges, generalizations) require a mapping from old-schema role-players and attribute owners to new-schema ones. The migration is the program that realizes this mapping over existing data. When a mapping is ambiguous, the system asks rather than guesses (Wang/Dillig).
- **Native validation as the correctness contract.** Anything the type system can express becomes the type system's responsibility. Application-level validation handles only what falls outside that surface (modeling pitfalls, GIST conformance patterns expressed as queries).

## Principles

- One voice to the user. Internal multi-agent decomposition is invisible to the conversation.
- Ask before proposing. Domain understanding precedes schema generation.
- Mirror the user's vocabulary in the upper ontology before introducing technical labels.
- Teach every primitive used; never assume the user knows what GIST:Activity means.
- The spec drives convergence; the user's CQs are the contract.
- Durable history beats reconstructable state.
- Partial answers from the conversational interface are a failure mode of the schema, not a feature of the agent.

## What this epic supersedes

- one-2xg.36 — framed only the schema-model substrate and not the conversational synthesis system that consumes it.
- one-2xg.38.3 — an intermediate framing that assumed a single-agent runtime with prompt edits, supplanted once multi-agent synthesis was understood as the right architecture.

## References

- Nayyeri et al., *Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Ontologies from Relational Databases* (RIGOR), arXiv:2506.01232, 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01232. Source of the iterative generate-and-judge loop with bounded retries and CQ-score as the headline quality metric. RIGOR walks a relational source schema table-by-table and terminates on structural coverage; the architecture here replaces that termination criterion with CQ-coverage convergence appropriate to a conversational setting.
- *SchemaAgent: A Multi-Agents Framework for Generating Relational Database Schema*, arXiv:2503.23886, 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.23886. Source of the multi-agent role-decomposition pattern adopted here.
- Wang, Feng, Bavishi, Dillig et al., *Synthesizing Database Programs for Schema Refactoring* (Migrator), arXiv:1904.05498, 2019 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.05498. Source of the value-correspondence formalism used here for non-additive schema migrations. The conversational setting often makes correspondences obvious from the user's natural-language description; the formalism is what tells the system when they are not.
- Lippolis et al., *Ontogenia: ontology generation with metacognitive prompting in large language models* (competency-question-driven ontology generation), 2025. Establishes competency questions as the convergence criterion for ontology-generation systems.
- TypeDB / TypeQL 3 — see the `typedb` skill in this workspace and the bundled `Resources/Packages/ontology-gist` package for the upper-ontology projection used as anchor points.
- GIST upper ontology — see https://www.semanticarts.com/gist/ for the upstream OWL definition; this workspace consumes the TypeQL projection bundled in `Resources/Packages/ontology-gist`.
- Swarm orchestration framework — https://christopherkarani.github.io/Swarm/. The Swift orchestration runtime this system is built on; vendored under `OneApp/SwarmAgent/` and consumed by the Ontology plugin.
acceptance_criteria:
- A domain expert who does not know TypeQL, GIST, or ontology modeling can sustain a conversation that produces or evolves a GIST-grounded TypeQL ontology answering their stated competency questions, without being asked to write or read schema language directly.
- The system observes its own convergence: it can report which CQs are answered, which remain unanswered, and which have been retired as obsolete.
- Every accepted schema change is judged against the live type system before reaching the user; structurally invalid candidates never reach the review surface.
- Every accepted schema change carries durable lineage tying it to the conversation that motivated it, the CQs it newly answered, and the data migration if non-additive.
- Non-additive changes preserve existing instance data unambiguously, surfacing clarifying questions to the user when value correspondences are ambiguous rather than guessing.
- Sessions survive interruption: a recoverable checkpoint exists at every committed change.
- The motivating one-2xg.36 failure ("are any relations in knowledge subclasses?") is answerable from the conversational interface against any GIST-grounded sandbox.
- All child features closed.

title: Provide Lingo with a complete schema object model
description: Give the ontology modification agent a complete, structured view of each database schema so it can reason over schema facts directly instead of relying on lossy summaries or blocked read-query workarounds.
design:
## Motivation

A Lingo session exposed a contract mismatch in the current schema-inspection surface. The user asked whether any relations in the `knowledge` database are subclasses. The agent correctly started with schema inspection, then attempted to query the stored `schemaSubTypeOf` facts when the parsed-schema summary did not expose enough information. That read was rejected by the `run_read_query` guard, which says schema/type/subtype inspection must go through `getParsedSchema`. The result was a dead end: the agent was directed to the right conceptual tool, but that tool only exposed a partial projection of the schema.

This is not primarily a bug in a single query. It shows that a schema modification agent cannot be built on fragments of schema context. Lingo needs a complete schema object model: a coherent, structured representation of the live database schema that captures the facts humans and agents need to reason about changes before proposing them.

## Conceptual Direction

The live TypeDB schema text should remain the import/export and provenance surface, but it should not be the primary reasoning surface. Lingo should parse the live schema into a Swift schema model that represents the schema as objects and relationships: types, supertypes, relations, roles, role overrides, ownership, played roles, attributes, functions, constraints, annotations, documentation, and declared versus inherited capabilities.

The agent-facing schema tool should expose a faithful serialized view of that same model. The serialized output is a transport format for the LLM boundary, not the model itself. Inside the app, UI, validators, diffing, proposal authoring, and agent tools should all depend on the same Swift representation so they agree about what the database schema currently says.

The goal is not to create many narrow tools for every possible schema question. The goal is to give Lingo one complete, stable schema contract it can build reasoning on. Specialized tools may still be useful later for token-efficient slices or convenience, but they should be views over the complete model, not substitutes for it.

## What The Model Must Enable

The complete schema model should let Lingo answer increasingly sophisticated questions without falling back to speculative text interpretation or forbidden data reads. Examples include:

- Which entity, relation, and attribute types exist?
- Which types are subtypes of which supertypes?
- Which relation roles are declared, inherited, or overridden?
- Which entities or relations own which attributes, and with what constraints?
- Which entity or relation types play which roles?
- Which capabilities are directly declared versus inherited?
- What functions exist and what schema concepts do they depend on?
- What schema facts would a proposed change add, replace, remove, or conflict with?
- Why is a proposal compatible with the current ontology, or why would it drift?

This model should become the foundation for richer schema modification behavior: reliable proposal generation, preflight validation, human-readable explanations, migration authoring, schema diff review, UI inspector state, and eventually CLI/CI parity.

## Design Principles

The schema model should be complete enough to reason over, stable enough to become a contract, and explicit about provenance. It should preserve TypeQL semantics rather than merely reshaping the text into JSON. The agent should receive schema facts, not a lossy list of names.

Separate the concerns clearly:

- TypeDB `typeSchema()` text is the source material and review/apply format.
- Swift schema objects are the app's canonical reasoning model.
- Agent tool output is a stable serialization of that model across the LLM tool boundary.
- Proposal TypeQL is generated or validated against the model, then shown to humans as the change artifact.

Avoid exposing implementation accident as contract. The public schema contract should be deliberate and documented, even if it is backed by existing parser structs internally.

## Expected Shape

The schema inspection surface should include, at minimum:

- complete type inventory grouped by kind
- each type's label, kind, abstractness, supertype, annotations, and provenance when available
- relation definitions with roles, role supertypes/overrides, cardinality, and inherited role context
- entity and relation ownership declarations, including cardinality and key/unique/distinct/cascade-style annotations where applicable
- plays declarations and whether they are direct or inherited
- attributes with value type and constraints
- functions with signature and enough structured metadata to reason about dependencies or at least preserve their source faithfully
- explicit declared-vs-inherited views where useful for proposal authoring and explanation
- the original TypeQL source or source references as optional provenance/debug material

The first usable version does not need to solve every advanced inference problem, but it must close the class of failures where Lingo is instructed to use parsed schema inspection and then cannot access fundamental schema facts such as relation subtyping.

## Relationship To The Observed Failure

After this work, the question "are any relations in knowledge subclasses?" should be answerable from the schema model alone. The agent should inspect relation objects, find those with relation supertypes, and respond with the concrete subtype-to-supertype pairs. It should not need to query stored schema-documentation facts, scrape TypeQL text, or explain that the available tool surface is insufficient.

The `run_read_query` guard can remain conceptually correct: data reads are for instance data, counts, and examples. But the alternative path must be complete. If schema inspection is blocked in read queries, the schema model must actually expose the schema.

## Future Payoff

This foundation lets the ontology system grow in a coherent direction. The same schema model can power:

- Lingo answers to schema questions
- schema proposal validation before apply
- drift detection and explanation
- migration generation
- richer inspector views
- schema diff visualizations
- CLI and CI checks that match the app
- safer agent planning because the agent reasons over one authoritative schema graph

The durable win is that Lingo stops being a prompt wrapped around partial tools and becomes a schema modification agent grounded in an explicit model of the database it is changing.
acceptance_criteria:
- A child bead exists under `one-2xg` describing the complete schema object model work.
- The design explicitly ties the work to the observed `run_read_query` / `getParsedSchema` failure.
- The design states that Swift schema objects are the app's canonical reasoning model and serialized tool output is only the LLM boundary representation.
- The design explains why this supports increasingly sophisticated schema questions and modification workflows.
- The acceptance criteria for implementation include answering relation subtype questions from schema inspection without using `run_read_query`.
- The bead is self-contained enough for a future agent or human to understand the architectural goal without reading this conversation.

title: Ontology upgrade keeps multiple cached versions in active package resolution
description: One App crashed during an ontology package upgrade from gist 2.0.4 to 3.0.0. The cache correctly held both release versions, but PackageManager fed both into active dependency resolution keyed only by manifest.name, triggering Swift Dictionary(uniqueKeysWithValues:) fatal error: Duplicate values for key: 'gist'.
design: Separate cached package versions from the active resolver input. During refresh/update, multiple cached releases of the same package may exist on disk, but PackageManager must choose one active package per manifest.name before dependency resolution and UI grouping. Preserve historical cached versions for migration/rollback; do not treat them as invalid repos or delete them as part of resolution.
acceptance_criteria:
- Reproduce the crash scenario with a focused PackageManager test containing gist@2.0.4 and gist@3.0.0 cached state.
- Dependency resolution no longer traps when multiple cached versions of one package exist.
- Active resolution deterministically chooses the intended/latest git package version while preserving old cache directories.
- Existing install/update registry behavior continues to persist only active packages.
close_reason: Fixed PackageManager active package selection so multiple cached releases of one ontology package collapse to a single active resolver entry; added regression coverage for gist 2.0.4 plus 3.0.0 cached state.

title: Refresh gist docs describing mapping decisions
description: Update local translation docs to remove stale flattening language and describe structural preservation of property hierarchies.
design:
Update local docs under docs/translation and related tooling docs to match the revised mapping decision.

docs/translation/mapping-summary.md currently says xsd date and datetime variants are flattened to TypeDB datetime. That is incomplete/stale after the new mapping: primitive values still collapse to TypeDB primitives at root attributes, but explicit datatype-property subPropertyOf edges become attribute subtype edges. Object-property hierarchy preservation and role specialization should also be described. Keep documentation concise and aligned with generated report strategy.
acceptance_criteria:
Acceptance tests:
1. docs/translation/mapping-summary.md no longer says DateTime hierarchy is flattened as the hierarchy-preservation mechanism.
2. Docs explicitly state rdfs:subClassOf -> entity subtyping, datatype-property subPropertyOf -> attribute subtyping, object-property subPropertyOf -> relation subtyping with role specialization.
3. Docs explain query helpers are convenience APIs over structural schema, not substitutes for hierarchy emission.
4. rg for 'flatten' in docs/manifests current generated outputs only finds historically versioned artifacts or deliberately qualified primitive value mapping text.
5. Documentation changes are included in release artifacts/checksums where applicable.
close_reason: Translation docs and generated release artifacts reflect structural hierarchy mapping.

title: Add generated docs hierarchy validation
description: Add validation that generated schema docs contain structural subtype metadata for emitted attribute, relation, and role subtype edges.
design:
Add documentation-level hierarchy checks after schema docs regeneration.

The generated docs are TypeQL data, not JSON. The simplest robust check can parse or search the generated structural metadata section for schemaSubTypeOf insert blocks matching each schema subtype edge. Prefer reusing parseTypeQLSchemaStructure() on schema text to derive expected edges, then verify data/gistCore-schema-docs.tql contains corresponding SchemaResource typeLabel matches and schemaSubTypeOf insert patterns.

This check should cover attribute subtype edges, relation subtype edges, and role subtype edges.
acceptance_criteria:
Acceptance tests:
1. Deleting a generated schemaSubTypeOf block for an attribute subtype causes validate:bootstrap to fail.
2. Deleting a generated schemaSubTypeOf block for a role subtype causes validate:bootstrap to fail.
3. The error message names the missing subtype and supertype labels.
4. The check ignores unrelated SchemaResource annotation text and only validates generated structural metadata.
5. Freshly regenerated docs pass.
close_reason: Implemented and locally verified with generated schema/docs checks; TypeDB runtime validation remains tracked separately.

title: Regenerate vibemachine schema docs after shared parser fix
description: Refresh vibemachine generated documentation metadata so existing hand-authored role specializations appear in SchemaResource structural metadata.
design:
Run ontology-vibemachine's package contract refresh after the shared parser changes in ontology-gist are available.

vibemachine uses node ../ontology-gist/tools/package_contract/bootstrap_hand_authored_package.mjs . for refresh. That script imports parseTypeQLSchemaStructure() from ontology-gist/tools/shared/schema_structure.mjs, so fixing the shared parser changes vibemachine generated docs without schema redesign.

The important existing schema examples are schema/vibemachine.tql relation submissionProvidedBy sub comesFromAgent and several sub hasParticipant relations, plus schema/vibemachine-process.tql assignmentPerformedBy/workStartedPerformedBy/verificationPerformedBy.
acceptance_criteria:
Acceptance tests:
1. After npm run refresh:package-contract in ontology-vibemachine, data/vibemachine-schema-docs.tql contains role subtype metadata for submissionProvidedBy:submission -> comesFromAgent:comesFromAgentSubject and submissionProvidedBy:submitter -> comesFromAgent:comesFromAgentObject.
2. Generated docs include role subtype metadata for process relations assignmentPerformedBy, workStartedPerformedBy, and verificationPerformedBy.
3. Existing hand-authored vibemachine schema files are not unnecessarily reformatted or redesigned.
4. npm run validate:bootstrap passes in ontology-vibemachine.
close_reason: Implemented and locally verified with generated schema/docs checks; TypeDB runtime validation remains tracked separately.

title: Assess whether documentation schema needs a role-specialization relation
description: Confirm whether existing schemaSubTypeOf is sufficient for role specialization metadata or whether the self-describing schema needs a dedicated relation.
design:
Review schema/self-describing-schema.tql and consumers of SchemaResource metadata before deciding on schema changes.

The existing model has SchemaResource(kind='role') plus schemaSubTypeOf between SchemaResources. TypeDB role specialization is structurally a subtype relationship, so schemaSubTypeOf is probably the right representation. A dedicated schemaRoleSpecializes relation would only be justified if consumers need to distinguish role specialization from other subtype edges without checking kind, or if TypeDB semantics require metadata beyond subtype/supertype.

Document the decision in docs/translation/mapping-summary.md or a nearby translation docs file so future schema-browser work understands why role specialization uses schemaSubTypeOf.
acceptance_criteria:
Acceptance tests:
1. Decision notes explicitly compare reusing schemaSubTypeOf vs adding a dedicated relation.
2. If schemaSubTypeOf is retained, generated metadata can query role specializations by matching SchemaResource kind 'role' on both sides.
3. If a new relation is added, schema/self-describing-schema.tql, synthetic SchemaResource docs, generated data, apply units, and validation are all updated consistently.
4. TypeDB bootstrap passes after whichever decision is implemented.
notes: Decision: keep the documentation schema unchanged. Existing SchemaResource(kind='role') plus schemaSubTypeOf is sufficient because TypeDB role specialization is itself a subtype relationship. Consumers can distinguish role specialization by matching both resources with kind='role'. No dedicated schemaRoleSpecializes relation is needed for this release.
close_reason: Implemented and locally verified with generated schema/docs checks; TypeDB runtime validation remains tracked separately.

title: Update translation report strategy and hierarchy coverage data
description: Update emit_structural.mjs report text and coverage fields so reports describe structural hierarchy preservation instead of DateTime flattening as a substitute.
design:
Update renderReport() in tools/gist_to_typeql/emit_structural.mjs and generated manifests/gist-v3.0.0.translation-report.json.

The report currently says DateTime properties are flattened to TypeDB datetime attributes. Replace that with the revised mapping decision: datatype subPropertyOf maps to attribute subtyping; object subPropertyOf maps to relation subtyping plus role specialization. Add explicit counts for IR edges discovered and schema edges emitted so validation failures are diagnosable from the report alone.

Do not overstate OWL semantics: transitive/symmetric/functional flags remain notes/report metadata unless separately implemented as rules or constraints.
acceptance_criteria:
Acceptance tests:
1. translation-report strategy text no longer describes DateTime hierarchy flattening as a substitute for structural subtyping.
2. report coverage includes datatypeSubPropertyEdgesDiscovered/emitted and objectSubPropertyEdgesDiscovered/emitted counts.
3. report includes roleSpecializationsEmitted count for object property hierarchy edges.
4. Counts match the regenerated schema and validation checks.
5. npm run validate:bootstrap verifies the report is fresh.
close_reason: Implemented and locally verified with generated schema/docs checks; TypeDB runtime validation remains tracked separately.

title: Raw TypeQL proposal is lost when parser finds no type declarations
description: Transcript lingo-20260501T001833Z shows propose_schema_change receiving a full TypeQL proposal made of existing-type plays clauses, but the returned proposal payload has typeQL='define' and only a synthetic 'Schema proposal' concept. The proposal model serializes parsed entities/relations/attributes and loses raw TypeQL when the parser cannot parse existing-type amendment statements.
design: Preserve raw TypeQL on EngineeringHierarchyProposalPart for proposals created from tool TypeQL. Use raw TypeQL as the canonical typeQL/sendable/plainText payload when present. Keep parsed structural fields for browser rows when the parser can derive them; if parsing yields no rows, the browser should still show the raw TypeQL in a proposal detail/summary surface. Edited structural proposals may continue to serialize from parsed structures.
acceptance_criteria:
- A proposal whose TypeQL is only existing-type plays clauses returns the original full TypeQL, not 'define'.
- The Lingo Browser has a visible proposal review surface for raw-TypeQL-only proposals.
- Existing structured entity/relation/attribute proposal tests still pass.
- Regression test uses fixture TypeQL and no AI provider.
close_reason: Fixed: proposal parts preserve raw TypeQL when parser yields no structural rows; Explorer shows a proposal overview for raw-TypeQL-only proposals; regression test covers amendment-only TypeQL.

title: Disable Lingo Type Editor as an active proposal surface
description: The app should stop using the Lingo Type Editor for now without deleting its code. Transcript lingo-20260501T001833Z shows the agent calling focus_proposal_in_editor after proposing a schema change, then telling the user the proposal opened in the Type Editor.
design: Remove Type Editor from active Lingo UI/tool paths. Do not delete LingoTypeEditorView or its model/tests unless required. Stop registering focus_proposal_in_editor with the Lingo agent, remove prompt references that tell the model to use the Type Editor, make any active proposal affordance route to the Lingo Explorer, and remove visible app affordances that open the Type Editor. The Lingo Browser/Explorer is the only active proposal review surface. Also update the schema-design prompt flow so the assistant does not jump directly to TypeQL: first seek to understand the user's domain and intent, then identify terms/relations/roles/attributes and definitions, and only then present a model proposal.
acceptance_criteria:
- propose_schema_change opens Lingo Explorer and does not mention switching to Type Editor.
- Lingo agent tools do not include focus_proposal_in_editor.
- In-app visible controls no longer open Lingo Type Editor.
- Existing Type Editor code remains in repository.
- The system prompt requires intent and vocabulary grounding before schema proposals.
- Focused tests updated to expect Explorer-only behavior and intent-first proposal behavior.
close_reason: Fixed: Lingo no longer registers or opens the Type Editor as an active proposal surface; prompt and visible affordances route to Lingo Explorer; tests cover Explorer-only catalog and intent-first proposal flow.

title: Lingo proposal collisions are rejected before browser review
description: propose_schema_change rejects proposals that mention existing live labels such as Collection and VibeEngineeringTask. This prevents the Lingo Browser from opening as the default proposal review surface and hides the proposal entirely. Collisions should be visible for review; unsafe redefinitions should be blocked at apply time.
design: Split proposal validation from apply validation. propose_schema_change should still reject structurally unusable TypeQL such as unknown plays roles, but live-label duplicate definitions should be recorded as proposal collisions/drift and shown in Lingo Browser. apply_schema_delta must continue to reject duplicate live definitions before TypeDB writes. Ensure propose_schema_change opens Lingo Browser by default even when collisions are present.
acceptance_criteria:
- Given a proposal containing existing labels Collection and VibeEngineeringTask, propose_schema_change records the proposal, returns live_schema_verification collision data, and opens Lingo Browser.
- The same duplicate-label TypeQL is still rejected by apply_schema_delta before TypeDB writes.
- Unknown plays role payloads remain rejected at proposal time.
- Regression tests require no AI provider.
close_reason: Allowed propose_schema_change to record live-label collisions for Lingo Browser review while preserving strict apply-time duplicate-definition validation and proposal-time unknown-role rejection.

title: Lingo Browser does not show the active proposal
description: The Lingo Browser can open without showing the schema proposal. The browser should always show the selected in-flight proposal section when a current proposal exists, even after multi-proposal state migration or legacy single-proposal compatibility paths.
design: Audit LingoChatView visibility conditions, currentLingoProposal vs lingoEngineeringHierarchyProposal, proposalParsedSchema cache use, and explorer expansion defaults. Make the browser render from currentLingoProposal, not only the legacy single proposal property. Ensure opening/focusing the explorer expands the proposal domain and proposal type section so the proposed types are visible immediately.
acceptance_criteria:
- With a current selected proposal in lingoProposals, LingoExplorerView appears even if legacy lingoEngineeringHierarchyProposal is nil.
- The proposal banner/domain and proposed types are visible after openLingoExplorer/focus_proposal_in_explorer.
- Multi-proposal and single-proposal compatibility paths both render the selected proposal.
- Regression test covers selected proposal collection without relying on legacy single-proposal field.
close_reason: Fixed first-send session start, removed noisy lifecycle transcript rows, silenced internal sandbox package fallback warnings, restored proposal rendering from current proposal state, and aligned Lingo entity rows with entity-browser hierarchy.

title: Lingo Browser exposes empty sandbox package fallback to users
description: The Lingo Browser shows 'Sandbox package versions are empty. Showing on-disk package contents.' This should not be a normal user-facing state, and the empty pinned package snapshot indicates the sandbox installed-package lookup returned no package records even though live ontology data should be available.
design: Find why active sandbox pinned packages can be PinnedLivePackages.empty. The likely source is SandboxInstalledPackagesService returning no installed package records from PackageBootstrapRegistry for the active sandbox. Fix the data path so a sandbox with no package registry records falls back silently to loaded live/on-disk package data without displaying an alarming error. Reserve user-facing warnings for actual stale/error states that require action. Add diagnostics/logging if useful, not transcript/UI noise.
acceptance_criteria:
- Normal Lingo Browser use does not show 'Sandbox package versions are empty'.
- Empty pinned package snapshots do not hide live ontology sections.
- Empty registry/no installed-package data is treated as silent fallback or a neutral loading state, not a warning.
- Root cause is documented in completion notes.
- Regression test covers active sandbox + empty pinned/installed package data.
close_reason: Fixed first-send session start, removed noisy lifecycle transcript rows, silenced internal sandbox package fallback warnings, restored proposal rendering from current proposal state, and aligned Lingo entity rows with entity-browser hierarchy.

title: Lingo chat requires explicit Start before first send
description: Opening Lingo chat and submitting the first input should start the conversation automatically. The current UI requires pressing a Start button first because canSend is gated by isLingoSessionActive and sendMessage returns if service is nil.
design: Change LingoChatView so the first submitted user turn starts the agent session automatically, then sends the message. The header should not require a prominent Start action for normal use. Preserve Restart/Stop behavior if useful, but first-send must be the primary happy path. Avoid double-start when a session is already active or a turn is in flight.
acceptance_criteria:
- First non-empty input can be submitted when no Lingo session is active.
- sendMessage starts the conversation and sends the first user turn in order.
- The old Start prerequisite is gone from the normal happy path.
- If provider configuration fails, the draft is not lost and the transcript shows a useful configuration error.
- Add focused view-model/view tests or extracted logic tests where practical; no AI provider/network is required.
close_reason: Fixed first-send session start, removed noisy lifecycle transcript rows, silenced internal sandbox package fallback warnings, restored proposal rendering from current proposal state, and aligned Lingo entity rows with entity-browser hierarchy.

title: Verify both Claude Code and Codex find the skills (incl. Unicode scanner)
description: The make-or-break compatibility check. Run Claude Code and Codex sessions in OneWorkspace and verify each can list and invoke swift-concurrency, ontology-repo-layout, and typedb via description triggers (or whatever skill discovery surface they use). Validate that APM's Unicode-hijack scanner doesn't reject the Greek letters in swift-concurrency (Γ, α, κ, ρ from the typing rules). If the scanner blocks, evaluate workarounds: (a) replace Greek with ASCII + prose, (b) move formal calculus to an external linked doc and keep only patterns inline, (c) override the scanner if APM allows it.
design: Codex install location: per APM docs it should write to whatever the configured Codex location is, but verify empirically. If Codex doesn't auto-pick up: check apm config, check whether Codex on this machine has its skill discovery surface configured, and consider whether a manual symlink from APM's Claude location to Codex's expected path is acceptable as a workaround.
acceptance_criteria: (1) Claude Code finds and invokes all 3 skills. (2) Codex finds and invokes all 3 skills. (3) Unicode scanner verdict documented — passed cleanly OR workaround applied with rationale. (4) Any deltas between agent installs (e.g., APM only writes to .claude/skills/ but not Codex's location) are documented as known issues for the rollout decision.

title: Lingo Browser omits installed live ontology sections
description: The Lingo Browser is only showing the schema proposal; installed live ontologies such as gist, beads, vibemachine, and gastown are not visible. This breaks the core review experience because users cannot compare the proposal against the existing ontology or navigate to live parents/relations.
design: Fix live ontology population in the Lingo Browser. The browser should always show proposal changes alongside relevant installed live ontology sections when package data or live schema data is available. If live packages are still loading, show an explicit loading/fallback state rather than silently omitting them. The data source should use sandbox-pinned packages when available and fall back to loaded package/live schema caches when no active sandbox exists.
acceptance_criteria:
- With fixture packages loaded, Lingo Browser rows include proposal section plus live ontology domain sections.
- With an active sandbox and pinned packages, live sections reflect pinned installed packages.
- With no active sandbox, live sections fall back to loaded on-disk/live schema data and display a clear fallback message.
- If live schema/package data is unavailable, the UI shows an explicit empty/loading/error state rather than only the proposal.
- Regression tests are view-model row tests using package fixtures; no AI provider required.
close_reason: Fixed with local TypeQL validation, read-only browser controls, role inspector state, and live package fallback tests.

title: Lingo Explorer marks live gist labels as new proposal types
description: The Lingo Explorer displayed Collection as a proposal-local NEW entity with parent 'entity'. In the gist ontology, Collection already exists and is a subclass of Composite. The Explorer/proposal verifier allowed proposal data to override or obscure live gist truth instead of surfacing a collision/redefinition issue.
design: Ensure proposal verification and Explorer rendering are based on a complete active live schema snapshot before assigning NEW/COLLISION/DRIFT badges. Proposal labels that already exist in gist or installed live packages must never appear as simple NEW items. The detail view should make collisions obvious and should let users compare the proposed declaration with the live declaration, including live parent such as Collection -> Composite.
acceptance_criteria:
- With gist loaded, a proposal containing 'entity Collection sub entity' yields a collision/redefinition warning, not a NEW badge.
- The Explorer can show that live gist Collection has parent Composite.
- The proposal-local Collection does not silently replace live Collection in navigation/inspection without collision context.
- Regression test uses fixture packages and proposal TypeQL directly; no AI provider required.
close_reason: Fixed with local TypeQL validation, read-only browser controls, role inspector state, and live package fallback tests.

title: Block invalid AI-generated TypeQL before proposal or apply
description: Lingo accepted/generated TypeQL such as 'entity Collection sub entity, plays isMemberOf:isMemberOfObject' and let it reach apply_schema_delta/TypeDB, producing a raw TypeQL parser error. The root issue is that AI-generated TypeQL crosses deterministic boundaries without a local schema contract check for existing labels, relation names, role names, and parseability.
design: Add deterministic validation around both propose_schema_change and apply_schema_delta. Treat assistant TypeQL as untrusted input. Validate against the active sandbox/live schema snapshot before recording a reviewable proposal or attempting TypeDB writes. The validator must catch: unknown relation labels in plays clauses, unknown role names for known relations, attempts to redefine existing live labels such as gist Collection, and TypeQL parser syntax failures. The apply path must fail before calling TypeDB when validation fails, and the transcript/tool result should report a concise actionable validation error instead of exposing raw TypeDB parse output.
acceptance_criteria:
- A canned bad payload with 'entity Collection sub entity, plays isMemberOf:isMemberOfObject' is rejected locally before TypeDB write.
- Test fake TypeDB client records no write/apply call for invalid TypeQL.
- Validation error names unknown relation 'isMemberOf' and/or unknown role 'isMemberOfObject'.
- Existing live label 'Collection' is reported as collision/redefinition risk, not accepted as a new proposal label.
- propose_schema_change and apply_schema_delta both exercise the same deterministic validation path or equivalent contract checks.
- Focused tool tests require no live AI provider and use fixture TypeQL payloads only.
close_reason: Fixed with local TypeQL validation, read-only browser controls, role inspector state, and live package fallback tests.

title: Profile and reduce VibeMachine activate() from 4.5s
description: VibeMachine plugin's activate() takes ~4.5s, dominating the plugin activation window. Identify which work inside activate() is blocking and either move it off the activation path or parallelize it.
design:
## Evidence
From the 2026-04-30 launch (PID 91891), AppState log:

  11:45:37.834  [AppState] Activating plugin: com.gamma.vibemachine
  11:45:37.835  [vibemachine:Plugin] runtime metadata logged
  11:45:37.836  [vibemachine:Plugin] registered lazy SwiftTerm backend
  11:45:37.835-.943  [beads:SuperviseManager] init, restored 11 sessions, 11x SuperviseSessionWorkspace "Initial terminal config"
  11:45:37.951  [vibemachine:Plugin] Using active repository
  11:45:38.137  [tmux:TmuxAgentClient] Connected to tmux agent mach service
  11:45:38.153  [ghosttyterminal:TmuxService] tmux agent bootstrap status ready=true
  ... ~4.2s of silence ...
  11:45:42.318  [AppState] Plugin activated: com.gamma.vibemachine

The 4.2s gap from 38.153 to 42.318 has no log lines. That gap is the budget to find.

## Files to investigate
- OneApps/VibeMachine/**/Plugin/*.swift (VibeMachine entry point + activate())
- com.gamma.beads SuperviseManager / SessionPersistence / SuperviseSessionWorkspace - these emit during VibeMachine activation, suggesting beads bootstrap runs synchronously inside VibeMachine activate()
- Active repository resolution (last log before the gap is "Using active repository")

## Approach
1. Add os_signpost or Date()-diff logs around each major step inside VibeMachine activate(): runtime metadata, backend registration, beads SuperviseManager bootstrap, repo discovery, tmux agent connection, anything after tmux ready.
2. Re-run launch and capture the same log window with the command in the parent epic's design.
3. Identify the dominant cost in the 4.2s gap.
4. Fix: prefer (a) move the work off activate() into a lazy/background task, (b) parallelize independent steps with async let / TaskGroup, (c) cache results across launches if recomputing on every cold start.

## Notes
- The 11 SuperviseSessionWorkspace "Initial terminal config" lines and "restored 11 sessions" suggest session restore for beads supervised processes runs at activation. If each one synchronously checks tmux state, that scales with session count.
- "Using active repository" + git work is a likely culprit for hidden synchronous IO.
acceptance_criteria: VibeMachine activate() returns in <500ms on a warm machine. Per-step instrumentation logs are checked in (or removed) so future regressions are catchable. Re-running the launch profile shows the gap eliminated.

title: Startup Performance
description: Reduce time-to-interactive after launch. Profiling on 2026-04-30 (PID 91891) showed plugin activation takes ~4.6s after the app window appears, dominated by a single plugin's activate(). Separately, the Knowledge view's first-open hangs ~30s on a TypeDB connect candidate even though plugin loading itself is already done. Both contribute to the user-perceived 'plugins are still loading' experience.
design:
## Goals
Cut perceived startup latency from app-launch to fully-interactive plugin UI.

## Baseline (2026-04-30, PID 91891)
- AppState begins activation at 11:45:37.724 with 9 plugins discovered.
- Plugin activation completes at 11:45:42.324 (4.60 s).
- Per-plugin activation duration:
  - ghosttyterminal 24 ms
  - eurorack 5 ms
  - muse 1 ms
  - flashbacks 0 ms
  - example 1 ms
  - proto01 0 ms
  - ontology 79 ms
  - vibemachine **4,484 ms**
  - producer 5 ms
- Activation runs sequentially in AppState; vibemachine alone accounts for ~97% of total activation time and pushes producer behind it.
- Separately, Ontology's TypeDB connect path stalls 30 s on the second candidate before failing (11:45:37.945 -> 11:46:07.946). This is post-activation but contributes to the user-perceived slowness when first opening Knowledge.

## Source of truth
Logs captured via:
  /usr/bin/log show --predicate 'processID == 91891' --start "2026-04-30 11:45:35" --end "2026-04-30 11:46:30" --style compact --info --debug

## Approach
Track work under one feature ("Faster plugin activation and post-launch responsiveness"); break individual investigations and fixes into tasks under that feature. Use blocking dependencies if a fix depends on an earlier investigation.

## Success criteria (rough targets - refine in tasks)
- Time from `AppState: Discovered N plugin(s)` to `Plugin load complete` under 1 second.
- No single plugin's activate() exceeds 250 ms on a warm machine.
- First open of Knowledge does not block UI for >2 s when TypeDB container is still booting.
acceptance_criteria: Each child task has its own measurable acceptance. Epic closes when all children close and re-running the launch profile shows: (a) plugin activation total < 1s, (b) Knowledge view first-open does not block on a 30s TypeDB connect.

title: Index SKOS altLabels and editorial notes in ontology memory corpus
description: StaticSchemaProvider parses altLabels, editorialNotes, historyNotes, seeAlso, domainIncludes, iri, and deprecated from each SchemaResource, but OntologyMemoryCorpus.typeDocRecord drops them before indexing. The largest loss is altLabels: when a user says 'task' but the canonical type is 'WorkItem' with altLabel 'task', BM25 cannot match. This blocks the AI+human interactive ontology goal because Lingo keeps inventing types that already exist under a synonym. Per-type structural records (entity/relation/attribute) also carry parent/owns/plays/value only with no description text, so structure and meaning never co-locate in a single retrieval chunk.
design: Extend OntologyMemoryCorpus.typeDocRecord to include altLabels, editorialNotes, historyNotes, seeAlso in the body so they participate in BM25 scoring; add iri, deprecated, and altLabels (joined) to record metadata. Optionally enrich typeRecord (entity/relation/attribute) by joining the matching TypeDocEntry by typeLabel and folding prefLabel + definition into the body so a single chunk carries both shape and meaning. Bump the corpus fingerprint input so existing stores rebuild on first launch after the change.
acceptance_criteria: typeDoc records contain altLabels, editorialNotes, historyNotes, seeAlso text. iri, deprecated, and altLabels appear in record metadata. Searching the corpus by an altLabel returns the canonical type. Existing OntologyMemoryCorpusTests are updated and a new test asserts altLabel retrieval against a fixture with synonyms. Fingerprint changes when the new fields are added so old stores rebuild.
notes: Discovered while validating 15.36 — the SKOS layer is mostly indexed (definition, scope notes, examples, prefLabel) but the synonym/cross-reference fields are dropped.
close_reason: OntologyMemoryCorpus.typeDocRecord now indexes altLabels (body + metadata), editorialNotes (body), historyNotes (body), seeAlso (body), iri (metadata), and deprecated (metadata). StaticSchemaProvider.parseLegacyTypeDocEntries extended to extract altLabel/editorialNote/historyNote/seeAlso/example/deprecated/prefLabel from legacy TypeDoc statements. Tests in OntologyMemoryCorpusTests assert SKOS fields appear in record body + metadata and that altLabel-only fingerprint changes drive a corpus rebuild. Fixture gist Task now carries altLabel/editorialNote/seeAlso real data. Discovered an unrelated pre-existing parser bug (semicolons inside quoted values truncate the parsed statement); filed as one-cwy.

title: Migrate LingoDiagnosticSessionRecorder to Swarm RunHooks
description: LingoDiagnosticSessionRecorder pattern-matches a 30-case OneAgentEvent switch (LingoDiagnosticSessionRecorder.swift) re-bridged from baseService.events through OntologyAgentService.startEventConsumer. The bridging Task re-iterates an AsyncStream that already had one consumer, which causes events to be lost on restart (the underlying cause of one-3u7). Replace the post-hoc event-stream observer with Swarm.RunHooks fed directly into ReActAgent.run/stream — RunHooks fires synchronously inside the agent's run loop, eliminating the AsyncStream re-iteration and halving the recorder code.
design:
Files: Vendor/Swarm/Sources/Swarm/Core/RunHooks.swift (read-only, hooks contract); OneApp/SwarmAgent/AgentService.swift (BaseAgentService.send call site); OneApps/Ontology/Agent/LingoDiagnosticSessionRecorder.swift (the consumer); OneApps/Ontology/Agent/OntologyAgentService.swift (startEventConsumer/handleAgentEvent).

Approach:
1. Define a OneAgentRunHooks adapter in OneApp/SwarmAgent/Facade that mirrors Swarm.RunHooks but exposes One*-prefixed types (no plugin Swarm imports).

title: OntologyTests: SwarmToolToMCPAdapter maps argument errors to MCP internal-error code instead of invalid-params

Likely lives in OneApps/Ontology/MCP/OntologyMCPServer.swift or OneApp/SwarmAgent/Adapters/ around the SwarmToolToMCPAdapter / OneMCPError mapping introduced during the one-2xg.31 facade migration.

title: OntologyAgentService.startEventConsumer re-iterates baseService.events on restart (events lost)
description: OntologyAgentService bridges OneAgentEvents from BaseAgentService through its own AsyncStream by spawning an event-consumer Task that does 'for await event in baseService.events'. After cancel() and startConversation() are called, cancelEventConsumer() cancels the prior Task and startEventConsumer() spawns a new Task that iterates baseService.events again. AsyncStream only delivers events to its first iteration, so the new Task receives no events; subsequent send() calls dispatch a turn that the agent runs to completion but the user-facing service.events stream never sees the response — the LingoChatView would appear stuck and tests that wait on .completed hang. Fix likely: hold a single long-lived consumer Task that survives across cancel/restart, or rewrite OntologyAgentService to forward events without an intermediate AsyncStream (use a Continuation-driven pattern). This is independent of the conversation-memory wiring landed in BaseAgentService (see one-0um).
acceptance_criteria: A two-turn integration test that calls cancel() between turns, restarts the conversation, and asserts the second turn's .completed event is observed on service.events.

title: Prebuild SwarmAgent.xcframework once plugins are decoupled
description: Phase 2 of the Swarm/Wax build migration. Runs after one-2xg.31 (facade) completes.
