title: Lingo transcripts support manual feedback loops
description: Make Lingo chat/session transcripts reliable feedback artifacts for the Engineering hierarchy vertical slice so manual verification failures can be collected and fed back into prompt, memory, canned-query, and widget improvements.
design:
Implementation approach:
- Audit the existing LingoDiagnosticSessionRecorder, which already writes JSONL session traces under ConfigPaths.base/sessions/lingo and records session_started, user_turn, agent events, tool calls, output chunks/tokens, errors, and provider context.
- Ensure the Engineering hierarchy walking-skeleton flow records enough transcript data to diagnose failures: user text, assistant text, generated UI part identifiers/payload summaries, widget actions, action results, tool calls, sandbox/database context, and user-facing errors.
- Add explicit diagnostic events for generative UI parts and widget actions because those are app-level transcript events, not necessarily GammaAgent events. Keep payloads sanitized/truncated consistently with the existing recorder.
- Surface the current transcript log path somewhere useful for manual verification, such as a debug transcript entry, Lingo debug view, or developer-only copy/reveal action.
- Define a small manual feedback artifact format or convention: a failed session can be identified by sessionID/fileURL plus a short human note about what went wrong. Do not automate the improvement loop yet; the loop is intentionally manual.
- Preserve privacy/safety behavior: diagnostic tracing must never break a chat session, must redact likely secrets, and must avoid unbounded payload growth.

- The transcript includes user turns, assistant text, tool calls/results, errors, active database/sandbox context, generated UI part metadata, and widget action/result events.

title: Engineering hierarchy widgets resolve from plugin data shapes
description: Extract the proven EngineeringTask walking-skeleton widgets into the minimal data-shape registry needed for Lingo: plugin-registered SwiftUI widgets are selected by typed ontology data shapes and rendered inside transcript messages.
design:
Implementation approach:
- Do this after the concrete Engineering hierarchy request/proposal widgets are manually verified. This bead is an extraction/generalization step, not the first implementation step.
- Start from the working Lingo-local types introduced for the Engineering hierarchy slice and promote only the pieces that have proven useful.
- Add the smallest Swift-native data-shape-to-widget mechanism needed by the Engineering hierarchy workflow. Prefer protocols, enums/structs, @Observable stores, and SwiftUI view builders over web-style JSON component trees.
- Define a generative UI part type that carries shape identifier, schema version, payload, source, and action metadata.
- Define a widget contribution/registry pattern aligned with GammaCore contributions if the abstraction should be shared; otherwise keep it in Ontology and leave a clear path to GammaCore promotion.
- Ontology should register widgets for the shapes already exercised by the Engineering hierarchy slice: request understanding, sandbox affordance, schema proposal/review, apply progress/result, validation evidence, compact schema snapshot, and compact intent timeline.
- Matching should prioritize exact shape identifiers and fall back to a safe textual/JSON renderer.
- Widgets may compose by asking the registry to render child generative UI parts, but avoid an arbitrary model-authored UI tree.

Relevant files likely involved:
- OneApp/GammaCore/Contributions/Contribution.swift and ContributionRegistry.swift if promoted to GammaCore
- OneApps/Ontology/Plugin/OntologyPlugin.swift
- OneApps/Ontology/Views/Lingo/LingoChatView.swift
- new generative UI model/registry/widget files under OneApps/Ontology or GammaCore
- OneApps/Ontology/OntologyTests/* for registry and fallback tests.

- Lingo transcript rows can render a generative UI part by resolving its shape through a plugin/widget registry.
- Ontology registers widgets for all Engineering hierarchy shapes needed by the vertical slice.
- Unknown shapes render through a safe fallback instead of crashing or disappearing.
- Widget actions are typed and dispatch through Swift code, not arbitrary model-generated handlers.
- Tests cover exact shape resolution, fallback rendering model, and at least one composed child-part rendering path.
notes: Design reference: planning-n-design/muse-lingo-generative-ui-architecture.md. Extract the widget/data-shape registry from the working vertical slice; do not make generic workflow abstraction the starting point.
close_reason: Added a minimal data-shape widget registry. LingoTranscriptPart now exposes a stable shape identifier; LingoWidgetRegistry resolves a transcript part to a SwiftUI view via shape-keyed renderers, falling back to LingoUnknownShapeFallbackView for unregistered shapes. LingoBuiltinWidgets registers the three Engineering hierarchy walking-skeleton widgets (request, proposal, validation evidence) — those views are no longer file-private so the registry can resolve them. LingoTranscriptPartView now dispatches through the registry instead of switching on the closed enum, and LingoWidgetRegistry.shared auto-registers builtins. Tests in LingoWidgetRegistryTests cover shape registration, exact resolution, fallback rendering, override behavior, and a composing-widget pathway that re-enters the registry to render an embedded child shape. title: Engineering hierarchy validation renders as chat evidence

design:

- The final chat state should show the evidence that validation ran; the inspector should show the latest cumulative state for human verification.
- Reuse CandidateSchemaView/IntentTimelineView presentation logic through inspector sections where possible.

title: Engineering hierarchy refinement stays inside transcript
description: Support follow-up conversational refinement of the EngineeringTask hierarchy after the initial proposal, including vocabulary changes, rationale updates, regenerated in-chat review surfaces, and synchronized inspector state.
design:
Implementation approach:
- Treat follow-up user turns as edits to the active proposal or active sandbox, depending on whether the proposal has been confirmed.
- For pre-confirmation refinements, update the existing proposal surface or append a new revision surface with clear supersession state.
- For post-confirmation refinements, use normal confirmed schema-change flow: show review, wait for confirmation, then apply paired writes.
- Required scenario coverage should include renaming/refining labels such as Top Level Feature vs TLF, Sub Feature vs Sub-feature, and adding rationale/typedoc-style annotations.
- The transcript should show what changed between proposal revisions using a compact diff/revision summary widget.
- The inspector should always reflect the current cumulative state: active proposal, superseded revisions where useful, accepted labels, active sandbox, applied changes, and latest intent grouping. Chat owns event-shaped review/revision actions; the inspector owns current-state inspection.

- OneApps/Ontology/Views/Lingo/LingoChatView.swift

- OneApps/Ontology/Agent/LingoTranscriptItem.swift

- OneApps/Ontology/Agent/Tools/ChangeIntentTools.swift
- OneApps/Ontology/Diff/SchemaDiff.swift
- OneApps/Ontology/Migration/MigrationAuthor.swift if codification-preview structures are useful.
acceptance_criteria:
- A follow-up turn can revise the Engineering hierarchy proposal before confirmation without applying schema.
- The transcript clearly identifies the current proposal and marks superseded proposal revisions.
- A follow-up turn after confirmation produces a new review-and-confirm cycle instead of silently mutating the sandbox.
- Rename/refinement intent records include previous and new labels where applicable.
- The inspector reflects the latest active proposal or applied sandbox state after each refinement.
- Tests cover pre-confirmation revision, post-confirmation revision, transcript supersession behavior, and inspector state projection.

Added EngineeringHierarchyProposalPart.revision/supersedes/revisionDiff and EngineeringHierarchyProposalStatus.superseded; LingoProposalRevisionDiff.compute() captures added/removed concept and relationship labels. OntologyViewModel+Lingo.recordEngineeringHierarchyProposal supersedes pre-confirmation proposals in place (revision++, marks prior transcript copies as .superseded, records compact diff) and opens a fresh review-and-confirm cycle for post-confirmation follow-ups (status.isPostConfirmation). markEngineeringHierarchyProposal propagates status into the matching transcript copies. ProposeSchemaChangeTool routes through the helper and surfaces revision/supersedes/revision_diff in the tool result. EngineeringHierarchyProposalCard renders revision badge, diff strip, and superseded-by-revision N hint. LingoInspectorSnapshot.proposalRevision exposes the cumulative state. System prompt updated. Tests in LingoTranscriptTests cover pre-confirm supersession, post-confirm fresh cycle, and inspector cumulative state; SchemaEvolutionToolsTests covers tool-level supersession metadata.

title: Confirmed engineering hierarchy applies through chat actions
description: Complete the vertical slice where the user confirms the in-chat Engineering hierarchy proposal and Lingo applies the schema deltas, records intents, refreshes state, and renders results in the transcript.
design:
Implementation approach:
- Wire the schema review widget confirm action to the existing paired-write path: apply_schema_delta plus ChangeIntent records. The action dispatch should be typed Swift code and should not require the LLM to reissue an untrusted arbitrary command after the user presses confirm.
- Support applying the Engineering hierarchy proposal as one or more schema deltas while preserving atomicity expectations from ChangeIntentWriter. If multiple deltas are required, surface progress as an in-chat activity.
- After apply, refresh active sandbox schema from TypeDB and update OntologyViewModel.liveIntrospectedEntities/Relations/Attributes plus intentLog/intentGroups.
- Render an in-chat result widget showing applied changes, new/changed schema elements, and recorded motivations.
- Update the inspector immediately after apply so active sandbox/database, accepted concepts, current schema snapshot, and intent timeline reflect the committed sandbox state.
- Tool-call events should become structured activity/result parts in the transcript for apply_schema_delta and validate_candidate first; generic tools can keep text fallback until the registry/tool-shape abstraction is broader.
- Keep the old text transcript fallback for diagnostics and accessibility.

title: Engineering hierarchy proposal renders in-chat schema review
description: Build the vertical slice where Lingo turns the EngineeringTask hierarchy request into an in-chat schema proposal with gist placement, candidate TypeQL, rationale, and review actions.
design:
Implementation approach:
- Add a domain-shape-first generative UI part for ontology.schemaChangeReview.v1 or a narrower ontology.engineeringHierarchyProposal.v1. The model/tool should produce validated domain payloads, not arbitrary SwiftUI component trees.
- Payload should include proposed concepts, relationships, role names, candidate TypeQL, rationale/motivation, and unresolved assumptions.
- For the supplied dialog, the review should cover at minimum:
  - Umbrella as a grouping/container concept for Top Level Features.
  - Top Level Feature -> Sub Feature -> Task hierarchy semantics.
  - Whether hierarchy is modeled by specialization, composition relations, or parent/child relation patterns, with the selected approach explained.
  - Proposed TypeQL statements and ChangeIntent metadata.
- Render this proposal as an in-chat SwiftUI widget with sections for vocabulary, structure, TypeQL preview, and decisions.
- The widget must expose typed actions such as confirm/apply, revise names, and ask follow-up, routed through Swift actions rather than raw model-generated button handlers.
- Also project the active proposal into the Lingo inspector so the user can inspect current pending decisions without scrolling back through the transcript.
- Reuse CandidateSchemaPresentation and existing TypeQL parser structures where useful, but the candidate schema preview should be inspectable through the inspector and summarized in chat.

title: Engineering hierarchy request starts a generative Lingo turn
description: Replace the first-screen Lingo experience for the EngineeringTask scenario with a chat-first generative turn: the user asks for Umbrella -> Top Level Feature -> Sub Feature -> Task modeling, Lingo responds with in-chat understanding and a bounded sandbox affordance, and cumulative state remains available through the Lingo inspector.
design:
User utterance to support:

"I want to extend the vibe machine ontology such that engineering tasks can exist in a hierarchy. Essentially, I want to model Top Level Feature -> Sub Feature -> Task. And I want to have Umbrellas that are collections of TLFs."

Implementation approach:
- Build this as a walking skeleton before generalizing the widget registry. It is acceptable for this bead to introduce a small Lingo-local enum/struct such as LingoGenerativePart.engineeringHierarchyRequest and render it directly in LingoChatView.
- Refactor the Lingo root for this slice so chat is the primary conversation/action surface. Do not remove cumulative state inspection; the follow-on inspector bead moves state inspection into a native SwiftUI inspector modeled after EuroRack ModulesRootView.
- Extend the transcript model beyond kind/title/message just enough for this concrete request so a Lingo message can contain text parts plus typed Engineering hierarchy UI parts. Keep Swift-native types; do not adopt a web JSON UI protocol directly.
- Add a typed in-chat part for the opening turn carrying the user goal, inferred concepts, unresolved vocabulary, and next actions.
- On this first turn, Lingo should gather canonical context from ontology repo memory if available and live state from TypeDB tools when needed. Treat repo memory as design precedent and TypeDB as current runtime state.
- Render only a bounded in-chat sandbox affordance when none is active: a one-shot create/select action needed to continue the conversation. Do not parallel-implement the full SandboxSelectorView in chat.
- As concrete decisions are made, update shared view-model state so the inspector can reflect active sandbox/database and decided/proposed concepts.

- OneApps/Ontology/Views/Lingo/LingoRootView.swift
- OneApps/Ontology/Views/Lingo/LingoChatView.swift
- OneApps/Ontology/Agent/LingoTranscriptItem.swift

- OneApps/Ontology/Agent/Tools/SandboxTools.swift
- new Lingo-local generative UI model/renderer files under OneApps/Ontology/Views/Lingo/.

- Starting from no active sandbox, the exact Engineering hierarchy utterance appears as a user turn and produces an assistant turn containing a typed in-chat generative UI part, not only plain text.
- The assistant turn shows the inferred modeling goal: Umbrella groups Top Level Features; Top Level Feature contains Sub Features; Sub Feature contains Tasks.
- The assistant turn provides a bounded in-chat create/select sandbox affordance only when needed.

- The workflow keeps cumulative state in view-model state so the inspector can reflect it; chat is not the only inspection surface.
- Add focused tests for transcript part modeling and sandbox widget action behavior using real implementations, not mocks.

title: Configure Claude Code and Codex MCP from Settings
description: Add an end-user Settings experience for Lingo/Ontology MCP setup. A user should be able to open OneApp Settings, discover exactly how to connect Claude Code and Codex to the local MCP server, and preferably let OneApp write the user-scope home-directory configuration for them after explicit confirmation.
design:
Settings UX:
- Add an MCP configuration screen/section under OneApp Settings for the Ontology/Lingo plugin.
- Present two separate setup rows/cards/sections: Claude Code and Codex.
- Each client section shows: detected install/config status, the target config location or command, the configured server name, the stable MCP URL, and current server health.
- Provide a primary action for automatic configuration when safe: Configure Claude Code, Configure Codex.
- Provide fallback actions: copy command, copy config snippet, open containing config folder/file if possible, and refresh status.
- Use clear status states: not configured, configured to this OneApp endpoint, configured to a different endpoint, config file missing, config parse error, app/CLI not found, server offline, port conflict.

Claude Code target:
- Prefer user-scope configuration so the server is available across projects and remains private to the user account.
- Official Claude Code docs describe user-scoped MCP servers as stored in ~/.claude.json and addable via commands such as: claude mcp add --transport http NAME --scope user URL.
- Implementation may use the Claude CLI if available, or carefully merge ~/.claude.json. If editing the file directly, preserve unrelated user settings and existing MCP servers.

Codex target:
- Official OpenAI/Codex docs describe MCP servers under ~/.codex/config.toml, shared by Codex CLI and IDE extension.
- Prefer a user-home config entry like [mcp_servers.oneLingo] with url = "http://127.0.0.1:PORT/mcp".
- Merge TOML structurally. Preserve unrelated config, comments where feasible, profiles, approval settings, and existing MCP servers.

Safety and consent:
- Never silently modify home-directory agent configs on plugin activation or app launch.
- Automatic configuration requires an explicit user action and a preview of the change.
- Create a timestamped backup before writing a home config file.
- Writes must be idempotent: pressing Configure again should update the OneApp server entry only, not duplicate entries or rewrite unrelated config.
- If an existing OneApp/Lingo entry points at a different endpoint, show a reconfigure/update action and explain that Claude/Codex may need reconnect/reload after client config changes.

Stickiness:
- The Settings flow must consume the sticky endpoint from 13.3.
- OneApp restarts should leave Claude Code/Codex config valid. Users may reconnect their MCP client session, but should not need to edit config or restart the tool due to a new port.

Implementation notes:
- Keep client-specific config read/write logic in small services so it can be tested without rendering Settings UI.
- Use structured JSON/TOML parsing rather than string concatenation.
- Add documentation in MCP_INTEGRATION.md for manual setup, matching the Settings snippets.

Suggested tests:
- ClaudeCodeMCPConfigTests: detect missing/configured/different endpoint states; merge ~/.claude.json without dropping unrelated keys; idempotent update; backup created.
- CodexMCPConfigTests: parse/merge ~/.codex/config.toml; preserve unrelated MCP servers/settings; idempotent update; backup created.
- Settings view/view-model tests: surface both clients, endpoint health, and conflict states.
- Manual human verification: use Settings to configure both clients, restart OneApp, then reconnect from Claude Code and Codex without changing config.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] Settings exposes an MCP configuration screen/section for Lingo/Ontology
- [ ] Claude Code and Codex have separate visible setup/status entries
- [ ] Each entry shows configured/unconfigured/different-endpoint/error status against the sticky OneApp MCP URL
- [ ] User can automatically configure Claude Code user-scope MCP after explicit confirmation, or copy exact fallback instructions
- [ ] User can automatically configure Codex user-home MCP after explicit confirmation, or copy exact fallback TOML
- [ ] Home config writes are backed up, idempotent, and preserve unrelated user configuration
- [ ] No home-directory agent config is modified on app launch/plugin activation without a user action
- [ ] OneApp restart leaves the configured Claude Code/Codex URL unchanged and reconnectable
- [ ] Unit tests cover config detection, merge/update, backup, idempotency, and divergent endpoint states
- [ ] MCP_INTEGRATION.md includes manual Claude Code and Codex setup matching the Settings UI
close_reason: Added Lingo MCP Settings UI, Claude Code and Codex config detection/update services with backups and snippets, sticky endpoint status display, documentation, and config merge tests.

title: Quiet TmuxService.hasSession probe failures
description: TmuxService.run() logs every non-zero tmux exit at .error level. hasSession() uses run() to probe whether a session exists on a given socket, then catches the throw and returns false. When SuperviseManager.tmuxSessionConnection probes the current socket and falls back to legacy (the architectural design), each probe miss spams an .error log. Observed at ~6 errors/sec sustained for stale legacy sessions. Fix: thread a 'quietOnFailure' option through run() so hasSession suppresses the error-level log; the throw still propagates so callers behave identically.

title: Record Lingo diagnostic session traces
description: Persist redacted JSONL diagnostic traces for Lingo sessions under ~/.config/one/sessions/lingo so failed assistant/tool interactions can be inspected after the fact without relying on os.Logger replay data.
design: Add a lightweight session recorder used by OntologyAgentService. It writes JSONL events only for diagnostics: session start/end metadata, user turns, agent events, tool lifecycle, errors, provider/model metadata, and TypeDB context. Redact secrets and truncate large strings/results. Do not log API keys or attempt replay completeness.
acceptance_criteria:
- Lingo creates a per-session JSONL file under ~/.config/one/sessions/lingo/YYYY-MM-DD/
- Events include provider/model, user turns, tool calls/results, completion/error, and TypeDB context

title: Migrate Producer assistant configuration to GammaAgent provider settings
description: Producer has its own Assistant settings section, provider/model JSON file, Keychain service, and runtime env injection. After GammaAgent ProviderResolver and OneApp Assistant settings exist, Producer should not ask for duplicate provider/model/API key configuration. It should consume the shared assistant selection/key path and inject the correct provider-specific endpoint/model/key environment into the Producer server.
design: Audit ProducerSettingsView, ProducerSettings.swift, ProducerPlugin.moduleEnvironment, and Web/producer server env reads. Remove or replace the Producer-specific assistant section once Producer can use GammaAgent AssistantConfigStore/ProviderKeyStore/ProviderResolver. Align injected env vars with the server's actual model selection path: today Web/producer reads ZAI_BASE_URL, ZAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, and AI_MODEL while ProducerPlugin only injects AI_API_KEY. Decide whether Producer server should be taught a provider-neutral env contract or whether ProducerPlugin maps ResolvedProvider to the existing env names. Endpoint URLs must come from ProviderPreset/defaults or explicit advanced override, not manual Producer settings.
acceptance_criteria:
- Producer settings no longer has a duplicate Assistant provider/model/API key section once shared GammaAgent config is wired
- Producer runtime uses shared GammaAgent assistant selection and per-provider keys
- ProducerPlugin injects env vars that Web/producer actually consumes, including model and endpoint/base URL as needed
- Manual Web/producer npm run dev mode can consume the same provider/model/key configuration or has a documented, low-friction bridge to it
- TypeDB endpoint resolution remains lane-aware for dev/sandbox/etc. (for example gamma-typedb.dev.eurorack.internal vs gamma-typedb.sandbox.eurorack.internal)
- OneApp/EuroRack publishes or otherwise exposes an active-lane manifest so an independently-run Producer dev server can discover the right lane/TypeDB endpoint; explicit --lane and TYPEDB_HTTP_URL overrides still win
- Users are not asked to manually supply provider API endpoints in Producer settings
- Misconfiguration errors are translated into actionable user-facing diagnostics for missing key, expired/incorrect key, wrong provider auth shape, unknown model, unreachable AI endpoint, wrong/unreachable TypeDB lane endpoint, and no active lane manifest
- Existing Producer assistant/chat/status paths work with the shared configuration
- Follow-up tests cover env mapping for ZAI/OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic paths, TypeDB lane endpoint mapping, active-lane manifest discovery/override precedence, plus diagnostic mapping for common provider/auth/endpoint failures
notes:
Additional context from user: Producer must support both EuroRack-managed runtime and manual dev-mode server runs from Web/producer via npm run dev, where the user opens http://localhost:4200/assistant and the server reports Next 4200, Express API 4101, Hocuspocus 4100, and TypeDB at gamma-typedb.dev.eurorack.internal:8000/v1. Provider config must work in both modes. Current misconfiguration errors can surface as vague messages like 'Error: token expired or incorrect'; this bead should improve validation and diagnostics so end users get actionable guidance for missing/wrong/expired API keys, wrong provider, wrong model, or unreachable endpoint.
Additional TypeDB lane context: Producer cannot assume one fixed TypeDB host. The database endpoint depends on how OneApp/Producer is launched and which EuroRack lane is active. Known examples include gamma-typedb.sandbox.eurorack.internal and gamma-typedb.dev.eurorack.internal. The migration must preserve lane-aware endpoint resolution for both EuroRack-managed Producer and manual Web/producer dev mode, and diagnostics should clearly show which TypeDB endpoint is being used when assistant/status calls fail.
Design clarification: manual Producer dev mode needs a discoverable lane/runtime source. Today Web/producer/src/server/dev.ts supports --sandbox and --lane <name>, sets ONE_EURORACK_LANE, and resolveTypeDBBaseUrl() maps that to gamma-typedb.<lane>.eurorack.internal. OneApp launch --sandbox sets ONE_TMUX_NAMESPACE=sandbox, and EuroRackBuiltinNetwork.currentIdentity() uses ONE_EURORACK_LANE, then ONE_TMUX_NAMESPACE, then build channel, then dev. Missing piece: when OneApp starts, it should publish/discoverably expose its active EuroRack lane/network/runtime endpoints so a separately-run Web/producer dev server can pick the correct lane/TypeDB endpoint without manual guesswork. Candidate design: write a small lane manifest under Application Support/OneApp or app group container with active lane identifier, dnsDomain, TypeDB HTTP URL, Producer API URL, and timestamp/process identity. Producer dev server can read it by default, with --lane / TYPEDB_HTTP_URL explicit overrides still taking precedence.
Design refinement: active runtime discovery should be a multi-instance registry, not a single mutable 'current lane' file. Multiple OneApp instances may run at once (for example dev and sandbox), so each instance should publish an entry keyed by stable instance identity/lane/process and remove or mark stale on shutdown. Store this registry under the user's OneApp config directory, preferably ~/.config/one/, rather than only Application Support. Use atomic writes/locking or per-instance files plus an index to avoid concurrent writer corruption. Producer must be able to switch TypeDB targets at runtime, not only at process startup: the web backend should expose/read selectable runtime entries and reconnect/reconfigure TypeDB/Hocuspocus/assistant state as needed. Explicit env/CLI overrides still win for scripted runs, but the default dev UX should discover available OneApp runtimes and let the user choose.
close_reason: Producer duplicate assistant settings removed; Producer now consumes shared GammaAgent assistant config/keychain env, publishes runtime registry entries under ~/.config/one, and web Producer can discover/select runtime TypeDB endpoints.

title: NormalizedSchema: fail loudly on unparseable statements
description: NormalizedSchema.canonicalize currently uses compactMap to drop any statement its regex cannot parse. The regex handles 'entity|relation|attribute' with simple identifiers and the common clauses; anything else (struct declarations, functions, annotation-carrying top-level declarations, future TypeQL grammar) is silently discarded on both sides of the comparison. That means NormalizedSchema.equal can return true for schemas that actually differ outside its grammar.
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/OntologyTests/Support/NormalizedSchemaEquals.swift

Change normalizeStatement to a throwing API that returns a Statement or throws UnparseableStatement(text:). Update canonicalize to collect parseable statements AND a list of unparseable originals. equal(lhs, rhs) becomes throws and returns Bool: if either side has unparseable statements, throw UnparseableStatementError with both offending texts so the failure message pinpoints the grammar gap. Callers in SandboxManagerTests.swift use 'try #expect(try NormalizedSchema.equal(...))' or equivalent; tests fail with a message naming the unparseable line instead of silently returning true.

Optionally: widen the regex to cover 'struct' and '@annotation' prefixes before the main identifier. Not required — the point of this bead is detection, not coverage. Future grammar changes should be explicit follow-up.
acceptance_criteria:

title: Implement normalizedSchemaEquals test helper for TypeQL schema comparisons
description: A shared test helper that compares two TypeDB typeSchema() outputs for semantic equality — ignoring whitespace variance, line ordering, and owns-clause ordering. Every test under one-2xg.1 through one-2xg.7 that currently asserts raw typeSchema() string equality switches to use it. Stops the tests from being flaky on reformatting that doesn't change semantics.
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/OntologyTests/Support/NormalizedSchemaEquals.swift (or Support/ subfolder alongside the existing LiveTypeDBFixture).

Public API:
  public enum NormalizedSchema {
    public static func equal(_ lhs: String, _ rhs: String) -> Bool
    public static func canonicalize(_ schema: String) -> String
  }

canonicalize algorithm:
  1. Split the typeSchema string into logical "declaration blocks." A block is one top-level declaration — entity X …, relation Y …, attribute Z …, etc. — possibly spanning multiple lines. TypeDB's typeSchema output is close to this shape already; blocks typically end at a semicolon at line start or at a blank line.
  2. Within each entity / relation block, collect the `owns` clauses into a set, then re-emit them in sorted order by attribute name.
  3. Within each relation block, collect `relates` clauses into a set, sorted by role name.
  4. Trim trailing whitespace from every line; collapse runs of blank lines to a single blank line; ensure trailing newline.
  5. Sort blocks alphabetically by the declaration's primary name (entity name, relation name, attribute name).
  6. Return the concatenated result.

Equality:
  NormalizedSchema.equal(a, b) == (canonicalize(a) == canonicalize(b))

Edge cases to handle explicitly:
  - Block comments in the input (if TypeDB emits any) — strip them in canonicalize.
  - Cardinality annotations (@card(...)) — preserve verbatim on their owns clauses; their ordering is implicit in the attribute-name sort.
  - Sub clauses (entity X sub Y) — preserve verbatim; don't reorder the `sub` relationship.
  - Plays clauses on entities — sort alphabetically within the entity.

Tests:
  Location: OneApps/Ontology/OntologyTests/Support/NormalizedSchemaEqualsTests.swift
  - testIdenticalSchemasAreEqual
  - testWhitespaceDifferencesAreIgnored
  - testOwnsOrderDifferenceIgnored — "owns a, owns b;" vs "owns b, owns a;" equal
  - testDifferentAttributeNamesNotEqual
  - testCardinalityDifferenceNotEqual
  - testSubClauseDifferenceNotEqual

Adoption:
  After landing, grep for typeSchema equality asserts and switch them:
    rg "typeSchema\(\)" OneApps/Ontology/OntologyTests/ -l
  Update each assertion to use NormalizedSchema.equal instead of raw string equality. Tasks affected: one-2xg.1.1, one-2xg.2.3, one-2xg.2.4, one-2xg.2.5, one-2xg.5.x (where diff tests compare schemas).

This task is purely the helper + its tests. Adopting it across existing test files is implicit in each affected test task's acceptance.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] NormalizedSchema type exists in OneApps/Ontology/OntologyTests/Support/NormalizedSchemaEquals.swift
- [ ] canonicalize(_:) returns a stable, order-normalized representation of a typeSchema string
- [ ] equal(_:_:) is symmetric (equal(a, b) == equal(b, a)) and reflexive (equal(a, a) == true)
- [ ] Six unit tests above all pass
- [ ] Test helpers are a sibling to existing LiveTypeDBFixture — documented in a brief comment so future test authors can find it
- [ ] Grep output documented: list of files currently using raw typeSchema() equality that will adopt this helper as each is touched
notes: On closing 2.1: left SandboxManagerTests.testCreateFromKnownSource using raw '==' on typeSchema() strings, per acceptance. When 2.7 lands and canonicalize(_:) exists, adopt it here too — the sandbox comes from the same driver so schemas should already be byte-equal in practice, but normalized equality is the safer long-term invariant.
close_reason:
Implemented NormalizedSchema helper at OneApps/Ontology/OntologyTests/Support/NormalizedSchemaEquals.swift. canonicalize(_:) strips # line comments and /* */ block comments, splits on top-level ';' (respecting paren depth for @card(...)), and reparses each entity/relation/attribute declaration into (kind, name, sub, clauses). Clauses inside each declaration are whitespace-collapsed and sorted; declarations themselves are sorted by kind+name. sub parents and cardinality annotations are preserved verbatim — they're semantic differences, not reformats. equal(_:_:) just compares canonicalized forms; symmetric and reflexive by construction.

Tests at Support/NormalizedSchemaEqualsTests.swift (9 tests, all pass in <1ms):
- testIdenticalSchemasAreEqual
- testWhitespaceDifferencesAreIgnored
- testOwnsOrderDifferenceIgnored
- testDifferentAttributeNamesNotEqual
- testCardinalityDifferenceNotEqual
- testSubClauseDifferenceNotEqual
- testEqualIsSymmetricAndReflexive
- testDeclarationOrderingIsIgnored
- testLineCommentsAreStripped

Adoption: raw '==' on typeSchema strings was present in three spots at close time:

- TypeDBDriverTests.swift:315 (delete-isolation test) — switched to NormalizedSchema.equal

All still green after swap. Future tests in one-2xg.2.3/2.4/2.5/5.x should use NormalizedSchema.equal from day one.

title: Human verify: 'ontology new' from a fresh terminal completes cleanly

Verification procedure:
1. Open a fresh terminal with `ontology` installed via Homebrew.
2. cd to a temp directory.
3. Run the simplest form:
     ontology new test-ontology-1
   Observe the output. Confirm:

   - `ontology validate --repo ./test-ontology-1` exits 0
4. Run with flags:
     ontology new test-ontology-2 --domain "Just a test" --first-version 1.0.0 --no-git

   - `ontology validate` passes
5. (Optional, if you have a test GitHub account) Test --remote:
     Create an empty repo on GitHub: test-ontology-3

   Confirm:
   - Local scaffold exists

6. Run `ontology new --help`. Confirm examples are clear and flags are well-described.

title: Human verify: create two new ontologies end-to-end via Lingo
description: A human creates two brand-new ontologies through Lingo conversation — one private, one public — and confirms the repos exist on GitHub with v0.1.0 tagged. Then they add a first concept to one of them and codify v0.2.0. The full new-ontology-into-evolution flow works.
design:
Verification procedure:

Part A: Create ontology 1 (private, empty start)
  1. Launch OneApp. Sign in to GitHub if not already.
  2. In Lingo chat: "I want to start a new ontology for acoustics testing."
  3. Agent asks: name (accept "ontology-acoustics"), domain (paste something like "Acoustic testing schemas for audio hardware"), GitHub org (your username or a test org), visibility (private).
  4. Agent summarizes, user confirms.
  5. Observe:
     - Local scaffolding in ~/SoftwareProjects/.../ontology-acoustics/ (file system check)
     - GitHub: new private repo exists with first commit + v0.1.0 tag (browser check)
     - Chat transitions: "<name> is ready. Shall we add your first concept?"

Part B: Create ontology 2 (public, with first concept)

  2. Say yes to "add your first concept": "Let's add a concept for Microphone."
  3. Agent walks the gist placement (Category vs Specification), applies to sandbox, surfaces diff.
  4. User says "codify". Agent proposes minor bump (v0.2.0).
  5. Walk through F22 (push + PR) and F23 (merge + refresh).
  6. Verify: v0.2.0 exists on the new ontology repo; concept queryable in the new ontology's knowledge.

Part C: Spot-check validation

  - For the one that has v0.2.0: run `ontology diff --repo <path> --from v0.1.0 --to v0.2.0`: shows the first-concept migration.

If anything's off (repo not created, visibility wrong, tag missing, transition awkward, `ontology validate` fails), file follow-ups.

title: Handoff from new ontology to first-concept exploration
description: After scaffolding + repo creation + first push + tag, the agent smoothly transitions into "let's add your first concept" — picking up the exact same conversational pattern Lingo uses for evolving an existing ontology. The user doesn't notice a seam.
design:
Post-scaffold flow:
  1. New-ontology tool returns successfully with the scaffolded path + github URL + first version.
  2. Agent says: "<ontology name> is ready at <path>. I've created its first release (v0.1.0) with an empty schema. Shall we add your first concept?"
  3. If user says yes (or describes a concept): agent creates a sandbox from the new ontology's knowledge (which is currently empty), and drives the same evolution flow as any enhancement.
  4. From this point, the experience is identical to enhancing an existing ontology — everything in F1-F15 just works because the new ontology is now a regular ontology.

Implementation:
  - After new_ontology succeeds, set the new ontology as the "active target" in the OntologyViewModel (by registering it with the plugin's knowledge-DB manager, even if empty)
  - First sandbox creation: SandboxManager.create(from: "<new-name>-knowledge")  — bootstraps from the empty schema
  - ChangeIntentWriter, SchemaDiff, all subsequent tools work as usual

The agent's system prompt has the handoff language baked in (previous task).

Test: full new-ontology-then-evolve flow in a manual scenario.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] After successful scaffold + push + tag, agent proposes adding the first concept
- [ ] User acceptance creates a sandbox from the new ontology's knowledge
- [ ] Evolution flow (F1-F15) works seamlessly against the new ontology
- [ ] No code duplication: new ontology and enhancement flows share all downstream tools
- [ ] Manual scenario: create new ontology + add first concept + codify v0.2.0 works end-to-end

title: Add 'new ontology' entry to Lingo chat via agent tool
description: After this lands, the user can say "let's start a new ontology for X" in Lingo and the agent recognizes it as a new-ontology intent, walks the conversation through the required info, and invokes scaffolding when ready.
design:
Agent system-prompt extension:
  "When the user expresses intent to start a new ontology (phrases like 'create a new ontology', 'start fresh', 'I want a new ontology for X'):
   1. Acknowledge and gather:
      - Domain or purpose ('What's this ontology for?')
      - Name ('What should it be called?' — suggest a name based on the domain)
      - GitHub target ('Do you have an empty repo, or should I create one under <your org>?')
   2. Once all info is gathered, summarize and ask for confirmation.
   3. On confirm: invoke new_ontology tool with the gathered params.
   4. After scaffold, seamlessly transition into evolution mode: 'Your new ontology is ready. Let's add your first concept.'"

Tool:
  name: "new_ontology"
  description: "Scaffold a new ontology at a target location and optionally create its GitHub repo. Call after gathering name, domain, and GitHub target from the user."
  input: {
    "name": String,
    "domain": String?,
    "destination_path": String,   // e.g., "~/SoftwareProjects/collection-vibe-machine/ontology-acoustics"
    "github_org": String?,        // if null, don't create remote
    "github_repo": String?        // if provided, point at existing empty repo
  }
  output: {
    "scaffolded_path": String,
    "github_url": String?,
    "first_version": String       // "0.1.0"
  }
  implementation: calls OntologyCore.scaffold + OneApps/Ontology/NewOntology/RemoteCreator.swift for the GitHub part (next task)

Tests: manual chat scenario — walk the new-ontology conversation end-to-end.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] System prompt updated with the new-ontology conversation pattern
- [ ] new_ontology tool registered with LingoAgent
- [ ] Agent gathers domain, name, GitHub target conversationally
- [ ] Summarizes and confirms before scaffolding
- [ ] Transitions to evolution mode after scaffold
- [ ] Tool output structure documented and stable

title: Implement scaffolding function in ontology-core (from ontology-template)
description: After this lands, ontology-core exposes a scaffolding function that creates a valid, empty ontology at a target path — matching the ontology-template layout. Both the CLI's `ontology new` and Lingo's GUI flow call into this.
design:
Location: rust/ontology-core/src/scaffolding.rs

Public Rust API:
  pub struct ScaffoldOptions {
    pub name: String,
    pub domain: Option<String>,
    pub destination: PathBuf,
    pub first_version: Version,  // default v0.1.0
  }

  pub fn scaffold(options: ScaffoldOptions) -> Result<ScaffoldReport, ScaffoldError>

  pub struct ScaffoldReport {
    pub root: PathBuf,
    pub manifest: PathBuf,
    pub schema: PathBuf,
    pub migrations_root: PathBuf,
  }

Algorithm:
  1. Reference: collection-vibe-machine/ontology-template/ for the canonical layout.
  2. Write a package manifest (package.json) with:
     - name
     - version: first_version
     - domain (description)
     - required scripts (refresh:package-contract, validate:bootstrap, test:typedb-bootstrap — per the ontology-tooling contract, even though we're moving to Rust, preserve the contract)
  3. Write schema/<name>.tql — an empty schema root file with a placeholder comment.
  4. Write migrations/ directory with an initial triple for v0.0.0 → v0.1.0:
     - preflight/<file>.tql — sanity check that no existing data conflicts
     - v0.0.0-to-<first_version>.tql — the migration (initially empty since there's nothing to define yet; user adds via Lingo later)
     - verify/<file>.tql — post-apply assertions
  5. Write README.md with name + domain description.
  6. Write .gitignore (standard template).
  7. Return ScaffoldReport.

Post-scaffold: scaffolded directory must pass `ontology validate`. Add a test asserting this.

Tests:
  - Happy path: scaffold to a temp dir; assert structure + validate passes
  - Name-collision path: destination exists → ScaffoldError.destinationExists
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] rust/ontology-core/src/scaffolding.rs exists with scaffold(options) function
- [ ] Reference: ontology-template layout is the source of truth
- [ ] Scaffolded output passes ontology-core's validate_package
- [ ] Structure includes: manifest, schema/<name>.tql, migrations/{preflight,v*.tql,verify}, README.md, .gitignore
- [ ] Destination-exists case throws ScaffoldError.destinationExists
- [ ] Tests: happy path (scaffold + validate) and destination-exists failure

title: Expose scaffolding via FFI for OneApp
description: After this lands, Swift can call OntologyCore.scaffold to create a new ontology on disk — used by F26's GUI flow and (via its own path) F27's CLI.

title: Handle semver edge cases: empty diff, new ontology's first version, mixed-scope
description: After this lands, the semver flow behaves correctly at boundary conditions: refusing to codify nothing, auto-classifying a new ontology's first version, and clearly explaining mixed-scope scenarios so users can confirm with their eyes open.
design:
Edge cases:

1. Empty diff:
   - classify_semver returns None/nil
   - Agent says: "Nothing has changed in this sandbox compared to its base. Add or modify a concept before codifying."
   - Codify action refuses to proceed

2. First version of a new ontology (F26 flow):
   - Sandbox doesn't have a base version (or base is 0.0.0 sentinel)
   - classify_semver is skipped; bump auto-set to initial (v0.1.0)
   - Agent announces: "This is a new ontology — first version will be 0.1.0."

3. Mixed-scope (e.g., 3 adds + 1 remove):
   - Classification is major (remove wins)
   - Rationale explicitly lists the major-triggering item: "Major: removed attribute 'X' (other additions would have been minor)."
   - Agent surfaces the additions and removals as a structured summary so the user understands what they're about to do

4. Rename without an existing consumer:
   - If the renamed item is newly introduced in this same sandbox exploration, it's not breaking (nothing downstream uses it yet)
   - Heuristic: only count renames as major if the renamed-from label existed in the base version
   - Unit test for this case

Implementation: this task extends F24.1's classifier with these edge-case rules, and extends F24.3's agent integration to surface them correctly in chat.

Tests:
  - Empty-diff case
  - First-version (new-ontology) case
  - Mixed-scope case
  - Rename-of-new-item-not-major case
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] Empty diff: agent refuses to codify with a helpful message
- [ ] First version of a new ontology: auto-classifies to v0.1.0 without asking
- [ ] Mixed-scope: rationale explicitly lists the major-triggering item
- [ ] Rename-of-new-item (not pre-existing in base) does not trigger major
- [ ] Unit tests cover each edge case
- [ ] Integration tested via chat scenarios (manual or scripted)

title: Human verify: semver classifier suggests the right bump across realistic scenarios
description: A human walks 5+ different explorations through codify and confirms the agent's semver proposal matches their own judgment — the heuristic is good enough to trust as a default.
design:
Verification procedure:

Walk at least five scenarios through Lingo:

1. Add one new entity → expect minor proposal.
2. Add an entity + a relation + a couple of attributes → expect minor (bigger but still additive).
3. Add one new doc annotation to an existing concept → expect patch.
4. Rename an attribute used in the base schema → expect major (with rationale explicitly mentioning the rename).
5. Add an entity + remove an attribute that was in the base → expect major, with rationale highlighting the removal.

For each scenario:
  - Drive the exploration via Lingo chat
  - When triggering codify, observe the agent's proposal
  - Judge: does the proposal match your intuition?
  - If no: is the heuristic wrong, or is your intuition non-standard? Document the disagreement.
  - Confirm or override; walk it to completion if you want, or abort

Sixth scenario (optional): empty diff — start a sandbox, immediately try to codify without changes. Agent should refuse.

Seventh scenario (optional): first version of a new ontology via F26. Classification should auto to 0.1.0.

If any scenario's proposal is off, file a specific case against F24.1 (the heuristic) or F24.3 (the surfacing) with a minimal repro.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] At least 5 realistic scenarios walked through; each classification matches human judgment or the disagreement is documented
- [ ] Empty-diff case refuses to codify with the expected message
- [ ] First-version case auto-classifies without prompting
- [ ] Rationale text reads naturally in chat — no jargon, no machine-generated-looking phrases
- [ ] Any heuristic disagreements filed as follow-ups with specific repro
- [ ] Bead closed only after all scenarios verified

title: Teach the Lingo agent to propose a semver bump during codify
description: After this lands, when the user says "make this real," the agent calls classifySemver, surfaces the suggested bump with rationale, and asks the user to confirm or override. The chosen bump drives F21's manifest version.
design:
Extension to the LingoAgent's system prompt:
  "When the user confirms an exploration is ready to codify:
   1. Invoke classify_semver tool.
   2. Surface the classification and rationale in chat: 'I think this is a {bump} release because {rationale}.'
   3. Ask: 'Does that look right? [Yes / No, use <other> / Cancel]'
   4. On user override, capture the chosen bump.
   5. Pass the chosen bump into codify's version-bump step."

Tool:
  name: "classify_semver"
  description: "Classify the active sandbox's accumulated changes as patch / minor / major. Returns the recommended bump with rationale. Call before asking the user to confirm codify."
  input: {}
  output: { "bump": String, "rationale": String, "triggers": [...] }
  implementation: wraps OntologyCore.classifySemver

Edge cases:
  - Empty diff: classify_semver returns null; agent tells user "There's nothing to codify yet — keep exploring."
  - Major bump: agent emphasizes the breaking nature, mentions downstream consumers, suggests the user confirm consciously

This task depends on F24.1 (classifier) + F24.2 (FFI). Integration happens here.

Test: manual chat scenario — add one entity, ask to codify, confirm agent proposes "minor" with the right rationale.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] classify_semver tool registered with LingoAgent
- [ ] System prompt teaches the agent to call it before each codify
- [ ] Agent surfaces bump + rationale in chat
- [ ] User can confirm or override via chat ("use patch", "use major")
- [ ] Chosen bump flows into F21's codify flow
- [ ] Empty-diff case surfaces "nothing to codify" message
- [ ] Major-bump case emphasizes the breaking nature

title: Implement semver classifier in ontology-core Rust crate
description: After this lands, ontology-core exposes a pure function that classifies a SchemaDiff as patch / minor / major along with a human-readable rationale. The same logic is used by the CLI (`ontology dry-run --bump auto`) and the Lingo agent (during codify).
design:
Location: rust/ontology-core/src/semver_classifier.rs

Public API:
  pub fn classify(diff: &SchemaDiff) -> SemverClassification

  pub struct SemverClassification {
    pub bump: BumpKind,
    pub rationale: String,
    pub triggers: Vec<BumpTrigger>,  // which specific changes drove the decision
  }

  pub struct BumpTrigger {
    pub kind: TriggerKind,  // AddedEntity, RemovedEntity, Rename, etc.
    pub label: String,      // the entity/attr/relation label
    pub level: BumpKind,    // what bump level this trigger alone implies
  }

Heuristic:
  - removedEntities / removedRelations / removedAttributes non-empty → major
  - renames (detected via intent log, passed as a parallel input — see note) → major (breaking for consumers)
  - cardinality tightening (e.g., @card(0..1) → @card(1..1)) → major
  - cardinality loosening → minor
  - addedEntities / addedRelations / addedAttributes / addedOwnsClauses → minor
  - only annotate-doc entries in intents → patch

Rationale:
  - One-sentence summary of the strongest trigger
  - Examples:
    * "Patch: only documentation annotations were added."
    * "Minor: 2 new entities and 1 new relation."
    * "Major: removed attribute 'projectName' from Project — consumers depending on it will break."

Note on renames: rename-detection requires the intent log, not just the diff. Extend the signature to accept intents too:
  pub fn classify(diff: &SchemaDiff, intents: &[ChangeIntentRecord]) -> SemverClassification

Mixed-scope: the strongest trigger wins (major > minor > patch).

Tests:
  - Pure-add scenario → minor
  - Rename scenario → major, rationale mentions rename specifically
  - Only-annotations scenario → patch
  - Mixed adds+removes → major, rationale highlights the major-triggering removal
  - Empty diff → no classification (return Option::None); callers handle as "nothing to codify"
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] rust/ontology-core/src/semver_classifier.rs exists
- [ ] classify(diff, intents) returns SemverClassification with bump, rationale, triggers
- [ ] Heuristic: removals/renames/cardinality-tightening → major; adds/cardinality-loosening → minor; annotate-doc only → patch
- [ ] Strongest trigger wins in mixed-scope cases
- [ ] Empty diff returns None (or Option::None) so callers handle as "nothing to codify"
- [ ] Unit tests: pure-add, rename, annotation-only, mixed, empty

title: Expose semver classifier via FFI to Swift
description: After this lands, OntologyCore.classifySemver is callable from Swift, returning a structured classification that Lingo's agent and UI can use.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] OntologyCore.classifySemver exposed in OntologyCoreFFI
- [ ] Swift types (SemverClassification, BumpKind, BumpTrigger) mirror Rust
- [ ] Returns nil for empty-diff case
- [ ] Swift-side tests mirror Rust tests (same scenarios)

title: Archive the sandbox with a pointer to the merged PR and tag
description: After the merge + refresh completes, the sandbox used for the exploration is archived — dropped from the active list but retained as metadata linked to the merged PR and release tag. Users can still find their history; the active-sandboxes view stays clean.
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Sandbox/SandboxArchiver.swift

Public API:
  public final class SandboxArchiver {
    public init(manager: SandboxManager)
    public func archive(
      sandbox: SandboxHandle,
      mergedPR: URL,
      releaseTag: URL,
      version: Version
    ) async throws -> ArchivedSandbox
  }

  public struct ArchivedSandbox {
    public let name: String          // was knowledge-sandbox-<uuid>
    public let archivedAt: Date
    public let mergedPR: URL
    public let releaseTag: URL
    public let version: Version
  }

Behavior:
  - Write an archive record in a known location: ~/Library/Application Support/OneApp/lingo/archives.jsonl (append-only)
  - Drop the live sandbox TypeDB database via SandboxManager.drop (the intent log is preserved in the archive record; the live DB isn't useful after merge)
  - Alternative (optional, future): retain the DB for offline reference but mark it "archived" — for v1, drop is fine since archives.jsonl has the intent log snapshot

Archive record structure:
  {
    "name": "knowledge-sandbox-abc123",
    "archivedAt": "2026-04-20T15:30:00Z",
    "mergedPR": "https://github.com/.../pull/42",
    "releaseTag": "https://github.com/.../releases/tag/v1.3.6",
    "version": "1.3.6",
    "sandboxName": "knowledge-sandbox-abc123",
    "intentLogSnapshot": [ ... ]  // all intents at time of archive
  }

UI implications (for F15's SandboxSelectorView, not this task):
  - Archived sandboxes don't appear in the active list
  - A "history" view (future) shows archived sandboxes with their PR/tag links

Tests: unit test for archive-record writing + sandbox drop; integration test for full archive flow.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] SandboxArchiver.swift exists
- [ ] archive(...) writes a record to ~/Library/Application Support/OneApp/lingo/archives.jsonl
- [ ] Archive record includes: name, archivedAt, mergedPR, releaseTag, version, intent log snapshot
- [ ] Live sandbox DB dropped via SandboxManager after archive record is written
- [ ] archives.jsonl is append-only (no rewrites; tolerant of concurrent writes if ever relevant)
- [ ] Tests cover archive + drop; archive record JSON shape validated

title: Human verify: full merge → tag → refresh → query flow in a real session
description: A human completes a full Lingo session end-to-end: explore, codify, push, CI green, merge, tag, refresh, then queries the new concept against their real knowledge database from the app. This is the proof that the whole pipeline delivers.
design:
Verification procedure:
1. Prerequisite: completed F22's verification (PR exists, CI green). Sign-in active. Real ontology-vibemachine checked out.
2. In Lingo chat: "merge it".
3. Confirm merge prompt; agent asks for strategy if settings allows or confirms default. User confirms.
4. Observe chat:
   - "Merging PR #N..." → "Merged."
   - "Tagging release v1.3.6..." → "Tagged."
   - "Refreshing your knowledge with ontology-vibemachine 1.3.6..." (progress updates)
   - "Your knowledge now has <new concept names>. Try asking about them."
5. Verify via GitHub browser:
   - PR shows Merged state
   - New tag v1.3.6 (or whatever) exists on the repo
6. Verify via TypeDB console:
   - Connect to gamma-typedb, open knowledge DB
   - Query: match $x type <NewConcept>; fetch $x;  → concept exists
7. Verify sandbox archived:
   - In Lingo's sandbox selector, the sandbox no longer appears (or shows "archived" status)
   - ~/Library/Application Support/OneApp/lingo/archives.jsonl has a record for it
8. Back in Lingo chat, start a new conversation: "Create an instance of <NewConcept>." Agent should now be able to use the concept (it exists in knowledge).

If any step fails (merge fails, refresh hangs, concept not in knowledge, sandbox not archived), file specific follow-ups. This is the load-bearing verification — it's how a user experiences Lingo end-to-end.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] Merge triggered from chat; completed successfully
- [ ] Release tag pushed to origin; visible on GitHub
- [ ] Local knowledge refreshed to the new version
- [ ] New concept is queryable in the knowledge DB via TypeDB console
- [ ] Sandbox archived; no longer in active list; archive record present in archives.jsonl
- [ ] Agent can use the new concept in a subsequent conversation (it's in real knowledge)
- [ ] Full flow completed entirely from inside OneApp — no terminal, no browser, no git commands
- [ ] Bead closed only after all above confirmed

title: Trigger local knowledge re-bootstrap to the new version
description: After tag push, Lingo triggers the existing local knowledge-DB re-bootstrap path — pulling the new package version into the user's running TypeDB. The newly-minted concept is immediately queryable against real data.
design:
The Ontology plugin already has code to upgrade the local knowledge database (per the user's note: "we already have code for that"). This task wires Lingo's codify flow to invoke it.

Location: OneApps/Ontology/Codify/KnowledgeRefresher.swift

Public API:
  public final class KnowledgeRefresher {
    public init(plugin: OntologyPlugin)  // or similar host reference
    public func refresh(toVersion version: Version, ofPackage packageName: String) async throws -> RefreshReport
  }

  public struct RefreshReport {
    public let fromVersion: Version
    public let toVersion: Version
    public let migratedRecords: Int
  }

Algorithm:
  1. Delegate to the plugin's existing knowledge-DB upgrade code path.
  2. Surface progress in chat: "Refreshing your knowledge with ontology-vibemachine 1.3.6... 42% complete."
  3. Return a summary on completion.

Progress reporting:
  - The existing upgrade code should expose a progress callback or async sequence
  - Lingo surfaces milestones in chat (not every tick)
  - On completion: chat confirms "Your knowledge now has <new concept names>. Try asking about them."

Error handling:
  - Refresh failure: surface full error; agent offers to retry. The user is not blocked — they can keep using the old version until the refresh completes successfully.

Tests: integration test against the existing knowledge-upgrade path with a fixture ontology.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] KnowledgeRefresher.swift exists
- [ ] refresh(...) delegates to the existing Ontology plugin upgrade path
- [ ] Progress surfaced in chat as milestones (not tick-by-tick)
- [ ] Completion message references the new concepts added
- [ ] Refresh failures surface clearly; agent offers retry; user not blocked
- [ ] Integration test against the existing upgrade code path

title: Tag the release after merge via ontology-core
description: After merge, Lingo invokes OntologyCore's release function against the target repo to create the version tag (per the existing ontology-* release convention). The tag is pushed to origin automatically.
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Codify/ReleaseTagger.swift

Public API:
  public final class ReleaseTagger {
    public func tagAndPush(repo: URL, version: Version, tokenStore: GitHubTokenStore) async throws -> ReleaseTag
  }

  public struct ReleaseTag {
    public let version: Version
    public let sha: String
    public let url: URL  // GitHub release or tag URL
  }

Algorithm:
  1. Pull main locally: git fetch origin main && git checkout main && git reset --hard origin/main
  2. Confirm HEAD matches the merged PR's sha (safety check)
  3. Invoke OntologyCore.releaseTag(at: repo, version: version) — wraps the Rust release function in dry_run=false, push=true mode
  4. The Rust release function: validates, creates tag, pushes tag (uses Swift-side git credentials from the token store)
  5. Return ReleaseTag

Error handling:
  - Main doesn't match expected SHA (someone else pushed mid-flight): surface in chat; offer to retry after local update
  - Tag already exists: unusual but possible; treat as success if it matches the expected version; error otherwise
  - Push failure: retry with backoff; re-auth on 401

This task requires OntologyCore.releaseTag to exist, which wraps F16's port of package-release.mjs. If that wrapping isn't yet in OntologyCoreFFI (F19), add it as part of this task.

Tests: integration test against a test repo; unit test for edge cases.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] ReleaseTagger.swift exists
- [ ] tagAndPush creates the version tag on main after merge
- [ ] Tag push uses the stored GitHub token
- [ ] Main-SHA drift between merge and tag is detected and handled
- [ ] Tag-already-exists path handled (success if matching, error if not)
- [ ] OntologyCore.releaseTag exposed via FFI (added if not already present in F19)
- [ ] Integration test exists (gated on token)

title: Merge the PR via GitHub API with configurable strategy
description: After this lands, once CI is green and the user confirms, Lingo merges the PR using the user's preferred strategy (squash, merge, rebase — stored in GammaAgent settings). Chat acknowledges the merge result.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] PullRequestMerger.swift exists
- [ ] merge(...) calls GitHub's merge endpoint with the chosen strategy
- [ ] Strategy sourced from GammaAgent settings (default: squash)
- [ ] 405 / 409 / 401 / transient errors each handled with appropriate UX
- [ ] Commit message editable before squash
- [ ] Integration test exists (gated on token)

title: Handle auth expiration and network flakes during push/PR/monitor
description: After this lands, any transient failure in the push-open-monitor flow (expired token, network drop, rate limit) is handled gracefully — re-auth fires, backoff kicks in, the in-flight operation resumes after recovery. The user sees clear chat messages at each step.
design:
Apply consistent error policy across BranchPusher, PullRequestOpener, PRCheckMonitor:

Transient errors (retry with exponential backoff, max 3 attempts):
  - Network timeouts
  - 5xx from GitHub
  - 429 rate-limit with backoff-hint header

Auth errors (401):
  - Re-trigger F20's sign-in flow
  - Resume the original operation after successful re-auth

Semantic errors (4xx other than 401, 429):
  - Surface in chat with the GitHub error message
  - No automatic retry
  - Agent may offer to help (e.g., "PR already exists" → offer to reuse it)

All error paths produce a chat-visible message; silent failures are disallowed.

Shared retry helper: OneApp/GammaAgent/Sources/HTTP/RetryPolicy.swift (since F20 also needs this). Document once, apply everywhere.

Tests: unit tests that simulate 401, 429, 500, network timeout. Confirm behavior per policy.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] Shared RetryPolicy helper exists in GammaAgent and is used by all GitHub HTTP operations
- [ ] Transient errors retried with exponential backoff (max 3, respect Retry-After)
- [ ] Auth errors (401) trigger re-auth and resume the original operation
- [ ] Semantic errors surface in chat with GitHub's error message; no silent failures
- [ ] Unit tests cover 401, 429, 500, timeout

title: Human verify: push + PR + CI round-trip, including an intentional failure
description: A human walks a codified branch through push → PR → CI green, then intentionally breaks the branch, watches CI go red, lets the agent propose a fix, and watches the loop return to green. All from inside chat.
design:
Verification procedure:
1. Prerequisite: codify an exploration (from F21's verification) but don't delete the branch.
2. In Lingo chat, trigger push/PR: "push this and open the PR".
3. Observe chat:
   - "Pushing branch lingo/..." → "Pushed."
   - "Opening pull request..." → "Opened #N."
4. Visit the PR URL in a browser; confirm it exists with the agent-drafted title + body, labeled "lingo".
5. Wait for CI. Watch chat stream status transitions. Confirm:
   - "CI started" appears within ~30s
   - Individual check updates appear as they happen
   - "All checks passed" or equivalent green state appears when done
6. Now intentionally break the branch (on the ontology-* repo clone, edit one of the preflight files to have malformed TypeQL, commit, push).
7. Watch chat. Within a minute:
   - Failure event surfaces with specific annotation
   - Agent proposes a fix ("I can revert the malformed statement and re-validate. Shall I?")
8. Confirm. Watch:
   - Agent applies the fix
   - Local validation passes
   - Force-push happens
   - CI re-runs and goes green
9. Close the PR without merging (test-only).

Any step that fails silently, hangs, or surfaces a confusing message: file specific follow-ups against F22.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] Codified branch pushed successfully; chat announces each step
- [ ] PR created with agent-drafted title + body, labeled "lingo"
- [ ] CI status transitions stream into chat within reasonable latency (<60s end-to-end)
- [ ] Intentional break on the branch surfaces as a failure annotation in chat
- [ ] Agent proposes a targeted fix and executes it on user confirmation
- [ ] Force-push re-triggers CI; CI returns to green
- [ ] Full round-trip never required the user to leave the app
- [ ] Any confusing or missing feedback filed as follow-ups
- [ ] Bead closed only after full round-trip (including failure + recovery) verified

title: Poll PR check runs and push status updates into the chat
description: After this lands, after the PR opens, Lingo periodically checks GitHub for the status of CI checks and surfaces state changes in chat: "CI started", "ontology-validate passed", "all checks green". The user doesn't have to leave the app to know what's happening.
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Codify/PRCheckMonitor.swift

Public API:
  public actor PRCheckMonitor {
    public init(tokenStore: GitHubTokenStore)
    public func monitor(pr: PullRequest, interval: TimeInterval = 15) -> AsyncStream<PRCheckEvent>
    public func stop()
  }

  public enum PRCheckEvent {
    case checksStarted(count: Int)
    case checkUpdated(name: String, status: String, conclusion: String?)
    case allChecksComplete(success: Bool)
    case error(Error)
  }

Implementation:
  - Periodically GET /repos/<owner>/<repo>/commits/<sha>/check-runs (head SHA from the PR)
  - Diff against the previous snapshot; emit events for changes
  - Stop on completion (all checks conclude) or when caller cancels

Integration with chat:
  - LingoAgent subscribes to the event stream
  - Each event becomes an agent-mediated chat message: "Ontology validation passed." / "Package validator failed — see details."
  - For failures, the agent fetches the check's output and surfaces the annotation

Polling interval: 15s default, but respect GitHub's rate limits. If rate-limited (429), back off gracefully.

Tests: unit test the event-diffing logic with snapshots; integration test against a test PR.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] PRCheckMonitor actor exists
- [ ] Polls GitHub check-runs API at a configurable interval (default 15s)
- [ ] Emits PRCheckEvent for state changes (started, updated, complete)
- [ ] LingoAgent subscribes and turns events into chat messages
- [ ] Rate-limit handling: backs off gracefully on 429
- [ ] Event-diffing logic unit-tested
- [ ] Integration test against a real PR (gated on test token)

title: Surface CI failure annotations and offer an iterate-to-green loop
description: After this lands, when CI fails, Lingo surfaces the specific annotation (file, line, message) in chat, the agent offers to diagnose and propose a fix, and — with user confirmation — amends the branch and force-pushes to re-trigger CI. The user stays in chat through the whole iteration.
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Codify/CIFailureHandler.swift

Flow on CI failure:
  1. PRCheckMonitor emits a failure event with the check's conclusion + annotations (fetched via GET /repos/<o>/<r>/check-runs/<id>/annotations).
  2. Chat shows: "Ontology validation failed at migrations/v1.3.6-to-v1.3.7.tql:12: '<error message>'."
  3. Agent proposes: "I can try to fix this by [specific proposal]. Shall I?"
  4. On user confirm:
     a. Agent generates the fix (LLM)
     b. Agent applies the fix to the local branch (modifies files)
     c. Re-runs local validation (OntologyCore.validatePackage)
     d. If local validation passes: amend the commit (git commit --amend --no-edit, or a new commit — user preference), force-push-with-lease, re-trigger CI
     e. If local validation fails: iterate (up to a safety limit, say 3 attempts, before asking the user to take over)
  5. On user decline: close the loop; user deals with it manually (clone branch, push fixes directly, or abandon)

Safety:
  - --force-with-lease on push, never --force
  - Never silently abandon a PR; always surface the state

Tests: simulate a CI failure with fixtures; verify agent proposes a fix, applies it, revalidates, and force-pushes. Use a test repo.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] Failure annotations surfaced in chat with file + line + message
- [ ] Agent proposes fix; user must confirm
- [ ] On confirm: fix applied, local validation re-runs, force-push-with-lease to re-trigger CI
- [ ] On local validation failure after fix: iterate (up to 3 attempts) before handing off
- [ ] --force-with-lease never --force
- [ ] User decline closes the loop; PR and branch left in whatever state they're in for manual follow-up
- [ ] Integration test simulates a failure-and-fix loop

title: Draft PR title and body from the intent log via the agent
description: After this lands, the agent produces a good PR title and body from the intent log — motivations grouped by concept, clear structure, honest about what changed. Users can edit before submission but the defaults are good enough to merge as-is.
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Agent/PullRequestDrafter.swift (or a tool the LingoAgent invokes)

Tool signature (AnyJSONTool):
  name: "draft_pull_request"
  description: "Draft a PR title and body from the sandbox's intent log. Returns a title (<=72 chars) and a markdown body."
  input: { "intents": [intent records JSON], "sandbox_name": String }
  output: { "title": String, "body": String }

Draft algorithm (agent applies):
  - Title: one sentence in imperative mood summarizing the dominant change. Examples: "Add Umbrella concept to vibemachine", "Rename workspaceName to workspaceLabel".
  - Body sections:
    1. "## What changed" — bulleted list of concept-level changes (from groupedUnder)
    2. "## Why" — bulleted list of motivations (from intents)
    3. "## Migration path" — note the semver bump and whether any action is needed from consumers
    4. Footer: "Authored via Lingo from sandbox <sandbox_name>"

The agent has the creative latitude to write better prose; the structure above is the minimum. Keep it scannable — a reviewer glancing at it should understand the change in <30 seconds.

Editable by the user:
  - Before PR creation, CodifyConfirmationView (F21.8) shows the draft title and body
  - User can edit both inline before submitting
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] draft_pull_request tool registered with LingoAgent
- [ ] Returns a title (<=72 chars) and a markdown body with "What changed", "Why", "Migration path" sections
- [ ] Body includes footer referencing the sandbox name
- [ ] User can edit title and body in CodifyConfirmationView before submission
- [ ] Agent-drafted defaults are good enough to merge unedited (subjective — human-verify task checks this)

title: Push branch to origin using the stored GitHub token
description: After this lands, right after codify, Lingo pushes the branch to the target repo's origin using the stored GitHub token. On success, chat confirms the push. On failure (auth expired, network, branch already exists), Lingo surfaces a clear state.
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Codify/BranchPusher.swift

Public API:
  public final class BranchPusher {
    public init(tokenStore: GitHubTokenStore)
    public func push(repo: URL, branch: String, force: Bool = false) async throws -> RemoteBranch
  }

  public struct RemoteBranch {
    public let name: String
    public let url: URL  // e.g., https://github.com/org/ontology-vibemachine/tree/lingo/...
  }

Implementation:
  - Subprocess git push with credential helper sourcing the token from GitHubTokenStore
  - OR use libgit2 with a credential callback
  - --force-with-lease for the force path (F22.7's iteration loop)
  - Capture stderr for diagnostics; surface any "remote rejected" messages

Error handling:
  - 401 (token invalid / expired): throw BranchPushError.authExpired → triggers F20's re-auth flow → retry
  - Network failure: retry with exponential backoff (up to 3 attempts)
  - "Updates were rejected" (branch exists with different history): throw BranchPushError.staleRemote — F22.7 handles

Tests:
  - Integration test against a test repo (requires a test token — skip in CI if absent)
  - Unit tests for error translation
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] BranchPusher.swift exists
- [ ] push(repo:branch:force:) pushes using the stored token
- [ ] Chat surfaces success with a link to the branch on GitHub
- [ ] Auth failure: BranchPushError.authExpired → triggers re-auth from F20
- [ ] Network failure: retried with exponential backoff (up to 3)
- [ ] Stale-remote failure: distinct error type for F22.7 to handle
- [ ] Integration test exists (may be gated on test token availability)

title: Open the pull request via GitHub REST API
description: After this lands, right after the push, Lingo creates a pull request on GitHub with the branch as head and main (or the repo's default) as base. Title and body are drafted by the agent from the intent log. The PR is labeled 'lingo' for identification.
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Codify/PullRequestOpener.swift

Public API:
  public final class PullRequestOpener {
    public init(tokenStore: GitHubTokenStore)
    public func open(
      repo: URL,
      branch: String,
      baseBranch: String,   // usually "main"
      title: String,
      body: String
    ) async throws -> PullRequest
  }

  public struct PullRequest {
    public let number: Int
    public let url: URL
    public let nodeID: String  // for GraphQL subscriptions later
  }

Implementation:
  - POST /repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls via GitHub REST API
  - Auth: bearer token from GitHubTokenStore
  - Accept: application/vnd.github+json
  - API version: 2022-11-28 (or current)

Agent drafts title + body:
  - Title: one-line summary of the change
  - Body: markdown — sections for "What changed", "Why" (motivations from intent log), "Migration path"
  - Body includes a footer: "Authored via Lingo from sandbox <sandbox-name>"

Label the PR:
  - POST /repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<number>/labels with ["lingo"]
  - If label doesn't exist in repo, create it first (idempotent)

Error handling:
  - 422 Unprocessable (PR already exists for this branch): surface clear state, link to existing PR
  - 401: re-auth
  - Other errors: surface API message in chat
