title: Scaffold rust/ontology-core/ crate with cross-platform build targets
description: After this lands, a Rust library crate exists at rust/ontology-core/ in OneWorkspace. It builds cleanly on macOS and Linux, exposes a minimal starter API, and has a test suite skeleton ready to receive the ports from the subsequent tasks.
design:
Location: rust/ontology-core/ (new top-level rust/ directory in OneWorkspace).

Cargo.toml:
  - name = "ontology-core"
  - edition = "2021"
  - [lib] type = ["staticlib", "cdylib", "rlib"]  — allow both Swift linkage and Rust-native use
  - Dependencies (starter set — expand as modules arrive):
    - thiserror (error types)
    - serde + serde_json (manifest parsing)
    - semver (version logic)
    - tokio (async runtime, gated behind feature flag)

Targets configured: macOS arm64, macOS x86_64, Linux arm64, Linux x86_64. CI uses matrix build.

Initial src/lib.rs exposes:
  pub fn version() -> &'static str { env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION") }

Test: tests/smoke.rs asserts version() returns the expected string.

rust/Cargo.toml at workspace root defines the members:
  members = ["ontology-core", "ontology-cli"]

(ontology-cli is created in F17.)

mise.toml at OneWorkspace root adds cargo tasks if useful (`mise run rust-build`, `mise run rust-test`).
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] rust/ontology-core/ exists with Cargo.toml and src/lib.rs
- [ ] rust/Cargo.toml workspace root exists listing ontology-core (and ontology-cli as placeholder for F17)
- [ ] cargo build succeeds on macOS arm64 locally
- [ ] cargo test passes on macOS arm64 locally
- [ ] CI matrix configured (or issue filed) for macOS arm64/x86_64 + Linux arm64/x86_64
- [ ] Starter dependencies (thiserror, serde, semver, tokio-with-feature-gate) declared
- [ ] crate version set to 0.1.0

title: Research and decide Rust–Swift binding strategy
description: After this lands, we have a written decision with rationale for which Rust-to-Swift binding approach the ontology plugin will use, plus a working toy proof-of-concept. All subsequent FFI work (F19) and the ontology-core API surface (rest of F16) build on this decision. Goal: avoid a dumb choice in a fast-moving area — do the research once, up front.
design:
Evaluate current landscape (as of implementation date — this may shift; re-verify):

Candidates:
  - UniFFI (Mozilla) — https://mozilla.github.io/uniffi-rs/
  - swift-bridge — https://github.com/chinedufn/swift-bridge
  - cargo-swift — https://github.com/antoniusnaumann/cargo-swift
  - Raw C ABI + cbindgen — https://github.com/mozilla/cbindgen
  - Any emerging option discovered during research

Evaluation matrix (populate for each candidate):
  - Swift 6 / Xcode 26 actor isolation behavior (any workarounds needed?)
  - Error-type ergonomics across FFI (throws vs result codes vs enums)
  - Async support (cancellation propagation, Sendable compatibility)
  - XCFramework generation (built-in, scripted, or manual?)
  - Swift Package Manager integration path
  - Generator speed / incremental build impact
  - Maintenance status: last commit, open-issue count, contributor diversity
  - License compatibility
  - Toy PoC feasibility in <1 day

Toy PoC:
  - Standalone sandbox project under rust/fft-toy/ (FFI-feasibility toy) — delete after decision, or move to docs
  - One sync Rust function: validate a dummy TypeQL string → Result<ValidationReport, ValidationError>
  - One async Rust function: simulate a 200ms parse with tokio, return the result
  - One opaque-handle-returning function: parse something and return an owned handle Swift can later free
  - Swift consumer: a test that calls all three, handles success and error, and runs under Xcode 26

Decision doc:
  Location: OneDocumentation/OneDocumentation/Documentation.docc/ForAgents/RustSwiftBindings.md
  Sections:
    - Chosen tool + version pin
    - Evaluation matrix summary
    - What won and why
    - Build pipeline integration (cargo invocation → xcframework → Swift import)
    - Known edge cases and their workarounds
    - When to revisit (e.g., "revisit if UniFFI ships native cancellation")

This doc is load-bearing for F16 and F19. Every later FFI task references it.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] Evaluation matrix filled in for at least UniFFI, swift-bridge, cargo-swift, and raw C ABI + cbindgen
- [ ] Toy PoC committed (or documented as deleted) with one sync, one async, one opaque-handle round trip
- [ ] PoC builds and passes its tests under current Swift 6 / Xcode 26 — no hand-sed'd `nonisolated` workarounds in the generated code
- [ ] Decision document exists at OneDocumentation/.../ForAgents/RustSwiftBindings.md with chosen tool, rationale, build-pipeline plan, and revisit triggers
- [ ] Chosen tool pinned to a specific version in the decision doc
- [ ] Decision reviewed and signed off by at least one other human (bead comment or PR review)

title: Start a brand-new ontology by describing what it's for
description: A user can start a new ontology the same way they evolve one — through conversation. They tell Lingo what the domain is, what matters in it, what to call it. Lingo scaffolds from the template, walks the initial concepts, codifies version 0.1.0, and creates the GitHub repo. The user can start evolving it immediately.
design:
Entry point: "new ontology" action in Lingo, or a conversational trigger ("I want to start a new ontology for acoustics").

Conversation flow (agent-led):
  1. Domain and name ("What's this ontology for? What should it be called?")
  2. Target GitHub location ("Do you have an empty repo, or should I create one under <org>?")
  3. Initial concepts (optional — agent offers to walk through a few, or user can defer and start empty)
  4. Gist placement reasoning for each initial concept (same system-prompt discipline as enhancement flow)
  5. First codification produces v0.1.0 with the initial concepts captured as the first migration from a template baseline

Scaffolding:
  - Uses the existing ontology-template structure from collection-vibe-machine/ontology-template
  - Creates: package manifest, empty schema root, validating migration contract, initial README with domain description
  - Invoked via OntologyCoreFFI (the same scaffolding logic the CLI uses in F27)

GitHub repo creation:
  - Optional: if user has a blank repo, point at it
  - Otherwise: create via GitHub API under the user-specified org using the F20 token
  - First commit pushed; branch protection left at org defaults

Out of scope:
  - Importing from Excel, SysML, or other source formats (deferred)
  - Forking/branching existing ontologies as a starting point (deferred)
acceptance_criteria:
- User can trigger "start new ontology" from Lingo chat
- Agent conducts the conversation: domain, name, GitHub target, initial concepts
- Scaffolding matches the ontology-template shape and passes `ontology validate`
- First version is v0.1.0 with a valid package contract
- GitHub repo created (or pointed at existing blank repo); first commit pushed
- User can immediately begin evolving the new ontology with the same conversational flow
- Scaffolding shares a code path with F27's CLI `ontology new` command (no duplication)

title: Merge the change and see the new concept live in knowledge immediately
description: When CI is green, the user confirms merge and Lingo merges the PR, tags the release per the existing ontology release convention, and refreshes the local knowledge database. The concept they just invented is now queryable against their real data — no manual steps.
design:
Merge:
  - Via GitHub API
  - Merge strategy: user preference stored in GammaAgent settings (default: squash — matches ontology-* current convention)
  - Confirms merge commit with appropriate message

Tag and release:
  - After merge lands on main, Lingo triggers `ontology release --repo <path> --version <new>` via OntologyCoreFFI (the same Rust code F17's CLI uses)
  - Tag pushed to origin
  - Release notes drafted by the agent from the intent log

Local knowledge refresh:
  - Existing re-bootstrap code in the Ontology plugin is invoked automatically
  - Progress surfaced in chat: "Refreshing your knowledge with vibe-machine 1.3.6..."
  - On completion: sandbox used for the exploration is archived (with a pointer to the merged PR + tag) and closed

Failure paths:
  - Merge conflict (someone else landed a change mid-flight): agent offers to rebase F21's branch and re-run CI
  - Release tag failure: retried automatically; falls back to manual tag creation as a guided step
acceptance_criteria:
- User can merge a green PR from Lingo with one explicit confirmation
- Merge strategy respects user preference set in GammaAgent settings
- Release tag created on the target ontology-* repo per the existing convention
- Local knowledge DB re-bootstraps to the new version automatically
- Progress visible in chat throughout
- Sandbox archived with a pointer to the merged PR + release tag
- User can query the new concept against their real knowledge immediately after completion
- Merge conflicts trigger a guided rebase + re-run loop without leaving chat

title: Suggest and confirm whether a change is a patch, minor, or major version
description: When it's time to codify, the agent proposes whether this is a patch, minor, or major version bump — based on what actually changed — and the user confirms. The semver label travels with the commit and drives the version bump in the migration.
design:
Heuristic (agent applies, user can override):
  - Pure additions (new entities, relations, attributes) → minor
  - Removals, renames affecting public surface, cardinality tightening → major
  - Documentation annotations, typos, internal-only fixups → patch

Implementation:
  - Agent analyzes the SchemaDiff (via OntologyCoreFFI)
  - Proposes the classification with a one-sentence rationale in chat
  - User accepts or overrides (patch / minor / major)
  - Chosen classification captured as part of the codify payload consumed by F21 to bump the manifest version

Edge cases:
  - Empty diff: cannot codify (rejected with explanation)
  - Mixed-scope diff (additions + removals): agent highlights the major-triggering change explicitly
  - First version of a new ontology (F26): always v0.1.0; classification skipped

Heuristic documented in code and surfaced in agent prompt so behavior is predictable to users.
acceptance_criteria:
- Agent proposes a semver classification (patch/minor/major) during codify with a one-sentence rationale
- User can accept or override
- Chosen semver is recorded and drives F21's version bump
- Heuristics documented in code + agent prompt
- Empty-diff codify attempts are rejected with a clear message
- Mixed-scope diffs surface the major-triggering item explicitly
- First version of a new ontology (F26 flow) auto-classifies to v0.1.0

title: Turn a finished exploration into a real commit on a branch
description: When a user says "make this real," Lingo takes the sandbox's intent log and produces the preflight / migration / verify file triple in the target ontology-* repo on a new branch — locally, not yet pushed. The user can see the diff the next commit would introduce before anything leaves their machine.
design:
Lingo resolves the target ontology from the active sandbox's origin (e.g., sandbox cloned from "knowledge" bootstrapped against ontology-vibemachine). Uses the user's local checkout of that ontology repo (prompts to clone if not present).

Branch name: lingo/<agent-drafted-slug>-<YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS>. Slug comes from the agent summarizing the exploration's dominant concept.

Authoring:
  - Migration triple per ontology-tooling's contract: preflight/, v<old>-to-v<new>.tql, verify/
  - The TypeQL middle file comes from MigrationAuthor (F7), now invoked via OntologyCoreFFI (F19)
  - preflight/ and verify/ drafted by the agent; validated by the Rust engine before commit
  - Package manifest bumped to the new version per F24's classification

Commit:
  - Author-identified via `git config user.name` / `user.email` in the target repo (falls back to OneApp defaults if absent)
  - Message format: "<concept-summary>\n\n<agent-drafted paragraph from intent log>\n\nCo-authored-by: Lingo <noreply@...>"
  - Uses libgit2 (via a Rust extension of ontology-core, if practical) or shells out to git if simpler. Decision at impl time.

Strictly local. No push in this feature — that's F22.
acceptance_criteria:
- User can trigger "codify" from Lingo chat after confirming the exploration is complete
- A new branch exists locally on the target ontology-* repo with: migration triple, bumped manifest, descriptive commit message
- The commit passes local `ontology validate` against the branch
- User can view the diff through Lingo UI or by running `git diff` in the repo
- Nothing has been pushed — verify via `git log origin/main..HEAD` showing only the new commit locally
- If the target repo isn't checked out locally, Lingo prompts the user to clone it first (offers to do it automatically with gh/git)

title: Open the pull request and watch CI from inside the conversation
description: After codification, Lingo pushes the branch to GitHub, opens a pull request with an agent-drafted description, and streams CI status back into chat. The user sees green checks land without leaving the app. If CI fails, the agent can propose a fix and iterate.
design:
Push:
  - Uses the token from F20
  - Branch from F21 pushed to origin with a human-readable remote name
  - Failure surfaces as a clear chat message (auth expired → re-auth; network → retry; branch conflict → agent offers rebase)

Pull request:
  - Opens via GitHub REST API
  - Title: one-line summary from the agent
  - Body: rendered from the intent log — grouped by concept, motivations as bullet points
  - Labels the PR with "lingo" (for identifying Lingo-authored PRs)
  - Links back to the sandbox name for traceability

CI tracking:
  - Polls PR check runs every N seconds (or uses webhooks if feasible, but polling is acceptable for v1)
  - Updates OntologyViewModel on status change
  - Chat shows status transitions: "CI started", "Ontology validation passed", "All checks green"
  - On failure: surfaces the specific annotation (file + line) from the failed check; agent offers to diagnose

Iteration UX on CI failure:
  - Agent reads the failure annotation and proposes an edit
  - User confirms → agent amends the branch, force-pushes, CI re-runs
  - Loop continues until green or user abandons
acceptance_criteria:
- Codified branch pushed to GitHub under the user's credentials
- PR opened with a title and body drawn from the intent log's motivations
- PR is labeled "lingo" for identification
- CI status streams into Lingo chat in near-real-time
- Green checks clearly announced in chat
- On CI failure: specific annotation surfaced; agent offers to diagnose and iterate
- Amend-and-force-push loop works without the user leaving chat
- Auth expiration during push triggers re-auth flow gracefully

title: Let users sign in to GitHub once inside OneApp
description: The first time a user wants to codify an ontology change, OneApp walks them through a GitHub sign-in flow. The resulting token lives in Keychain. After that, pushing branches and opening PRs from Lingo is seamless.
design:
OAuth device flow via GitHub's device authorization endpoint — the pattern used by the `gh` CLI.

Flow:
  1. User hits "Sign in to GitHub" in GammaAgent settings (same pane as provider config from F9)
  2. App requests a device code from GitHub; displays the code and a short URL
  3. User pastes the code at github.com/login/device in their browser
  4. App polls for the token; on success, stores it in Keychain via GammaAgent.KeychainService

Token scopes:
  - repo (read + write to ontology-* repos)
  - workflow (read CI check status)

Sign-out clears the Keychain entry. Re-sign-in flow on token expiry is automatic.

Token never appears in logs, UserDefaults, or on disk outside Keychain.
acceptance_criteria:
- User can sign in to GitHub from GammaAgent settings
- Device flow completes end-to-end: user pastes code on github.com, returns to OneApp, token is saved
- Token stored in Keychain under a well-known key, per-provider convention matching F9
- Lingo can read the token whenever it needs to push a branch or open a PR
- Sign-out clears the token; next codify prompts re-auth
- Token scopes are repo + workflow (minimum viable)
- Token never appears in logs or disk outside Keychain

title: Gate every ontology PR with the same validation the app uses
description: When someone opens a PR against an ontology-* repo, GitHub Actions runs the same checks Lingo runs locally. A PR can't merge unless the schema is valid, the migration contract is satisfied, and the package bootstraps cleanly.
design:
A reusable GitHub Actions workflow installs the `ontology` CLI (from F17's releases) and runs `ontology validate --repo .` against the PR head. Failures surface as PR check annotations pointing at specific files and lines.

Layout:
  - .github/workflows/ontology-validate.yml in the OneWorkspace repo (or a dedicated share-workflows repo) — the reusable workflow
  - Each ontology-* repo has a thin .github/workflows/validate.yml that calls the reusable one

CI speed optimizations:
  - CLI binary cached across runs
  - Validation runs in parallel with other checks
  - Typical PR validates in <2 minutes

Failure UX on the PR page:
  - Check run title: "Ontology validation"
  - Details link to annotation lines in changed .tql files
  - Error messages from the Rust validator surface directly (no wrapper translation)
acceptance_criteria:
- Reusable workflow exists at a shared location
- All current ontology-* repos reference it
- A valid PR produces a green check
- A broken PR (migration contract violation, schema error, bootstrap failure) produces a red check with specific error annotations on the offending lines
- CI runs in under ~2 minutes for a typical change
- No Node.js dependencies in the CI path (pure Rust CLI)

title: Let the Ontology plugin speak to the Rust engine directly
description: Lingo doesn't shell out. It links the Rust engine through a Swift wrapper that makes every validation, diff, and authoring operation feel like a native Swift call.
acceptance_criteria:
- OntologyCoreFFI Swift module exists and links OntologyCore.xcframework
- Swift API covers the operations Lingo needs: validate, diff, author_migration, compute_next_version, bootstrap_package
- Error codes become Swift errors; handles are RAII-managed under ARC
- Round-trip tests: every Rust unit test has a corresponding Swift test exercising the FFI surface
- No memory leaks detected by Instruments under the FFI surface
- Memory management convention documented for future extensions

title: Build the Rust engine that understands ontologies, migrations, and packages
description: The validation, migration contract, diff computation, semver logic, package authoring, executable package loading, and ontology corpus execution that currently live in scattered tooling move into a single Rust crate. One source of truth for every consumer: ontology repo mise tasks, the CLI, GitHub Actions checks, and the OneApp Ontology plugin all call into the same engine.
design:
Location: rust/ontology-core/ (new top-level rust/ directory in OneWorkspace).

Public Rust API covers the operations currently provided by collection-vibe-machine/ontology-tooling/src/lib/*.mjs:
  - validate_package — package-contract validation
  - compute_schema_diff — diff between two schema states
  - author_migration — produces the TypeQL statement block from a diff + intent log
  - validate_migration_contract — preflight / migration / verify triple shape
  - compute_next_version — semver bumping logic
  - bootstrap_uniqueness — confirms a package bootstraps without identity collisions
  - executable_package — loads a package into TypeDB for testing

The Rust engine also becomes the home for executable ontology corpora. An ontology package is not only schema/data/manifests; it may also ship a corpus of executable examples that describe how agents and developers should query and model against that ontology. The corpus is stored with the ontology repo, while ontology-core owns loading, validation, execution, reporting, and export.

Corpus responsibilities added to ontology-core:
  - discover_corpus — find corpus manifests/items in an ontology repo
  - validate_corpus_manifest — validate corpus item shape, fixture references, tags, and expected answer declarations
  - load_corpus_fixture — load corpus-specific schema/data overlays into an isolated TypeDB database after package bootstrap
  - run_corpus_query — execute a known-good TypeQL query against the bootstrapped package + fixture and compare the observed answer shape to the expected result
  - validate_corpus — run selected corpus items by repo, package, tag, or query class
  - export_prompt_examples — produce a compact, deterministic artifact that Lingo/agent prompts can consume without copying ad hoc examples from tests

Corpus source of truth:
  - ontology-gist owns GIST-grounded examples and fixture data
  - ontology-vibemachine, ontology-beads, and other domain ontologies own domain-specific examples layered on their dependencies
  - ontology-tooling and ontology repo mise tasks are thin CLI surfaces over ontology-core
  - OneWorkspace/Ontology plugin consumes exported prompt/example artifacts and eventually calls ontology-core directly through the binding work tracked separately

Implementation strategy: port existing Node.js behavior without breaking contracts, but allow the corpus lab as a new vertical slice that exercises executable_package early. The corpus lab should start with ontology-gist because all other ontology packages depend on it. Node.js ontology-tooling stays live during this work. Retirement is post-v1, once the Rust crate has parity and all consumers (Lingo, CLI, CI) are on it.

The corpus lab is deliberately not a live-LLM test harness by default. The deterministic path validates checked-in corpus examples against TypeDB. Optional live generation/repair modes may be added as explicit mise tasks, but they must never run as part of normal tests.

C ABI surface is added in F19. This feature delivers the Rust-native library only.
acceptance_criteria:
- rust/ontology-core/ crate exists with Cargo.toml and compiles via cargo build
- Public Rust API covers the functional surface of ontology-tooling: validate_package, compute_schema_diff, author_migration, validate_migration_contract, compute_next_version, bootstrap_uniqueness, executable_package
- Public Rust API includes executable corpus operations: discover_corpus, validate_corpus_manifest, load_corpus_fixture, run_corpus_query, validate_corpus, export_prompt_examples
- Unit tests port alongside each migrated module
- Parity fixtures: for each ported function, a test fixture produces identical output to the current .mjs implementation given the same input
- At least one ontology-gist corpus fixture can bootstrap GIST, load fixture data, execute known-good TypeQL queries, and verify expected answer shapes through ontology-core
- Ontology repo mise tasks can delegate corpus validation/export to the shared engine without duplicating runner logic
- OneWorkspace/Ontology plugin has a documented consumption path for exported prompt examples, even before direct Rust binding is complete
- Node.js ontology-tooling remains intact and functional; no retirement in this feature

title: Ship a brew-installable CLI that does everything Lingo does from a terminal
description: A single command-line tool called `ontology` becomes available via Homebrew. It validates, diffs, releases, creates new ontologies, and migrates — everything Lingo does — from a terminal. Power users, scripts, and GitHub Actions all depend on it.
design:
Location: rust/ontology-cli/ — a binary crate linking ontology-core (F16).

Commands (first version):
  ontology validate --repo <path>
  ontology diff --from <version> --to <version> --repo <path>
  ontology dry-run --repo <path> --bump <patch|minor|major>
  ontology release --repo <path> [--bump <patch|minor|major> | --version <x.y.z>]
  ontology new <name> [--domain <domain>] [--path <path>] [--git]
  ontology refresh --repo <path> --version <x.y.z>

Distribution:
  - Built for macOS arm64 + x86_64 and Linux arm64 + x86_64
  - Signed binaries attached to GitHub releases
  - Homebrew tap under the same GitHub org (or homebrew-core once stable)
  - Formula auto-updates on each release via a lightweight bumper workflow

Versioning: the CLI's version is locked to ontology-core's Cargo.toml version. 1.0.0 ships once the Rust port reaches parity with ontology-tooling.
acceptance_criteria:
- rust/ontology-cli/ binary crate exists and builds for macOS and Linux
- `brew install ontology` installs the CLI from a maintained tap
- Commands implemented: validate, diff, dry-run, release, new, refresh
- Each command has clear `--help` that a power user can navigate unaided
- First tagged release of the CLI on GitHub with signed binaries for all four platforms
- CLI version is discoverable via `ontology --version` and matches the release tag

title: Human verify: walk EngineeringTask scenario through Lingo UI matches L5 output
description: A human sits down in front of Lingo and walks the full hierarchical EngineeringTask scenario (Umbrella → Feature-of-Umbrella → Sub-feature → Task-of-Sub-feature + a rename + a doc annotation) entirely through conversation. They confirm the final sandbox state matches the L5 (F7) programmatic test output, the sandbox survives quit/relaunch, and dropping the sandbox clears schema and intents together. This is the load-bearing milestone for Lingo v1.
design:
Prerequisites: all of F1-F14 landed and their verifications closed. F7's L5 test green. F15.1-F15.5 implemented.

Verification procedure:

Part A — Walk the scenario through chat:
1. Launch OneApp; open the Lingo sidebar item.
2. Create a new sandbox via the SandboxSelectorView's "+ New" action (or by asking the agent).
3. Have a conversation with Lingo to apply the 6 changes from the L5 scenario:
   a. "I want to group Features by shared commitment. Let's add an Umbrella concept." — confirm the agent proposes Umbrella sub Category with gist placement reasoning, ask for confirmation, apply.
   b. "Features belong to Umbrellas — add that relation." — confirm agent proposes featureOfUmbrella with role names, apply.
   c. "Sub-features are a kind of Specification that decompose Features. Add Sub-feature." — apply as specialization.
   d. "Tasks belong to Sub-features." — apply as taskOfSubFeature relation.
   e. "Rename umbrellaName to umbrellaLabel — it's display-visible, should follow the Label convention." — confirm agent uses the rename path, not undefine+define.
   f. "Add a doc annotation on Umbrella: 'An Umbrella groups Features by shared commitment.'" — confirm annotate-doc.
4. Throughout: CandidateSchemaView refreshes after each change; IntentTimelineView grows with motivations visible.

Part B — Compare to L5 programmatic output:
5. In parallel, run the L5 scenario test (from F7.2/7.3) and capture the MigrationAuthor output (or the final diff + intent log).
6. Compare against what you walked through in the UI:
   - Diff shape matches (same adds, same roles, same owns clauses).
   - Intent log order matches.
   - Migration TypeQL that would be generated from the UI-driven sandbox matches L5's output (bit-for-bit, or semantically equivalent).

Part C — Persistence and cleanup:
7. Quit OneApp (Cmd-Q, full exit).
8. Relaunch. Open Lingo. Confirm the sandbox you worked in is still there with all 6 intents and the expected schema.
9. Drop the sandbox via the SandboxSelectorView. Confirm:
   - Sandbox removed from list
   - Active sandbox state cleared
   - TypeDB console shows the sandbox DB is gone (cleanup complete)

If any part fails — wrong migration output, state doesn't survive restart, drop doesn't clean up — triage and file against the responsible feature.

Do not close this bead until all three parts (walk, compare, persist/cleanup) pass.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] Full 6-step EngineeringTask scenario completed entirely through the Lingo UI chat
- [ ] CandidateSchemaView refreshes after each change
- [ ] IntentTimelineView grows with motivations visible and correctly ordered
- [ ] Agent surfaces gist placement reasoning before each apply (required by system prompt)
- [ ] Rename handled via rename path, not undefine+define (confirmed by inspecting intent log)
- [ ] Final UI-driven sandbox state matches F7's L5 programmatic output (diff, intent log, generated migration)
- [ ] Quit + relaunch preserves sandbox with all intents and schema intact
- [ ] Drop sandbox clears schema AND intents together (verified via TypeDB console — DB is gone)
- [ ] Bead closed only after all above confirmed. This bead closes the Lingo v1 epic.

title: Implement IntentTimelineView
description: After this lands, IntentTimelineView renders the ChangeIntent log of the active sandbox as an ordered, grouped-by-concept timeline. Users can read the story of the exploration: what changed, when, why, grouped by what concept.
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Views/Lingo/IntentTimelineView.swift

Public view:
  struct IntentTimelineView: View {
    @ObservedObject var viewModel: OntologyViewModel
    var body: some View { /* ... */ }
  }

Data shape from view model:
- viewModel.intentLog: [ChangeIntentRecord] in precedes order
- viewModel.intentGroups: [String: [ChangeIntentRecord]] (concept label → intents)

Default display: grouped view.
- Section per group (concept label is section header).
- Within each section, list intents in chronological order.
- Each intent row shows:
  - Action badge (e.g., "define" / "undefine" / "rename" / "annotate-doc" / "untracked" — untracked highlighted in a warning color)
  - Target label + kind ("entity Umbrella", "attribute projectName")
  - Motivation (if present; italics; trimmed if very long)
  - Timestamp (relative format: "2 minutes ago", "yesterday", etc.)

View mode toggle: button to switch between "Grouped" and "Chronological" view. Chronological shows all intents in one list ordered by precedes.

Empty state: "No changes yet. Start describing what you want to evolve."

Untracked styling:
- Intents with action="untracked" render with a warning icon and a subtle color tint, plus a tooltip: "Detected outside the paired-write flow. Reconciled on reopen."

Tests: preview-based visual smoke.

Responsiveness: long motivations wrap; timeline scrolls when many intents exist.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] OneApps/Ontology/Views/Lingo/IntentTimelineView.swift exists
- [ ] Renders viewModel.intentLog and viewModel.intentGroups
- [ ] Default grouped view with concept-label section headers
- [ ] Each intent row shows action badge, target, motivation, relative timestamp
- [ ] Untracked intents visually flagged with warning styling + tooltip
- [ ] Toggle between Grouped and Chronological views
- [ ] Empty state renders with a call to action
- [ ] Long motivations wrap; view scrolls for many intents
- [ ] SwiftUI preview renders without crash
close_reason: Implemented IntentTimelineView with grouped/chronological modes and populated view-model intent groups from grouped queries

title: Compose LingoRootView from the four subviews with shared OntologyViewModel
description: After this lands, LingoRootView composes LingoChatView, CandidateSchemaView, SandboxSelectorView, and IntentTimelineView into a single layout. All four observe the same OntologyViewModel instance so state flows consistently. Replaces the placeholder from F14.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] OneApps/Ontology/Views/Lingo/LingoRootView.swift composes the four subviews with a shared OntologyViewModel
- [ ] Layout uses sidebar-first pattern matching other OneApp content views
- [ ] Sandbox selector + intent timeline on the left pane; chat + candidate schema on the right
- [ ] ontology/lingo route now builds LingoRootView, not LingoPlaceholderView
- [ ] LingoPlaceholderView.swift deleted
- [ ] OntologyViewModel wired with SandboxManager, ProviderResolver, client, LingoAgent factory
- [ ] Dark mode / Liquid Glass rendering verified (no bleed-through, text legible)
- [ ] SwiftUI preview renders the full composition

title: Human verify: Settings-configured Claude Code and Codex drive Lingo via sticky MCP
description: A human uses OneApp Settings to configure Claude Code and Codex for the Lingo/Ontology MCP server, then verifies both tools can reconnect after OneApp restarts without changing MCP client configuration. Each external agent drives at least one Lingo primitive and the OneApp UI reflects the change.
design:
Prerequisites:
- 13.1 / 13.2 / 13.3 / 13.5 landed.
- Claude Code and Codex installed on the same machine, or the manual fallback path clearly verified for any missing client.
- OneApp running with Ontology plugin active.

Procedure:
1. Launch OneApp and open Settings -> Lingo/Ontology MCP configuration.
2. Confirm Settings shows a stable MCP URL and separate Claude Code and Codex setup/status entries.
3. Configure Claude Code from Settings using the automatic action. If automation is unavailable, use the exact Settings-provided user-scope command/snippet.
   Expected user-scope shape per Claude Code docs: claude mcp add --transport http NAME --scope user URL, or equivalent ~/.claude.json merge.
4. Configure Codex from Settings using the automatic action. If automation is unavailable, use the exact Settings-provided TOML snippet.
   Expected user-home shape per OpenAI/Codex docs: ~/.codex/config.toml with [mcp_servers.NAME] url = URL.
5. Verify both client config entries point at the same stable OneApp MCP URL shown in Settings.
6. In Claude Code, verify the Lingo/Ontology tools appear and invoke listDatabases plus one mutating primitive such as create_sandbox or apply_schema_delta. Use actual tool names exposed by tools/list if they differ.
7. In Codex, verify the same MCP server appears and invoke at least listDatabases plus one Lingo primitive.
8. Switch to OneApp's Lingo view and confirm external changes are reflected in sandbox/schema/intent state.
9. Stop and restart OneApp. Confirm Settings shows the same MCP URL as before restart.
10. In Claude Code and Codex, reconnect/reload MCP if needed, but do not edit the MCP server definition and do not restart/reconfigure solely because the port changed.
11. Invoke another lightweight tool call from each client. Confirm OneApp UI still reflects the effects.

This proves the end-user flow: Settings discovery/configuration, dual-client setup, shared tool layer, and sticky endpoint behavior across restarts.

If the UI reflects first-run changes but fails after restart, triage 13.3 endpoint persistence before closing this bead. If users have to hand-edit a new port after restart, this bead fails.

If tool invocation fails, attach the latest redacted Lingo diagnostic JSONL trace from the configured session trace directory so the implementation bead can improve tool schemas, error messages, or provider behavior without relying on generic app logs alone.

title: Provide a sticky local MCP endpoint and lifecycle
description: After this lands, the MCP server exposes a stable local endpoint, persisted under the OneApp user config root, that Claude Code and Codex can be configured against once. OneApp restarts must not force the user to edit or recreate MCP client configuration. Any port/discovery internals are implementation details hidden behind the stable endpoint contract.
design:
Endpoint contract:
- Persist the chosen MCP endpoint via GammaCore.ConfigPaths under ~/.config/one. Prefer a documented Ontology/Lingo plugin-owned location such as ~/.config/one/plugin-data/com.gamma.ontology/ontology-mcp.json, or a documented OneApp-wide file under ~/.config/one/ontology-mcp.json if Settings needs shared discovery. Do not introduce a new Application Support config root for this.
- The client-facing URL must remain stable across normal OneApp stop/start cycles. Preferred shape: http://127.0.0.1:<persistedPort>/mcp with the same persisted port reused on restart, or a stable local proxy URL if the implementation introduces one.
- Avoid a per-launch random port file as the primary integration contract. Agentic tools often need restart/reload to pick up new MCP server definitions, so changing the configured URL is disruptive.

Lifecycle:
- First start: choose a suitable localhost port, persist it through ConfigPaths, start the server, and expose the full endpoint URL.
- Later starts: read the persisted endpoint and attempt to bind the same port.
- Stop: stop serving but keep the persisted endpoint configuration. Do not delete the persisted endpoint on normal shutdown.
- Unclean shutdown: persisted endpoint remains valid; the next start attempts the same endpoint.

Conflict handling:
- If the persisted port is occupied by this same OneApp server/process, treat it as already running/reconnectable.
- If the persisted port is occupied by another process, do not silently choose a new client-facing port. Surface the conflict in logs and Settings with recovery actions: retry, choose a new stable endpoint, or reset MCP configuration.
- If the user explicitly chooses reset/reconfigure, update the persisted endpoint and mark client configs as needing update.

Discovery metadata:
- Keep a machine-readable status file if helpful, but it should describe the stable endpoint and health, not be the client-facing contract that changes every launch.
- This endpoint config is separate from Lingo diagnostic session traces; do not mix replay/log data into the endpoint file.
- Document the endpoint persistence and conflict behavior in OneApps/Ontology/MCP/MCP_INTEGRATION.md.

Tests: OntologyTests/MCP/PortDiscoveryTests.swift or StickyEndpointTests.swift
- testEndpointPersistedOnFirstStart: start server; assert endpoint metadata exists under the ConfigPaths-backed ~/.config/one location and contains a numeric localhost URL.
- testEndpointReusedAcrossRestart: start, capture URL, stop, start again, assert URL unchanged.
- testEndpointNotDeletedOnStop: stop server; assert persisted endpoint remains.
- testPortConflictDoesNotSilentlyReconfigureClients: occupy persisted port with an unrelated listener; start server; assert conflict state/error and no automatic client-facing URL change.
- testExplicitResetChoosesAndPersistsNewEndpoint: invoke reset/reconfigure path; assert endpoint changes only by explicit action.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] First server start persists a stable localhost MCP endpoint via GammaCore.ConfigPaths under ~/.config/one
- [ ] Normal OneApp restart reuses the same client-facing endpoint
- [ ] Normal stop does not delete the persisted endpoint config
- [ ] Persisted-port conflict is surfaced instead of silently changing Claude/Codex config target
- [ ] Explicit reset/reconfigure path can choose and persist a new endpoint
- [ ] Settings can read endpoint status/health for user-facing configuration UI
- [ ] Endpoint config remains separate from Lingo diagnostic session traces
- [ ] MCP_INTEGRATION.md documents sticky endpoint semantics, config path, and recovery behavior
- [ ] Sticky endpoint lifecycle tests pass
close_reason: Added ConfigPaths-backed sticky MCP endpoint metadata, lifecycle reuse/reset/conflict handling, plugin integration, documentation, and focused lifecycle tests.

title: Implement SwarmToolToMCPAdapter (AnyJSONTool → MCP tool bridge)
description: After this lands, any Swarm AnyJSONTool implementation can be exposed through the local Lingo MCP server without re-implementing tool logic. The adapter must use the actual Swarm API: AnyJSONTool has name/description/parameters, normalizeArguments/validateArguments helpers, and execute(arguments:), with SendableValue arguments/results.
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/MCP/SwarmToolToMCPAdapter.swift

Current codebase constraints:
- AnyJSONTool does not expose a ready-made JSON Schema and does not have run(input:). It exposes parameters: [ToolParameter] and execute(arguments: [String: SendableValue]).
- Swarm already has MCP client-side types/protocols under Vendor/Swarm/Sources/Swarm/MCP, including MCPServer, MCPRequest/MCPResponse, MCPError, and ToolSchema parsing. Reuse compatible Swarm types where possible; only introduce modelcontextprotocol/swift-sdk types if 13.2 proves they are needed for serving external clients.

Adapter responsibilities:
1. Convert AnyJSONTool metadata into MCP tool metadata:
   - name -> tool name
   - description -> tool description
   - parameters [ToolParameter] -> JSON Schema object with properties, required, and additionalProperties=false.
2. Forward invocations:
   - Receive MCP tool arguments as [String: SendableValue]
   - Call tool.normalizeArguments / validateArguments where appropriate
   - Invoke tool.execute(arguments:)
   - Convert the SendableValue output into the MCP tool result shape expected by the server transport.
3. Translate errors into MCP invalidParams/internalError responses with useful messages.
4. Keep the adapter generic; Lingo-specific tools should require no special casing.

Tests: OntologyTests/MCP/SwarmToolToMCPAdapterTests.swift
- testAdapterExposesInputSchema: wrap a trivial AnyJSONTool, assert schema derived from ToolParameter matches expected JSON Schema.
- testAdapterForwardsInvocation: invoke through adapter with SendableValue arguments, assert execute(arguments:) receives normalized input and output round-trips.
- testAdapterTranslatesErrors: wrapped tool throws; assert MCP error response preserves the useful message.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] SwarmToolToMCPAdapter.swift exists with a generic wrapping API for any AnyJSONTool
- [ ] Adapter derives MCP-compatible input schema from ToolParameter definitions
- [ ] Adapter forwards MCP arguments through AnyJSONTool normalization/validation and execute(arguments:)
- [ ] Adapter converts SendableValue output into MCP tool result content
- [ ] Tool errors surface as MCP error responses with actionable messages
- [ ] Unit tests cover schema translation, invocation forwarding, and error translation
- [ ] Implementation matches the actual Swarm AnyJSONTool API in Vendor/Swarm
close_reason: Implemented SwarmToolToMCPAdapter with schema derivation, normalized invocation, result conversion, MCP error mapping, and focused tests.

title: Implement OntologyMCPServer over HTTP via swift-sdk
description: After this lands, a local HTTP MCP server runs inside or alongside the Ontology plugin and exposes the Lingo tool layer through SwarmToolToMCPAdapter. External agents such as Claude Code and Codex can list and invoke Lingo tools as MCP tools.
design:
Dependency/architecture notes:
- First inspect modelcontextprotocol/swift-sdk and Swarm's existing MCP types before adding a new dependency. Swarm already includes MCP client/protocol models, but not necessarily an embeddable HTTP server suitable for Claude Code/Codex.
- If swift-sdk is the right serving library, add it narrowly to the Ontology target or a small shared GammaAgent/GammaCore support target. If a minimal local JSON-RPC HTTP server is simpler and compatible, document why.

Location: OneApps/Ontology/MCP/OntologyMCPServer.swift

Public shape:
  actor OntologyMCPServer {
    init(tools: [any AnyJSONTool], port: Int? = nil)
    func start() async throws -> URL
    func stop() async
  }

Implementation:
1. Register every current Lingo tool from LingoAgent.makeTools(viewModel:) through SwarmToolToMCPAdapter. These are individual tools, not just the five original tool groups.
2. Serve MCP initialize, tools/list, and tools/call over HTTP in the transport shape accepted by Claude Code and Codex.
3. Bind to the requested localhost port, or a caller-selected free port for non-sticky test use. Sticky endpoint behavior belongs in 13.3.
4. Plugin activation should start the server only after the Ontology view model/tool context is available; plugin deactivation should stop it.
5. Emit os.Logger status for start/stop/conflict, and rely on Lingo diagnostic traces for tool-level behavior once calls enter the Lingo tool layer.

Tests: OntologyTests/MCP/OntologyMCPServerTests.swift
- testServerStartsAndListsTools: start server, call MCP initialize/tools/list, assert expected current Lingo tool names are present.
- testServerInvokesToolThroughAdapter: invoke listDatabases through MCP, assert response contains expected shape and view model updates where applicable.
- Do not proceed to 13.3 until the server can serve at least one real Lingo tool from a test.

- [ ] Serving transport chosen and documented: swift-sdk or minimal compatible HTTP JSON-RPC server
- [ ] OntologyMCPServer actor exists with start/stop lifecycle
- [ ] Current Lingo tools are registered via SwarmToolToMCPAdapter
- [ ] Server handles MCP initialize, tools/list, and tools/call
- [ ] Server binds to caller-specified localhost port or free test port
- [ ] Plugin lifecycle starts/stops the server when Ontology/Lingo context is available
- [ ] testServerStartsAndListsTools passes

Procedure:

3. Conversation turns, one per tool group:

   b. User: "Create a sandbox." → expect create_sandbox; viewModel.sandboxes adds entry; viewModel.activeSandbox set.

title: Let Claude Code and Codex drive Lingo over MCP
description: External agents such as Claude Code and Codex can connect over HTTP/MCP to a running OneApp instance and drive Lingo's sandbox primitives. The end-user path must make MCP setup discoverable and low-friction from OneApp Settings: users can see Claude Code and Codex configuration status, copy/view the exact config, and preferably apply user-scope home-directory configuration automatically. The configured endpoint must be sticky across OneApp restarts so already-configured agent tools can reconnect without requiring users to restart or reconfigure Claude Code/Codex.
design:
SwarmToolToMCPAdapter is a generic bridge: any AnyJSONTool implementation exposes to MCP by deriving an MCP input schema from the tool's actual Swarm metadata. The current Swarm API exposes name, description, parameters, normalizeArguments(_:), validateArguments(_:), and execute(arguments:); it does not expose a ready-made JSON Schema or run(input:) helper.

OntologyMCPServer runs a local HTTP MCP server, registers the current Lingo tools from LingoAgent.makeTools(viewModel:) through the adapter, and exposes a stable local HTTP endpoint intended for long-lived user-scope MCP client configuration. Before adding modelcontextprotocol/swift-sdk, inspect Swarm's existing MCP client/protocol types and choose either swift-sdk or a minimal compatible HTTP JSON-RPC server based on what is actually needed for Claude Code/Codex.

User experience requirement:
- OneApp Settings must include an MCP configuration screen for Lingo/Ontology.
- The screen must present separate Claude Code and Codex setup entries.
- Each entry must show whether that client appears configured, the target config path/command, and the exact endpoint URL.
- Ideal path: OneApp can configure the user's home-directory client config automatically after explicit user action/confirmation.
- Fallback path: OneApp provides copyable commands/snippets and clear status if automatic configuration is unavailable or unsafe.

Stickiness requirement:
- MCP client configuration is done once and should survive stop/start cycles of OneApp.
- Do not require new Claude Code/Codex config when OneApp restarts.
- Persist endpoint metadata via GammaCore.ConfigPaths under ~/.config/one, not a new Application Support root.
- Prefer a persisted endpoint contract (stable localhost port or stable local proxy URL) over a per-launch random port file. If a fallback dynamic port is unavoidable internally, hide it behind a stable endpoint that clients keep using.
- On restart, OneApp should rebind the previously configured endpoint or clearly surface a recoverable conflict in Settings rather than silently changing the client URL.

The MCP path is NOT on the v1 critical user path, but if included it must be an actual user experience, not a developer-only discovery file.
acceptance_criteria:
- SwarmToolToMCPAdapter wraps any AnyJSONTool as an MCP tool using the real Swarm AnyJSONTool API
- OntologyMCPServer starts on plugin activation and registers the current Lingo tools from LingoAgent.makeTools(viewModel:)
- MCP endpoint is stable across OneApp restarts once configured
- Endpoint metadata is persisted under ~/.config/one through GammaCore.ConfigPaths
- Settings includes separate Claude Code and Codex MCP configuration entries
- Settings can apply user-scope/home-directory MCP configuration automatically where supported, or provides exact copyable fallback instructions
- Human verify: configure Claude Code from Settings, restart OneApp, reconnect without editing Claude config, drive listDatabases plus one mutating Lingo primitive, observe effects in Lingo UI
- Human verify: configure Codex from Settings, restart OneApp, reconnect without editing Codex config, drive at least one Lingo primitive, observe effects in Lingo UI

title: Implement QueryTools (runReadQuery, runWriteQuery)
description: After this lands, LingoAgent can run read queries against any database (to answer user questions like "how many Features are there?") and write queries (to seed synthetic instances for the user to validate a candidate schema's lived feel).
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Agent/Tools/QueryTools.swift

runReadQuery:
  name: "run_read_query"
  description: "Execute a read-only TypeQL query against a named database. Returns a row list."
  input: { "database_name": String, "tql": String }
  output: { "rows": [[String: Any]] }  // each row is a dict of var name → string repr

  Implementation:
  - Open a .read transaction, execute tql, collect rows.
  - Convert each Concept to a stringified representation (a richer typed Concept representation is deferred; per the design doc, this is acceptable for v0).

runWriteQuery:
  name: "run_write_query"
  description: "Execute a write TypeQL query (insert, delete) against a named database. Use to seed synthetic instances for exercising a candidate schema's shape. Writes commit immediately — use with care."
  input: { "database_name": String, "tql": String }
  output: { "committed": true, "row_count": Int }

  Implementation:
  - Open a .write transaction, execute, commit. Return summary.
  - Writes DO NOT get ChangeIntent records — this is by design (intents track schema changes, not data). If the agent needs to record "we seeded N instances of X", it should call ChangeIntentTools.record_intent with action="annotate-doc" and a motivation describing the seeding.

Errors:
- Database not found → clear tool error.
- TQL syntax / semantic error → surface TypeDB's error message back to the agent.

Safety: runWriteQuery against the base "knowledge" database should be blocked by convention (refuse with an error). The agent should only write to sandboxes. Enforce in the tool: if database_name == "knowledge", reject with a message nudging toward create_sandbox first.

Tests: OntologyTests/QueryToolsTests.swift
- testRunReadQueryReturnsRows: insert a few instances, read them back via the tool.
- testRunWriteQueryCommitsAndBlocksKnowledge: write to a sandbox works; write to "knowledge" is refused.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] QueryTools.swift exists with runReadQuery + runWriteQuery as AnyJSONTool
- [ ] runReadQuery returns row list; errors surface TypeDB error messages
- [ ] runWriteQuery commits and returns row count
- [ ] runWriteQuery refuses writes to "knowledge" with a clear nudging error
- [ ] Unit tests for both tools pass against gamma-typedb
close_reason: Implemented Lingo read/write query tools with sandbox write guardrails and focused unit coverage.

title: Implement ChangeIntentTools (recordIntent, queryIntents)
description: After this lands, LingoAgent can manually record an intent (e.g., for annotate-doc or for recording a commentary entry without applying a schema change), and can query the intent log with filtering — feeding the IntentTimelineView (F15) and enabling the agent to reason about the history of an in-progress exploration.
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Agent/Tools/ChangeIntentTools.swift

recordIntent:
  name: "record_intent"
  description: "Write a ChangeIntent record to the active sandbox without performing a schema change. Use to annotate or comment on the exploration (e.g., for commentary, observations). For actual schema changes, use apply_schema_delta instead."
  input: {
    "action": String,          // typically "annotate-doc" or "note"
    "target_label": String,
    "target_kind": String,
    "motivation": String?,
    "group_tag": String?
  }
  output: { "intent_id": String }

  Implementation: wraps ChangeIntentWriter.writeRawIntent (added in 6.2), appending to the log with proper precedes chain linkage.

queryIntents:
  name: "query_intents"
  description: "Query the ChangeIntent log of the active sandbox. Options: order by precedes chain, group by concept, filter by time window."
  input: {
    "mode": String,            // "ordered" | "grouped" | "between"
    "start": ISO8601String?,   // for "between"
    "end": ISO8601String?
  }
  output: depends on mode:
    ordered: [{ intent record as JSON }]
    grouped: { concept_label: [intent records] }
    between: [intent records in window]

  Implementation: dispatches to ChangeIntentReader's ordered() / grouped() / between() methods.

Errors:
- No active sandbox → clear error.
- Invalid mode → clear error listing valid modes.

- testQueryIntentsGroupedGroupsByConcept: record intents under two group tags; grouped mode returns them keyed correctly.

- [ ] recordIntent wraps writeRawIntent; links via precedes
- [ ] queryIntents supports ordered / grouped / between modes

title: Implement SandboxTools (createSandbox, dropSandbox)
description: After this lands, LingoAgent has two tools to manage sandboxes: createSandbox clones from a source DB (typically "knowledge") and returns the new sandbox's name; dropSandbox removes a sandbox by name. Both update OntologyViewModel so the UI stays current.
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Agent/Tools/SandboxTools.swift

createSandbox:
  name: "create_sandbox"
  description: "Create a new sandbox TypeDB database cloned from a source. Default source is 'knowledge'. The sandbox will have the ChangeIntent meta-schema loaded automatically. Returns the new sandbox's name."
  input: { "source": String? }  (nil → default "knowledge")
  output: { "name": String, "createdAt": ISO8601 String }

  Implementation:
  - let sandbox = try await sandboxManager.create(from: source ?? "knowledge")
  - viewModel.sandboxes.append(sandbox); viewModel.activeSandbox = sandbox
  - Return { "name": sandbox.name, "createdAt": ISO8601.string(from: sandbox.createdAt) }

dropSandbox:
  name: "drop_sandbox"
  description: "Drop a sandbox by name. Irreversibly deletes the sandbox database and its intent log."
  input: { "name": String }
  output: { "dropped": true }

  Implementation:
  - try await sandboxManager.drop(name: name)
  - viewModel.sandboxes.removeAll { $0.name == name }
  - If activeSandbox was this one, set activeSandbox = nil
  - Return { "dropped": true }

Errors:
- drop of non-sandbox (e.g., "knowledge") → clear error ("'{name}' is not a sandbox and cannot be dropped. Use drop_sandbox only on sandboxes created via create_sandbox.")
- drop of missing → clear error

Tests: OntologyTests/SandboxToolsTests.swift
- testCreateSandboxAppendsToViewModel: before 0 sandboxes, tool called, then 1 sandbox; activeSandbox set.
- testDropSandboxRemovesFromViewModel: after create + drop, sandboxes list empty.
- testDropKnowledgeErrorsClearly: attempt to drop "knowledge", assert error message matches.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] SandboxTools.swift exists with createSandbox + dropSandbox as AnyJSONTool conformances
- [ ] createSandbox uses SandboxManager.create(from:) and updates OntologyViewModel
- [ ] dropSandbox uses SandboxManager.drop and updates viewModel (removes + unsets activeSandbox if needed)
- [ ] Drop of non-sandbox surfaces a clear, actionable error
- [ ] Drop of missing surfaces a clear error
- [ ] Three unit tests above all pass

title: Implement SchemaEvolutionTools (applySchemaDelta, validateCandidate)
description: After this lands, LingoAgent can apply schema changes to a sandbox with motivation tracking, and can run a set of canned sanity queries against a sandbox to validate the shape is queryable before the user commits to it. Both are thin wrappers over F4 (paired-write) and F12's QueryTools.
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Agent/Tools/SchemaEvolutionTools.swift

applySchemaDelta:
  name: "apply_schema_delta"
  description: "Apply a schema change to the active sandbox as an atomic paired-write: schema change + ChangeIntent record. Use when the user has confirmed a proposed change. NEVER call without explicit user confirmation (the system prompt enforces this rule)."
  input: {
    "typeql": String,           // the define / undefine / rename TypeQL
    "action": String,           // "define" | "undefine" | "rename" | "annotate-doc"
    "target_label": String,
    "target_kind": String,      // "entity" | "attribute" | "relation" | "role"
    "rename_from": String?,
    "motivation": String?,
    "group_tag": String?
  }
  output: { "intent_id": String, "applied": true }

  Implementation:
  - Fetch active sandbox from viewModel; error if none.
  - writer = ChangeIntentWriter(client: ..., sandbox: active)
  - let id = try await writer.applySchemaDelta(typeql:, action:, targetLabel:, targetKind:, renameFrom:, motivation:, groupTag:)
  - After apply: re-fetch parsed schema and push to viewModel.currentSchema (so CandidateSchemaView refreshes).
  - Return { "intent_id": id.description, "applied": true }

validateCandidate:
  name: "validate_candidate"
  description: "Run a small set of canned sanity queries against the active sandbox to verify the candidate schema can answer typical questions. Use before asking for user commit-confirmation on a large change set."
  input: { }
  output: { "results": [{ "query": String, "rowCount": Int, "ok": Bool }] }

  Canned queries (configurable but start with a few sensible ones):
  - match $x isa thing; limit 5; — "top 5 entities"
  - For each top-level entity type: match $e isa <Type>; count;
  - For each relation type: match ($r) isa <Relation>; count;

  Implementation: iterate the queries, run via runReadQuery, capture results, return summary.

Errors:
- applySchemaDelta with no active sandbox → error ("No active sandbox. Call create_sandbox or set active first.")
- Any writer error propagates through as tool error with readable message.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] SchemaEvolutionTools.swift exists with applySchemaDelta + validateCandidate as AnyJSONTool
- [ ] applySchemaDelta wraps ChangeIntentWriter; requires active sandbox; pushes new schema to viewModel
- [ ] validateCandidate runs canned queries and returns summarized results
- [ ] Errors (no active sandbox, writer failure) surface as clear tool errors
- [ ] Unit tests for both tools against gamma-typedb
close_reason: Implemented schema evolution tools with active-sandbox guardrails, rollback handling, validation queries, and focused unit coverage.

title: Implement SchemaIntrospectionTools (listDatabases, getParsedSchema)

Both push their effects to the OntologyViewModel so UI state stays live.
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Agent/Tools/SchemaIntrospectionTools.swift

Tools (as AnyJSONTool from Swarm, re-exported via GammaAgent):

listDatabases:
  name: "list_databases"
  description: "List all TypeDB databases available to the agent — includes the base 'knowledge' database and any sandboxes."
  input: { } (no parameters)
  output: { "databases": [{ "name": String, "isSandbox": Bool }] }

  - Filter names; mark those starting with "knowledge-sandbox-" as isSandbox=true
  - Push to viewModel.databases (makes the list visible in the UI)

getParsedSchema:

  - Parse via TypeQLParser.
  - Push to viewModel.currentSchema (so CandidateSchemaView can render it).
  - Return JSON-serialized form of the parsed model.

title: Human verify: Lingo single-turn chat invokes a tool and updates UI
description: A human starts a trivial conversation with Lingo against a fresh sandbox and confirms the agent invokes at least one tool (listDatabases or getParsedSchema), streams a response, and updates the OntologyViewModel. This is the end-to-end smoke test that the conversational backbone is wired correctly.
design:
Prerequisite: at this point, F7 proves the backend; F9 provides provider config; F11.1-F11.3 wire the agent; F12 provides tools (at minimum, SchemaIntrospectionTools from 12.1 must be landed for this verification to be meaningful).

Procedure:
1. mise run dev to launch OneApp.
2. Configure a working provider in GammaAgent settings (preferably a cheap one — ollama local, OpenAI gpt-4o-mini, Claude haiku).
3. Create a sandbox via debug path (from 2.6).
4. Via a debug-only entry point (since the sidebar UI isn't built until F14), trigger a Lingo agent session against that sandbox.
5. Send the user turn: "What databases exist?"
6. Observe:
   - Agent streams a response (not a one-shot blob).
   - Response mentions the sandbox's name and/or "knowledge" by name, proving it invoked listDatabases.
   - The OntologyViewModel (observed via debug print or a test harness reading its state) shows a tool-call event with name="listDatabases".
7. If the agent doesn't invoke a tool, or if it invents database names instead of calling listDatabases, this is a prompt/tool-wiring regression — investigate before closing.

Send a second user turn: "Show me the schema of <sandbox-name>."
8. Observe the agent invokes getParsedSchema and mentions gist/vibemachine types in its response.

Do not close this bead until at least one successful tool invocation round-trip has been observed with a real provider + real sandbox.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] Working provider configured; sandbox created
- [ ] Single-turn chat to Lingo against the sandbox produces a streaming response
- [ ] At least one tool-call event observed (listDatabases or getParsedSchema)
- [ ] Tool output appears to have been used by the agent in its response (not ignored)
- [ ] OntologyViewModel state reflects the tool call (verified via debug print or test harness)
- [ ] Bead closed only after tool round-trip confirmed visually or via logs

Verification path: relaunch OneApp, open Ontology > Lingo, start a session after assistant provider config is set, send 'What databases exist?', then send 'Show me the schema of <database-name>'. title: Author opinionated gist-aware system prompt for LingoAgent (with function guidance)
description: After this lands, LingoAgent's system prompt teaches the agent the gist ontology's base types, vibemachine naming conventions, the specialization-vs-composition distinction, query-readability rules, the requirement to surface gist placement decisions before applying them, AND when to propose a function instead of a relation for derived or computed relationships. This prompt is the product differentiator versus "a generic chatbot that writes TypeQL."
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Agent/LingoSystemPrompt.md (Markdown for easy human review; loaded by LingoAgent at factory time via Bundle resource read OR via a Swift string constant — use whichever path matches the plugin's other runtime prompts).

Structure (minimum sections):

## Role
You are Lingo — a semantic workbench agent that helps users evolve TypeDB-based ontologies built on the gist upper ontology. You translate user intent into structured schema changes while surfacing semantic decisions for user confirmation.

## Gist base types and when to specialize each
- Category: things that group by shared *what*.
- Specification: things that describe intended properties or requirements.
- Commitment: things that represent agreements or binding relationships.
- Intention: things that represent what an actor wants to do.
- Determination: things that resolve or decide.
- Event: things that happened at a point in time.

(One sentence of placement guidance per base type.)

## Naming conventions (Vibe style)
- Attributes: camelCase for multi-word (workspaceName, projectId). NOT snake_case or PascalCase.
- Identifier attributes: snake_case is acceptable (item_id, user_id).
- Relations: present-tense verb phrases (motivatedBy, implementsFeature, fulfillsRequirement).
- Role names: domain-specific specializations so queries read like English.
- Functions: camelCase, noun phrases if returning a value (isGrandparentOf, totalEffortFor), verb phrases if performing a derivation.

## Specialization vs composition
When a user says "sub-feature of a feature": is SubFeature a *kind of* Feature (sub Feature), or a distinct thing that *participates in* a Feature (relation subFeatureOf)? Surface this distinction before applying.

## When to use a function vs a relation
Some relationships are DERIVED — they can be computed from existing data rather than stored. When a user describes something that follows FROM other facts (e.g., "X is a grandparent of Y if X is a parent of Z and Z is a parent of Y"), prefer a function over a relation:
  - A RELATION stores the fact directly; adding or removing it is an explicit data edit.
  - A FUNCTION computes the fact on demand from a pattern; it stays correct as the underlying data changes.
If the user says things like "if", "when", "whenever", "based on", "computed from" — that's a function signal. When they say "has a", "is part of", "is connected to" without conditionality — that's a relation.

When proposing a function:
1. Mirror back the user's intent in English — the derivation pattern, not the TypeQL.
2. Identify inputs and output ("given a Project, return its Contributors where contribution is non-zero").
3. Propose a name in Vibe style.
4. Ask for confirmation before applying.
5. Use TypeDB 3.x function syntax — verify the current form against https://typedb.com/docs/academy/ at the time of definition.

## Query-readability rule
A well-shaped TypeQL query reads like English. If a schema makes queries read awkwardly, reconsider role or function names.

## Required behavior
Before applying any schema change (including function definitions):
1. Mirror back the user's intent in structured English.
2. State the gist placement / function-vs-relation decision with reasoning.
3. Ask for confirmation.
4. Only then apply via applySchemaDelta, carrying the user's stated motivation into the ChangeIntent.

Never apply a change silently. Never emit raw TypeQL to the user without the English mirror.

## Tool catalog
(Brief one-line descriptions of each tool in the F12 set.)

## Example interactions
Include two worked examples:
1. A user proposes a concept that's a TYPE — agent walks the gist placement discussion.
2. A user proposes a derived / computed relationship — agent recognizes the function signal and walks the function-vs-relation decision.

---

Loading mechanism (Swift):
  let prompt = LingoSystemPrompt.markdown
  // or via Bundle if stored as a resource

Versioning: include a version string at the top (e.g., "version: 1.1.0" — bump on material changes). The prompt is the product — treat it as such in review.

Review: this file MUST be reviewed by someone with ontology knowledge before merge (the human verify in 11.4 gates this).
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] LingoSystemPrompt.md (or equivalent) exists and is loaded by LingoAgent at factory time
- [ ] Includes sections: Role, Gist base types, Naming conventions (with function-naming rules), Specialization-vs-composition, Function-vs-relation guidance, Query-readability, Required behavior, Tool catalog, Example interactions
- [ ] Function-vs-relation section teaches the agent to recognize "if/when/based on" signals and propose functions for derived relationships
- [ ] TypeDB 3.x function syntax referenced (link to current docs) so agent uses up-to-date form
- [ ] Version string present; bumped on material changes
- [ ] Reviewed by an ontology-knowledgeable human (signed off in PR review or bead comment)
- [ ] At least two worked examples: one type-placement, one function-vs-relation
close_reason: Added gist-aware Lingo system prompt covering role, naming, specialization/composition, function guidance, query readability, and tool behavior.

title: Build the Lingo conversational backbone

title: Implement OntologyAgentService actor
description: After this lands, the Ontology plugin has an OntologyAgentService actor that mirrors VibeMachine's AgentService shape — owns a Swarm ReActAgent, manages conversation state, streams events to the OntologyViewModel. It's the runtime host for all Lingo chat turns.
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Agent/OntologyAgentService.swift

Public API (conforms to GammaAgent.AgentService from 8.3):
  public actor OntologyAgentService: AgentService {
    public init(
      resolver: ProviderResolver,
      viewModel: OntologyViewModel    // so tools can push UI updates
    )
    public var eventStream: AsyncStream<OntologyAgentEvent> { get }
    public func startConversation(systemPrompt: String, tools: [AnyJSONTool]) async throws
    public func send(userTurn: String) async throws
    public func cancel() async
  }
  public enum OntologyAgentEvent {
    case userTurn(String)
    case agentTurnChunk(String)     // streaming partial content
    case agentTurnComplete(String)  // final content after streaming ends
    case toolCallStarted(name: String, input: [String: Any])
    case toolCallCompleted(name: String, output: Any?)
    case error(Error)
  }

Implementation:
- Resolve provider via resolver.resolve(selection: AssistantConfigStore().load()).
- Construct Swarm.ReActAgent with the resolved provider + tools (registered via 11.2's factory).
- Wire ReActAgent's event stream (however Swarm exposes it — AsyncSequence, callbacks, etc.) to eventStream.
- Inject viewModel into each tool (via a tool-construction closure) so tool effects can push UI state.

Concurrency:
- Actor isolation ensures conversation state is thread-safe.
- cancel() terminates the current turn cleanly.

Testing:
- OntologyTests/OntologyAgentServiceTests.swift: build the actor, start a conversation with a minimal tool set (one echo tool), send "Hello", assert at least one event flows through the stream.
- Uses real Swarm + real resolver with a test-only provider config (e.g., a local ollama endpoint to avoid real provider cost during CI).

title: Support ad-hoc endpoint URL override for local inference
description: After this lands, the user can override any preset's endpoint with their own URL — pointing the selected provider at a local inference server (lm-studio, ollama) or any OpenAI-compatible API. The auth header shape still follows the chosen provider's preset, but requests go to the override URL.
design:
Location: OneApp/GammaAgent/Sources/Providers/ProviderResolver.swift

Public API:
  public final class ProviderResolver {
    public init(keychain: KeychainService)
    public func resolve(selection: ProviderSelection) throws -> ResolvedProvider
  }
  public struct ResolvedProvider {
    public let endpoint: URL
    public let model: String
    public let authHeaders: [String: String]  // ready to attach to a URLRequest
  }

Algorithm:
1. Look up ProviderPreset by selection.providerID. If preset not found AND selection.providerID != .custom, throw ProviderResolutionError.presetMissing.
2. Determine effective endpoint:
   - if selection.endpointOverride is set → use it
   - else → preset.defaultEndpoint
3. Determine effective model: selection.model (pass-through, per 9.2).
4. Retrieve API key via keychain.retrieve(key: "api-key-\(selection.providerID.rawValue)"); throw ProviderResolutionError.missingApiKey if nil.
5. Construct authHeaders from preset.authHeader:
   - .bearer → ["Authorization": "Bearer \(key)"]
   - .anthropicVersioned → ["x-api-key": key, "anthropic-version": "2023-06-01"]  // verify current version at impl time
   - .custom(name, prefix) → [name: "\(prefix)\(key)"]
6. Return ResolvedProvider.

Precedence summary (document in the function's comment):
1. endpointOverride beats preset.defaultEndpoint
2. model string is passed through unchanged
3. authHeader shape always comes from the preset (never overridden — users pick a provider, and its auth shape comes with it; if they want a fundamentally different auth, they file an issue and we add a new preset)

Tests in 9.7.

Note: for local inference (ollama, lm-studio), users typically pick OpenAI as the provider (since those servers speak OpenAI-compatible APIs) and override the endpoint to http://localhost:11434/v1/... or similar.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] ProviderResolver.resolve(selection:) returns a ResolvedProvider with endpoint, model, authHeaders populated
- [ ] Endpoint override takes precedence over preset default
- [ ] Model string is passed through without modification
- [ ] Auth headers constructed per preset's authHeader shape
- [ ] Missing API key throws ProviderResolutionError.missingApiKey
- [ ] Unknown provider throws ProviderResolutionError.presetMissing
- [ ] Precedence rules documented in code comment
close_reason: Added ProviderResolver and ResolvedProvider. Resolution applies endpoint override precedence, passes model strings through unchanged, constructs bearer/Anthropic/custom auth headers from preset shape, and throws missingApiKey or presetMissing as appropriate.

title: Define ProviderPreset registry for ZAI, OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI
description: After this lands, GammaAgent exposes a ProviderPreset type and a registry containing four presets — ZAI, OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI — each with the endpoint URL, default model list, and auth header shape required to talk to that provider. This is the data layer that every subsequent selection / resolution task builds on.
design:
Location: OneApp/GammaAgent/Sources/Providers/ProviderPreset.swift

Public types:
  public struct ProviderPreset: Hashable, Codable {
    public let id: ProviderID            // enum: zai, openrouter, anthropic, openai, custom
    public let displayName: String
    public let defaultEndpoint: URL
    public let defaultModels: [String]   // e.g., ["claude-opus-4-7", "claude-sonnet-4-6"] for Anthropic
    public let authHeader: AuthHeaderShape
  }

  public enum ProviderID: String, Codable, CaseIterable {
    case zai, openrouter, anthropic, openai, custom
  }

  public enum AuthHeaderShape: Codable {
    case bearer                   // "Authorization: Bearer <key>"
    case anthropicVersioned        // Anthropic's "x-api-key" + "anthropic-version" pattern
    case custom(name: String, prefix: String)  // e.g., ("x-api-key", "")
  }

  public enum PresetRegistry {
    public static let presets: [ProviderPreset] = [
      .init(id: .zai, displayName: "ZAI",
            defaultEndpoint: URL(string: "https://api.z.ai/api/paas/v4/chat/completions")!,  // verify current endpoint at impl time
            defaultModels: ["glm-4.6", "glm-4.5v"],
            authHeader: .bearer),
      .init(id: .openrouter, displayName: "OpenRouter",
            defaultEndpoint: URL(string: "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions")!,
            defaultModels: ["anthropic/claude-opus-4-7", "openai/gpt-4o", "meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct"],
            authHeader: .bearer),
      .init(id: .anthropic, displayName: "Anthropic",
            defaultEndpoint: URL(string: "https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages")!,
            defaultModels: ["claude-opus-4-7", "claude-sonnet-4-6", "claude-haiku-4-5-20251001"],
            authHeader: .anthropicVersioned),
      .init(id: .openai, displayName: "OpenAI",
            defaultEndpoint: URL(string: "https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions")!,
            defaultModels: ["gpt-4o", "gpt-4o-mini", "o1-preview"],
            authHeader: .bearer),
    ]
    public static func preset(for id: ProviderID) -> ProviderPreset? {
      presets.first(where: { $0.id == id })
    }
  }

Notes:
- At implementation time: verify all four endpoint URLs against each provider's current docs. URLs in this design are provisional.
- Default model lists should reflect what's current on the provider's website as of implementation date. They're seeds for the UI picker, not exhaustive.
- ProviderID.custom is a sentinel for "user brought their own endpoint URL"; not in presets array but in the ID enum.

Tests: GammaAgent/Tests/ProviderPresetTests.swift
- testPresetsContainAllFourProviders: count == 4, IDs match the case list minus .custom.
- testPresetLookupReturnsCorrectEndpoint: lookup by .anthropic returns the Anthropic URL.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] ProviderPreset, ProviderID, AuthHeaderShape types exist in GammaAgent/Sources/Providers/
- [ ] PresetRegistry.presets contains exactly 4 entries (ZAI, OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI)
- [ ] Each preset has endpoint URL, default model list, and authHeader populated
- [ ] Endpoint URLs verified against current provider documentation at implementation time (documented in PR description or code comment)
- [ ] ProviderID.custom exists for user-supplied endpoints
- [ ] Tests pass: preset count, lookup by ID, endpoint values
close_reason: Added GammaAgent provider preset registry with auth shapes, fallback seed models, and live model-discovery metadata for OpenAI, Anthropic, and OpenRouter; Z.AI remains static fallback because no official model-list endpoint was found in docs.
