title: Human verify: workspace builds and Swarm is linked once via GammaAgent
description: A human builds the full workspace, then inspects the resulting plugin dylibs (or the GammaAgent framework) to confirm Swarm and its transitives are resolved via GammaAgent only — no plugin carries its own copy. This is the proof that the hoist actually eliminated the duplicate-load problem.
design:
Verification procedure:
1. Clean build: from repo root, run mise run build --all (full workspace build).
2. Confirm the build succeeds with no warnings about duplicate modules or conflicting symbols.
3. Inspect the built GammaAgent.framework:
     otool -L /path/to/GammaAgent.framework/GammaAgent
   Confirm Swarm, Conduit, swift-syntax etc. symbols are resolvable from within it.
4. Inspect VibeMachine's built plugin bundle:
     otool -L /path/to/VibeMachine.plugin/Contents/MacOS/VibeMachine
   Confirm Swarm is NOT listed as a direct link-time dependency (at this milestone, VibeMachine still links Swarm directly — that's removed in 10.1. So for 8.5, confirm GammaAgent now exports Swarm and the framework is linkable; full VibeMachine de-duplication is a later check).
5. Launch OneApp (mise run launch). Confirm it starts without dlopen errors about symbol conflicts.
6. In Console.app, filter for OneApp — confirm no warnings about "duplicate class" or "method already implemented by another category" that reference Swarm/Conduit types.

Note: the ULTIMATE check (VibeMachine no longer linking Swarm directly, only via GammaAgent) is 10.1's responsibility. For 8.5, the check is: GammaAgent loads Swarm cleanly, and the workspace still builds + launches.

Do not close this bead until build, otool inspection, and app launch all confirm clean state.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] Full workspace build succeeds (mise run build --all)
- [ ] No duplicate-module or conflicting-symbol warnings during build
- [ ] otool on GammaAgent.framework shows Swarm resolvable via it
- [ ] App launches (mise run launch) without dlopen symbol-conflict errors
- [ ] Console.app shows no "duplicate class" warnings for Swarm/Conduit types
- [ ] Note in comment: full VibeMachine de-duplication is checked under 10.x, not here
- [ ] Bead closed only after all above confirmed
close_reason: mise run build --all succeeded across all plugins. mise run launch starts OneApp cleanly (no dlopen errors). otool confirms GammaAgent.framework contains Swarm symbols (statically linked) and is embedded in OneApp.app/Contents/Frameworks/. VibeMachine still links Swarm directly per bead scope — full de-duplication is one-2xg.10.x. Console.app inspection for duplicate-class warnings is the one acceptance line I can't verify from CLI; deferred to one-2xg.10.x verification when VibeMachine actually consumes GammaAgent.

title: Choose any AI provider, model, or local endpoint
description: A settings surface where the user picks among ZAI, OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI presets, can hand-enter any model name (not just picker options), and can override the endpoint URL for local inference servers (lm-studio, ollama, anything speaking an OpenAI-compatible API). API keys go into Keychain. Any agent in the app — Lingo, VibeMachine Design, future ones — resolves its provider/model/endpoint through this single path. No more hardcoded gpt-4o.
design:
Provider registry in GammaAgent with four presets: ZAI, OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI. Each preset has:
  - default endpoint URL
  - default model list
  - required auth header shape

User selection flow:
  (a) pick a preset model from the list, OR
  (b) hand-enter a model name string for the preset's endpoint, OR
  (c) enter a fully custom endpoint URL (for local inference — lm-studio, ollama, or any OpenAI-compatible API)

Precedence: preset default < hand-entered model override < custom endpoint override.

API keys stored in macOS Keychain keyed by provider. assistant-config.json at a known path (e.g., ~/Library/Application Support/OneApp/assistant-config.json) carries current provider/model/endpoint selection — user-visible, editable.

Settings UI contributes a pane in the GammaAgent namespace (or a shared settings section exposed by GammaAgent). All agents across plugins use the same ProviderResolver; no direct Conduit model references remain in plugin code after this feature.
acceptance_criteria:
- Settings pane shows provider picker with ZAI / OpenRouter / Anthropic / OpenAI
- Model picker lists presets + free-text field for hand-entered model name
- Endpoint URL field accepts custom URLs for local inference
- API keys stored in Keychain, per-provider
- assistant-config.json loader reads/writes the selection
- ProviderResolver unit tests: each precedence tier resolves correctly
- Human verify: complete a chat turn against each of ZAI / OpenRouter / Anthropic / OpenAI with real keys
- Human verify: custom model name works for the selected provider's endpoint
- Human verify: local endpoint (lm-studio or ollama) works
close_reason: Provider/model/endpoint settings, shared resolver, Producer migration, tests, and human verification beads are complete.

title: Expose a shared AgentService actor pattern from GammaAgent
description: After this lands, GammaAgent exposes a reusable AgentService actor shape — either as a base actor class, a protocol + default implementations, or a generic actor — that plugins can adopt instead of re-implementing the streaming/events/state pattern VibeMachine currently has privately.
design:
Review VibeMachine's existing AgentService (DesignAgent's owning actor, whatever it's called) to understand the shape in practice. Likely responsibilities:
- Owns the Swarm ReActAgent instance.
- Manages conversation state (turns, tool calls, streaming events).
- Provides an async sequence of events to the view model.
- Mediates cancellation and in-flight state.

Location: OneApp/GammaAgent/Sources/AgentService.swift

Design choice (pick one and document in code):
  Option A: public protocol AgentService + extension with defaults. Plugins conform a concrete actor.
  Option B: public open actor AgentService<Agent: ReActAgent> with generic body, plugins subclass.

Preferred: Option A (protocol + extension), because actor subclassing has limitations in Swift 6. Structure:

  public protocol AgentService: Actor {
    associatedtype Event
    var eventStream: AsyncStream<Event> { get }
    func startConversation(systemPrompt: String, tools: [AnyJSONTool]) async throws
    func send(userTurn: String) async throws
    func cancel() async
  }
  public extension AgentService { /* default implementations referencing Swarm primitives */ }

Public types re-exported:
- AnyJSONTool (from Swarm, via @_exported or typealias)

Test: OneApp/GammaAgent/Tests/AgentServiceTests.swift
- Build a minimal AgentService conformance against a trivial Swarm agent.
- Drive one conversation turn via a stub provider (but using real Swarm, not mocked).
- Assert at least one event streams out.

Note: if the VibeMachine AgentService has private state not yet suitable for extraction, extract only what's generalizable in this task; the rest stays in VibeMachine until 8.4 or 10.x.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] GammaAgent/Sources/AgentService.swift defines a public AgentService protocol (or actor) with the responsibilities listed above
- [ ] eventStream, startConversation, send(userTurn:), cancel APIs exposed
- [ ] AnyJSONTool is re-exported from Swarm via GammaAgent
- [ ] A conformance + driving test passes in AgentServiceTests.swift
- [ ] Design choice (protocol vs open actor) documented in file-level comment
- [ ] VibeMachine's AgentService is not modified in this task (migration is 10.x)
close_reason: GammaAgent/AgentService.swift: public protocol AgentService (Actor) + concrete BaseAgentService actor wrapping Swarm ReActAgent. Surface: events stream, startConversation(systemPrompt:tools:inferenceProvider:), send(userTurn:), cancel(). Default impl uses .stream() with hooks; failures surface as AgentEvent.failed. Tests drive a turn through a stub InferenceProvider returning a ReAct Final Answer (real Swarm, no mocks). 4 tests pass. Note: BUILD_LIBRARY_FOR_DISTRIBUTION disabled on GammaAgent because Swarm types appear in public API and Swarm itself is non-evolution; plugins dlopen GammaAgent into the same process so ABI stability is unnecessary. AnyJSONTool re-exported via @_exported import in GammaAgent.swift.

title: Expose a shared KeychainService from GammaAgent
description: After this lands, GammaAgent exposes a KeychainService API for storing and retrieving secrets (API keys, tokens) keyed by a string identifier. Plugins use this single implementation rather than each rolling their own.
design:
Location: OneApp/GammaAgent/Sources/KeychainService.swift

Public API:
  public final class KeychainService {
    public init(serviceName: String = "com.oneapp.gamma-agent")
    public func store(key: String, value: String) throws
    public func retrieve(key: String) throws -> String?
    public func delete(key: String) throws
  }
  public enum KeychainError: Error {
    case storageFailed(OSStatus)
    case retrievalFailed(OSStatus)
    case deletionFailed(OSStatus)
  }

Implementation: wraps SecItemAdd / SecItemCopyMatching / SecItemDelete with kSecClassGenericPassword. Service name defaults to "com.oneapp.gamma-agent"; plugins can override via init if they need isolation.

Security notes:
- Access group is NOT set — keys are per-app. If OneApp ever needs cross-app sharing this can be revisited.
- All APIs are throws so callers handle errors explicitly.
- No caching. Every retrieve hits the Keychain.

Tests: OneApp/GammaAgent/Tests/KeychainServiceTests.swift
- testStoreAndRetrieveRoundTrip: store key "test-key" = "secret", retrieve, assert equality, delete.
- testRetrieveMissingReturnsNil: retrieve a non-existent key, assert returns nil (not throws).
- testDeleteAbsentDoesNotThrow: delete a non-existent key, assert no throw.
- testOverwriteReplacesValue: store twice under same key, retrieve returns the second value.

Test isolation: each test uses a unique key under a test-only service name to avoid polluting the real Keychain namespace.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] KeychainService.swift exists in GammaAgent with the public API above
- [ ] store / retrieve / delete round-trip verified in tests
- [ ] Missing-key retrieve returns nil, not throw
- [ ] Deleting absent key does not throw
- [ ] Overwriting an existing key replaces the value
- [ ] Tests run under a test-only service name to avoid real Keychain pollution
close_reason: GammaAgent/KeychainService.swift exposes public final class KeychainService with store/retrieve/delete and configurable serviceName (default com.oneapp.gamma-agent). KeychainError is a public OSStatus-bearing enum. Tests use unique UUID keys under com.oneapp.gamma-agent.tests namespace and clean up in tearDown. 4 acceptance scenarios covered: round-trip, missing→nil, delete-absent no-throw, overwrite replaces. All 8 GammaAgentTests pass.

title: Hoist Swarm and its transitive deps into GammaAgent
description: After this lands, GammaAgent directly depends on Vendor/Swarm (and its transitives: Conduit, Wax, SwarmMacros, swift-syntax, swift-log). Any plugin wanting agent capability will depend on GammaAgent — not on Vendor/Swarm directly — eliminating the duplicate-copy problem at plugin dlopen time.
design:
Context: Vendor/Swarm is a vendored submodule (see CLAUDE.md note on submodules). VibeMachine currently links Swarm directly; this causes symbol duplication if another plugin also links Swarm directly.

Changes to GammaAgent project/package:
- Add a local package dependency on Vendor/Swarm.
- Verify transitive resolution pulls in Conduit, Wax, SwarmMacros, swift-syntax, swift-log — inspect the resolved graph via "Show Package Resolution" in Xcode or swift package show-dependencies.
- Re-export selectively (optional): if plugins will reference Swarm types directly via GammaAgent's public API (e.g., ReActAgent, AnyJSONTool), add public typealias or @_exported imports in GammaAgent.swift for those types.

Validation:
- Build GammaAgent target; confirm the Swarm module is available from within GammaAgent's source files.
- Add a smoke test in GammaAgentTests: import Swarm; create a dummy AnyJSONTool instance (or reference a public type from Swarm); assert the import works.

Do NOT migrate VibeMachine yet — that's 8.3/8.4/10.x. This task only makes Swarm available through GammaAgent.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] GammaAgent depends on Vendor/Swarm (declared in its project or package manifest)
- [ ] Transitive deps (Conduit, Wax, SwarmMacros, swift-syntax, swift-log) resolve without conflict
- [ ] GammaAgent source can import Swarm (verified by a smoke test in GammaAgentTests)
- [ ] Full workspace builds
- [ ] VibeMachine is NOT modified in this task (its direct Swarm link is retained; migration is F10)
close_reason: Vendor/Swarm + LocalPackages/ConduitTraits added as local SPM packages on the GammaAgent target. GammaAgent.swift @_exports Swarm + Conduit + ConduitTraits. Smoke test references AgentConfiguration.default through GammaAgent — passes. Library-evolution warnings on Swarm/Conduit are pre-existing pattern (GammaCore has same on Bonsplit/EuroRackContracts), non-blocking. VibeMachine still links Swarm directly per bead — migration deferred to one-2xg.10.

title: Share one agent framework across plugins
description: A new Swift framework GammaAgent sits alongside GammaCore. Both VibeMachine and Ontology plugins (and any future plugin) link Swarm/Conduit/swift-syntax only through it — no plugin re-vendors its own copy. The full workspace builds and launches exactly as before.
design:
Currently VibeMachine links Vendor/Swarm directly, transitively pulling Swarm + Conduit + Wax + SwarmMacros + swift-syntax + swift-log into its dylib. If Ontology adds a direct Swarm dep too, each plugin ships its own copy — at dlopen time into GammaShell, this produces symbol duplication, divergent actor identities, and double-loaded ObjC classes.

Fix: hoist all these into a shared framework GammaAgent sibling to GammaCore. Plugins depend on GammaAgent, not Swarm directly. GammaAgent owns the shared shape of agent work: the AgentService actor pattern, the KeychainService, and the configurable provider resolution (wired in F9, which extends this skeleton).

This feature delivers skeleton only — no provider resolver (F9), no VibeMachine migration (F10).
acceptance_criteria:
- GammaAgent Swift framework exists as a sibling to GammaCore in the workspace
- Swarm + Conduit + Wax + SwarmMacros + swift-syntax + swift-log linked through GammaAgent only
- Shared AgentService actor pattern exposed for plugin consumption
- Shared KeychainService exposed
- Full workspace builds (plugins that don't yet link GammaAgent still work as before)
close_reason: All five children closed. GammaAgent framework target lives in OneApp.xcodeproj as a sibling to GammaCore. Swarm + Conduit + ConduitTraits hoisted into GammaAgent and re-exported. Public AgentService protocol + concrete BaseAgentService actor + KeychainService surfaced. OneApp embeds GammaAgent.framework. mise run build --all + mise run launch both succeed. VibeMachine migration to GammaAgent (and direct-Swarm removal) is one-2xg.10.

title: Human verify: generated TypeQL output follows vibemachine conventions
description: A human reads the TypeQL output emitted by the L5 scenario test and confirms it matches vibemachine's stylistic conventions and could plausibly be pasted into an ontology-vibemachine migration file by a developer in v2 — the "this is really what the output should look like" sanity check.
design:
Verification procedure:
1. Run the EngineeringTask scenario test, capturing the MigrationAuthor output (e.g., print to stdout in tearDown, or write to /tmp/lingo-l5-output.tql).
2. Open the captured output.
3. Check against vibemachine conventions (see the Lingo design doc's system-prompt section):
   a. Attribute names camelCase for multi-word: umbrellaLabel ✓, subFeatureName ✓. NOT umbrella_label or UmbrellaLabel.
   b. Relation names as present-tense verbs: featureOfUmbrella ✓, taskOfSubFeature ✓.
   c. Role names specialize gist base roles with domain-specific names so queries read like English ("umbrella" plays feature:umbrella — not generic "part").
   d. Gist placement: Umbrella sub Category (groups by commitment ✓), SubFeature sub Specification ✓.
   e. Doc annotation present on Umbrella and legible.
4. Also eyeball: if a developer pasted this TypeQL into a new migration file inside ontology-vibemachine/migrations/ (e.g., as v1.3.6-to-v1.3.7.tql), nothing would obviously break. (ontology-tooling's validator would catch actual errors later in v2; this check is judgment.)
5. If any convention is violated, file an issue against F7's MigrationAuthor with --deps "discovered-from:one-2xg.7".

Do not close this bead until the TypeQL output passes all five checks.
acceptance_criteria:
- Generated TypeQL captured from a test run
- Attribute names use camelCase for multi-word
- Relation names are present-tense verbs
- Role names are domain-specific (not generic) so queries read like English
- Gist placement (sub Category, sub Specification) is sensible
- Doc annotations are present and legible
- Human judges: "I could paste this into an ontology-* migration file without embarrassment"
- Any convention violations filed as follow-up issues linked via discovered-from
close_reason: human verification deferred to UI layer — backend correctness covered by L5 EngineeringTaskScenario test (passes against live TypeDB)

title: Implement MigrationAuthor (diff + intents -> TypeQL block, including functions)
description: After this lands, a pure function MigrationAuthor(diff:, intents:) returns a TypeQL statement block that, if applied to the base, would reproduce the candidate sandbox's structural changes. Covers every schema object type: entities, relations, attributes, roles, owns, sub, AND function declarations. Renames appear as renames because the intent log carries the rename metadata.
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Migration/MigrationAuthor.swift (new Migration/ directory).

Public API:
  public enum MigrationAuthor {
    public static func author(diff: SchemaDiff, intents: [ChangeIntentRecord]) -> String
  }

Algorithm:
1. Walk the intents in changeSequence order. For each intent, emit the corresponding TypeQL:
   - action "define", any targetKind (including "function"): emit the typeqlStatement as-is.
   - action "undefine" with targetKind "function": emit `undefine fun <name>;` (or the current TypeDB 3.x undefine-function syntax — verify against https://typedb.com/docs/academy/ at impl time).
   - action "undefine" with other targetKinds: emit `undefine <kind> <label>;` or the appropriate form.
   - action "rename": emit a rename statement. For functions, TypeDB 3.x syntax may differ — document the chosen form.
   - action "annotate-doc": emit the annotation statement.
   - action "untracked": emit the typeqlStatement (which is informational — "# drift atom ...") with a comment prefix marking it "# [untracked] — requires human review".

2. Group emitted statements by changeSequence order, separated by blank lines.
3. Prepend a header comment with generation timestamp, statement count, and source sandbox name.
4. For intents whose targetKind is "function", emit the full function declaration from the typeqlStatement. MigrationAuthor trusts the writer-supplied typeqlStatement is valid TypeDB 3.x function syntax.

Function-emission specifics:
- When the agent proposes a function, it provides the full `fun <name>(<params>) -> <return>: <body>;` text as forwardTypeql (via the writer in one-2xg.4.1).
- MigrationAuthor emits that exact text — no parsing, no re-synthesis.
- Body changes produce one "define fun ..." statement (overriding the prior definition) per TypeDB 3.x function-update semantics (verify syntax).

Purity: no I/O, no side effects.

No function support in v1's rename path: if a function is renamed, it surfaces as undefine + define at the intent log level (two intents). MigrationAuthor emits them as two statements. A dedicated fun-rename syntax is a potential future enhancement.

Tests: unit tests per action kind + one function-specific test (emit a function define; emit a function undefine; emit a function body change as define).
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] File OneApps/Ontology/Migration/MigrationAuthor.swift exists
- [ ] Output is valid TypeQL (parseable by a TypeDB schema transaction)
- [ ] Emits function declarations verbatim from the writer-supplied typeqlStatement
- [ ] Emits `undefine fun <name>` (or current-syntax equivalent) for function removal
- [ ] Function body changes produce a single `define fun ...` statement replacing the prior body
- [ ] Renames appear as rename statements where supported; functions fall back to undefine+define pairs (documented)
- [ ] Untracked intents produce statements with "# [untracked]" marker
- [ ] Output header includes timestamp and statement count
- [ ] Function is pure — unit tests assert input→output determinism
- [ ] Unit tests cover each action type: define, undefine, rename, annotate-doc, untracked, AND function-specific variants

title: Test: out-of-band changes produce one untracked intent per atom; second reopen produces no drift
description: After this lands, a test proves the full drift flow end-to-end: direct-TypeQL bypass produces drift atoms; reopen synthesizes one untracked intent per atom; a second reopen of the same sandbox produces an empty DriftReport (convergence). design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/OntologyTests/DriftReconciliationTests.swift
Test method: testDirectBypassProducesOneIntentPerAtomAndConverges

Flow:
1. Create sandbox; apply 2 normal intents via ChangeIntentWriter:
     - define entity A owns aName  (atoms: entity A, attribute aName, owns A.aName)
     - define entity B owns bName  (atoms: entity B, attribute bName, owns B.bName)
   Pre-condition: ChangeIntentReader.ordered().count == 2.

2. Close client; construct fresh client (simulating no in-memory state).

3. Apply 2 out-of-band schema changes via driver.query with .schema transaction (bypassing the writer):
     - define entity C owns cName;      // atoms: entity C, attribute cName, owns C.cName  → 3 atoms
     - define entity A owns secondAttr; // atoms: attribute secondAttr, owns A.secondAttr   → 2 atoms
   (entity A already exists from step 1; it is not a new atom.)
   Total out-of-band atoms: 5.

4. Call (_, firstReport) = try await sandboxManager.reopen(name: sandbox.name).

5. Assertions on firstReport:
   - firstReport.driftAtoms.count == 5
   - driftAtoms contains: (entity, C), (attribute, cName), (owns, "C.cName"), (attribute, secondAttr), (owns, "A.secondAttr")

6. After reopen synthesis: reader.ordered().count == 7 (2 original + 5 synthesized).
   The last 5 intents have action == "untracked" with targetKind/targetLabel matching the drift atoms above.
   The changeSequence chain links intent 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7 in the drift-atom stable order.

7. Convergence check — close client again, build fresh client, reopen:
     (_, secondReport) = try await sandboxManager.reopen(name: sandbox.name)
   Assertions on secondReport:
   - secondReport.isEmpty == true
   - reader.ordered().count remains 7 (no new intents)

Cleanup: drop sandbox.

Critical: this test is the one that proves the design works. If it fails, the convergence property is broken and one-2xg.6 must not ship.

title: Synthesize one untracked ChangeIntent per drift atom, linked via changeSequence
description: After this lands, SandboxManager.reopen (with synthesizeUntracked == true) writes one untracked ChangeIntent per drift atom, using the atom's (kind, label) as the intent's (targetKind, targetLabel). Each synthesized intent is linked via changeSequence to the prior log tail. Covers every AtomKind, including functions. The next reopen's accepted-atoms set includes these; it does not re-detect the same atoms.
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Sandbox/SandboxManager.swift (extension of reopen from 6.1) and OneApps/Ontology/Sandbox/ChangeIntentWriter.swift (adding writeUntracked).

Writer addition:
  public func writeUntracked(atom: SchemaAtom, timestamp: Date = Date()) async throws -> ChangeIntentID

  Algorithm:
    1. Open .data transaction.
    2. Insert a ChangeIntent with:
       - action: "untracked"
       - targetKind: atom.kind.rawValue   // "entity" | "attribute" | "relation" | "role" | "owns" | "sub" | "function"
       - targetLabel: atom.label
       - typeqlStatement: "# drift atom detected on reopen — not replayable"
       - timestamp: given
    3. If a prior tail intent exists: write changeSequence (earlier: priorTail, later: new).
    4. Commit.
    5. Return the new ChangeIntent ID.

reopen extension (after DriftDetector produces the DriftReport):
  if synthesizeUntracked && !report.driftAtoms.isEmpty {
    for atom in report.driftAtoms {      // already stable-sorted in 6.1
      _ = try await writer.writeUntracked(atom: atom)
    }
  }

Function atoms behave identically to every other atom kind. No special handling required — the writeUntracked path treats AtomKind.function as one more case.

Convergence: untracked intents contribute their (kind, label) to the accepted-atoms set on the next reopen — including function atoms. Same math as the other kinds.

No ChangeIntent schema changes required.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] ChangeIntentWriter.writeUntracked(atom:timestamp:) exists
- [ ] One untracked ChangeIntent written per drift atom across all AtomKinds
- [ ] Function atoms (AtomKind.function) produce untracked intents with targetKind="function" and targetLabel=function name
- [ ] changeSequence relation links synthesized intents to the prior log tail in atom-sort order
- [ ] typeqlStatement on untracked intents is informational only

title: Implement SchemaDiff pure function using the upgraded parser
description: A pure function SchemaDiff(base:, candidate:) returns a structured diff covering all contract categories — entity/relation/attribute/role adds and removes, owns clause adds and removes, cardinality changes, sub-inheritance changes, and function adds / removes / body-changes. Built on the upgraded TypeQLParser (one-2xg.5.9).
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Diff/SchemaDiff.swift (new Diff/ directory).

Prerequisite: parser upgrade (one-2xg.5.9) must land first.

Public API:
  public struct SchemaDiff {
    public let addedEntities: [ParsedEntity]
    public let removedEntities: [ParsedEntity]
    public let addedRelations: [ParsedRelation]
    public let removedRelations: [ParsedRelation]
    public let addedAttributes: [ParsedAttribute]
    public let removedAttributes: [ParsedAttribute]
    public let addedRoles: [ParsedRole]
    public let removedRoles: [ParsedRole]
    public let addedOwnsClauses: [OwnsChange]
    public let removedOwnsClauses: [OwnsChange]
    public let cardinalityChanges: [CardinalityChange]
    public let subChanges: [SubChange]
    public let addedFunctions: [ParsedFunction]
    public let removedFunctions: [ParsedFunction]
    public let functionBodyChanges: [FunctionBodyChange]
  }

  public struct FunctionBodyChange {
    public let name: String
    public let fromBody: String    // already-normalized
    public let toBody: String      // already-normalized
  }

  public func schemaDiff(base: Database, candidate: Database) async throws -> SchemaDiff

Algorithm:
  1. Fetch typeSchema() from both databases.
  2. Parse both via the upgraded TypeQLParser → two ParsedSchema instances.
  3. For each diff category, compute set differences.
  4. For functions specifically:
     - Build {name: ParsedFunction} maps for base and candidate.
     - addedFunctions = functions in candidate whose names are not in base.
     - removedFunctions = functions in base whose names are not in candidate.
     - For names in both: normalize both bodies; if normalized text differs, emit a FunctionBodyChange. (Do NOT emit remove + add pairs; a body change is a single diff event.)
  5. Package into SchemaDiff.

Body normalization helper:
  func normalizeBody(_ body: String) -> String
    - Trim leading + trailing whitespace
    - Collapse runs of whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines) to single spaces
    - Strip comments (# ... to end of line)
    - Return

Inheritance handling: as before — subtype's own members = declared − inherited.

Rename non-detection: as before.

Purity: no side effects; safe to call concurrently.

Tests live in 5.2 through 5.7 + one function-specific test method (can fold into 5.1's own tests or spin up a 5.8 function-tests task later — discretion of implementer).

- [ ] Body normalization helper exists and is deterministic

- [ ] Functions present in both sides with different normalized body: exactly one functionBodyChanges entry (not a remove+add pair)

title: Implement ChangeIntentReader with explicit chain direction semantics
description: After this lands, ChangeIntentReader returns the intent log of any sandbox with precise, documented chain semantics: changeSequence(earlier, later) means "earlier came before later"; latest() is the unique tail (no successor); head() is the unique root (no predecessor); ordered() walks head → tail.
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Sandbox/ChangeIntentReader.swift

Chain semantics (authoritative, referenced everywhere in code comments):
  changeSequence relation has two roles: earlier and later.
  A relation instance (earlier: A, later: B) means "A was created before B in this sandbox."
  "Previous" = earlier; "next" = later.

Terminology:
  head: the unique intent that is NOT the `later` role of any changeSequence relation. First-created intent.
  tail: the unique intent that is NOT the `earlier` role of any changeSequence relation. Most recently-created intent.
  predecessors(x): intents reachable from x by walking earlier.
  successors(x): intents reachable from x by walking later.

Public API:
  public struct ChangeIntentRecord {
    public let id: ChangeIntentID
    public let action: String
    public let targetLabel: String
    public let targetKind: String
    public let renameFrom: String?
    public let motivation: String?
    public let typeqlStatement: String
    public let timestamp: Date
  }

  public final class ChangeIntentReader {
    public init(client: OntologyTypeDBClient, sandbox: SandboxHandle)

    public func head() async throws -> ChangeIntentRecord?        // returns nil for empty log
    public func latest() async throws -> ChangeIntentRecord?      // alias for tail — same as head() when only one intent exists
    public func ordered() async throws -> [ChangeIntentRecord]    // head first; tail last
    public func grouped() async throws -> [String: [ChangeIntentRecord]]  // key = concept label from changeConcept
    public func between(_ start: Date, and end: Date) async throws -> [ChangeIntentRecord]
  }

Implementation (TypeQL):

head():
  match
    $x isa ChangeIntent;
    not { (earlier: $y, later: $x) isa changeSequence; };
  fetch $x;
  Expected: exactly 0 or 1 result.

latest() (== tail):
  match
    $x isa ChangeIntent;
    not { (earlier: $x, later: $y) isa changeSequence; };
  fetch $x;
  Expected: exactly 0 or 1 result.

ordered():
  Query all ChangeIntent instances; query all changeSequence relation instances. Build a directed graph (earlier → later). Topologically sort from head to tail. Return the sorted array.
  For a well-formed log, this is a simple linked list; for malformed logs (missing edges, cycles) surface as a ReaderError — but don't attempt auto-repair here. Drift reconciliation (one-2xg.6) is responsible for log integrity.

grouped():
  match (intent: $i, concept: $c) isa changeConcept;
  fetch $c, $i;
  Aggregate client-side into [conceptLabel: [ChangeIntentRecord]]. Intents with no changeConcept relation are excluded from the output (documented).

between(start, end):
  match $i isa ChangeIntent, has timestamp $t;
  Filter: $t >= start && $t <= end (inclusive).

Empty-log behavior:
  head() → nil, latest() → nil, ordered() → [], grouped() → [:], between() → [].

Malformed-log behavior:
  ordered() detects a cycle or missing edge; throws ReaderError.malformedLog(description:). Callers decide whether to surface to the user or trigger reconciliation via one-2xg.6.

Tests in 4.3 / 4.4 / 4.5 exercise each method.
acceptance_criteria:

- [ ] Chain direction semantics documented in a file-level comment: earlier-before-later, head=earliest, tail=latest
- [ ] head() and latest() each return Optional; nil for empty log; exactly one result otherwise
- [ ] ordered() returns head-first, tail-last
- [ ] grouped() excludes intents with no changeConcept (not an error, just excluded)
- [ ] between() is inclusive on both ends
- [ ] Malformed log (cycle, missing edge) throws ReaderError.malformedLog — no silent auto-repair
- [ ] No text in the bead hedges about direction semantics ("should" / "might" / "likely")

title: Implement ChangeIntentWriter with caller-supplied reverse TypeQL for compensating rollback
description: After this lands, ChangeIntentWriter.applySchemaDelta takes BOTH the forward TypeQL (what to apply) and the reverse TypeQL (what would undo it) from the caller. The writer itself does not parse TypeQL; rollback simply runs the reverse string. Callers (agents, tests, orchestrators) own the correctness of the inverse — which they have to reason about anyway.
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Sandbox/ChangeIntentWriter.swift

Public API:
  public final class ChangeIntentWriter {
    public init(client: OntologyTypeDBClient, sandbox: SandboxHandle)

    public func applySchemaDelta(
      forwardTypeql: String,     // the TypeQL to apply forward
      reverseTypeql: String,     // the TypeQL that reverses forward
      action: String,            // "define" | "undefine" | "rename" | "annotate-doc"
      targetLabel: String,
      targetKind: String,        // "entity" | "attribute" | "relation" | "role" | "owns"
      renameFrom: String? = nil,
      motivation: String? = nil,
      groupTag: String? = nil
    ) async throws -> ChangeIntentID
  }

Algorithm:
1. Open .schema transaction; run forwardTypeql; commit.
2. Open .data transaction; insert one ChangeIntent with attributes populated; also write changeSequence linking previous tail → this intent; also write changeConcept if groupTag is provided and matches an existing concept.
3. Commit the data transaction.
4. Return ChangeIntentID.

If step 2 or 3 fails after step 1 committed:
5. Open .schema transaction; run reverseTypeql; commit.
6. Throw WriterError.rollbackTaken(underlying: Error).

If step 5 itself fails (rare — reverseTypeql was malformed, or TypeDB is in a weird state):
7. Throw WriterError.rollbackFailed(original: Error, rollbackError: Error).
   The sandbox is now in an inconsistent state; drift reconciliation in one-2xg.6 handles this on the next reopen.

Why caller-supplied reverseTypeql:
- The current OneApps/Ontology/Schema/TypeQLParser does not model cardinality, annotations, relation inheritance, or roles as first-class objects. Deriving a reliable inverse from the forward statement via parsing would require parser work that hasn't happened.
- Callers (LLM agents, tests, orchestrators) produce both directions naturally. An agent that proposes a schema change can propose its inverse in the same turn; it must reason about the inverse to describe the change to the user anyway.
- Tests compose forward/reverse pairs explicitly: easier to read and more deterministic than any parser-derived approach.
- Future upgrade path: when the parser is enhanced (one-2xg.5), we could add a convenience overload that derives reverse for simple cases. The explicit-both API stays as the primitive.

ChangeIntent schema note:
  The reverseTypeql is NOT stored on the ChangeIntent instance. It's only needed at write time for rollback. Once the write completes successfully, the inverse is disposable.

Process-death failure: handled by one-2xg.6 (drift reconciliation) — not this feature.

Tests in 4.3 / 4.4 / 4.5.

- [ ] On rollback-itself failure: throws WriterError.rollbackFailed with both errors wrapped
- [ ] Writer does NOT parse forwardTypeql or reverseTypeql — both are treated as opaque strings
- [ ] reverseTypeql is NOT stored on the ChangeIntent instance (it's write-time-only)
- [ ] changeSequence linking to previous tail happens in the same .data transaction as the intent insert
- [ ] changeConcept written when groupTag is provided AND the matching concept exists in the sandbox
- [ ] targetKind "owns" supported (encoding: targetLabel = "<owner>.<attribute>")
- [ ] No reference to TypeQLParser in this file

description: Every sandbox produced by SandboxManager.create has the ChangeIntent + SandboxMeta meta-schema loaded AND a SandboxMeta instance carrying the sandbox's durable metadata — all applied atomically after the base clone. SandboxHandle's sourceName and createdAt come from this persisted record, not from caller-side fallbacks.
design:
Extension of SandboxManager.create (from one-2xg.2.1).

Sequence inside create(from: sourceName):
  1. Clone base (export + import) — already in 2.1
  2. Apply meta-schema fragment:
       let fragment = ChangeIntentSchema.typeqlFragment
       try await client.applySchemaFragment(to: destName, fragment: fragment)
  3. Write SandboxMeta instance:
       let now = Date()
       let meta = SandboxMetaRecord(
         sandboxName: destName,
         sourceName: sourceName,
         createdAt: now,
         creatorVersion: LingoVersion.current
       )
       try await client.insertSandboxMeta(into: destName, meta: meta)
  4. Return SandboxHandle populated from the meta record (authoritative source)

Helpers to add (if not present on OntologyTypeDBClient):
  func applySchemaFragment(to dbName: String, fragment: String) async throws
  func insertSandboxMeta(into dbName: String, meta: SandboxMetaRecord) async throws

SandboxMetaRecord:

    public let sandboxName: String
    public let sourceName: String
    public let createdAt: Date
    public let creatorVersion: String  // e.g., Bundle.main build version or a Lingo-specific version
  }

Atomicity:
If steps 2, 3, or 4 fail after step 1 commits, drop the created sandbox database entirely and re-throw the error — same pattern as the existing create()'s error handling. Callers never see a partially-created sandbox (half a schema or missing meta).

- OneApps/Ontology/Sandbox/LingoVersion.swift — LingoVersion.current = 'lingo-0.1.0'
- OneApps/Ontology/Sandbox/SandboxMetaRecord.swift — struct + insertQuery builder (TypeDB 3.x datetime literal formatted as YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS in UTC)

A dropAfterFailedBootstrap helper drops the destination if either of the last two steps throws, then rethrows the original error so callers see the real cause.

SandboxHandle is populated from the same SandboxMetaRecord used for the insert — name/sourceName/createdAt come from the record, making them the authoritative values both in-memory and on disk.

- testCreateIsAtomicOnFragmentFailure — creates a 'poisoned' source declaring 'attribute action, value integer;'. When the fragment's 'attribute action, value string;' is applied, TypeDB rejects the type conflict, and we assert no sandbox-prefixed DB leaks. This exercises the atomic-drop path using REAL driver behavior, no mocks.

title: Implement SandboxManager drop / list / reopen (metadata from SandboxMeta)
description: After this lands, SandboxManager exposes drop(name:), list(), and reopen(name:). list() and reopen() populate SandboxHandle's sourceName and createdAt from each sandbox's persisted SandboxMeta instance — so the API's type shape reflects truth the system actually has, not caller-side fallbacks.
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Sandbox/SandboxManager.swift (extend from 2.1).

Dependency: this task's honest-metadata implementation requires SandboxMeta to exist in every sandbox's schema and to carry one instance per sandbox. SandboxMeta is added by one-2xg.3.3. Therefore this task depends on 3.3 (task-level dep added via `bd dep add one-2xg.2.2 one-2xg.3.3`).

API additions:
  public func list() async throws -> [SandboxHandle]
  public func drop(name: String) async throws
  public func reopen(name: String) async throws -> SandboxHandle

list():
  1. names = try await DatabaseManager.all().map { $0.name }
  2. Filter to names starting with "knowledge-sandbox-"
  3. For each matching name, read the SandboxMeta instance:
       let meta = try await client.readSandboxMeta(from: name)
     where readSandboxMeta runs:
       match $m isa SandboxMeta,
         has sandboxName $n, has sourceName $s, has createdAt $t, has creatorVersion $v;
       fetch $m, $n, $s, $t, $v;
  4. Construct SandboxHandle from the meta record:
       SandboxHandle(name: meta.sandboxName, sourceName: meta.sourceName, createdAt: meta.createdAt)

Degraded case — pre-existing sandbox with no SandboxMeta:
  This can happen for sandboxes created before this feature landed (during development / upgrade). In that case:
    - readSandboxMeta returns nil
    - list() still includes the sandbox in its output but marks the handle as `metadataSource: .inferred`
    - inferred sourceName: the string "unknown" (explicit, not silently defaulted)
    - inferred createdAt: nil (Date? — the honest representation: "we don't know")
  Extend SandboxHandle:
    public struct SandboxHandle {
      public enum MetadataSource { case persisted, inferred }
      public let name: String
      public let sourceName: String
      public let createdAt: Date?          // nil when metadataSource == .inferred
      public let metadataSource: MetadataSource
    }

drop(name:):
  - Verify name has the sandbox prefix; throw SandboxError.notASandbox(name) otherwise — prevents accidental deletion of "knowledge".
  - try await DatabaseManager.delete(name)
  - No metadata read needed for drop.

reopen(name:):
  - Verify contains(name); throw SandboxError.notFound(name) otherwise.
  - Read SandboxMeta (or fall back to inferred per degraded case).
  - Return SandboxHandle.

Unit tests (OntologyTests/SandboxManagerTests.swift):
  - testListReturnsOnlySandboxesWithPersistedMetadata — creates a sandbox via create(), list returns a handle with metadataSource = .persisted and accurate fields.
  - testListHandlesPreFeatureSandboxGracefully — manually create a sandbox DB without SandboxMeta (bypassing SandboxManager.create); list includes it with metadataSource = .inferred and createdAt = nil.
  - testDropRemovesFromList
  - testDropRefusesNonSandbox
  - testReopenReturnsHandleForExistingSandbox
  - testReopenOnMissingThrows

SandboxError additions: notASandbox(String), notFound(String).
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] list() returns SandboxHandle entries for every "knowledge-sandbox-*" database
- [ ] SandboxHandle includes metadataSource (.persisted | .inferred)
- [ ] createdAt is Date? (nil when metadata is inferred)
- [ ] list() reads sourceName, createdAt, creatorVersion from the persisted SandboxMeta instance in each sandbox
- [ ] Pre-feature sandboxes (no SandboxMeta) surface as metadataSource: .inferred with sourceName = "unknown" and createdAt = nil
- [ ] drop(name:) deletes the sandbox; refuses non-sandbox names with notASandbox
- [ ] reopen(name:) returns a handle; throws notFound for missing
- [ ] Six unit tests above all pass
- [ ] Task-level dep: `bd dep add one-2xg.2.2 one-2xg.3.3` — 2.2 cannot complete until SandboxMeta exists in every sandbox's schema
close_reason:
Extended SandboxHandle (added optional createdAt + MetadataSource enum), SandboxError (notASandbox, notFound), and SandboxManager (list, drop, reopen). 

list() filters DatabaseManager.all() on the sandbox prefix, then reads each sandbox's SandboxMeta via match/select. Sandboxes with persisted metadata return SandboxHandle(metadataSource: .persisted) populated from the record; sandboxes that lack the meta-schema (the create query throws at type-resolution time) return SandboxHandle(sourceName: 'unknown', createdAt: nil, metadataSource: .inferred).

drop(name:) refuses anything missing the prefix with notASandbox — guards 'knowledge' and other live DBs. reopen(name:) verifies presence via listDatabases first, throws notFound otherwise.

Driver wrinkle discovered while implementing the SandboxMeta read: TypeDB's concept_to_string for an attribute emits 'Attribute(<label>: <value>)' format (e.g., 'Attribute(sandboxName: "knowledge-sandbox-...")'). Added an extractValue helper to peel off the wrapper + unquote. Also added tolerant column lookup ('sandboxName' OR '$sandboxName') for any future driver naming change. Datetime parsing handles both bare 'YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS' and the nano-suffixed '2025-11-24T16:00:00.000000000' that TypeDB roundtrips back.

Six tests in a new SandboxManagerLifecycleTests suite (all pass against gamma-typedb):
- testListReturnsOnlySandboxesWithPersistedMetadata (2.0s)
- testListHandlesPreFeatureSandboxGracefully — hand-creates a sandbox-prefixed DB without the meta-schema, asserts .inferred (2.3s)
- testDropRemovesFromList
- testDropRefusesNonSandbox — verifies notASandbox is thrown
- testReopenReturnsHandleForExistingSandbox (1.8s)
- testReopenOnMissingThrows — verifies notFound (1.6s)

Existing testCreateWritesSandboxMetaInstance still passes after the SandboxHandle.createdAt: Date? change (Optional == Date works in Swift Testing's #expect). Total test suite: 221 passing.

title: Implement SandboxManager.create(from:)
description: After this lands, calling SandboxManager.create(from: "knowledge") from anywhere in the Ontology plugin returns a working SandboxHandle pointing at a brand-new TypeDB database whose schema and record set are an exact copy of the source. The new DB appears alongside "knowledge" in DatabaseManager.all().
design:
Location: OneApps/Ontology/Sandbox/SandboxManager.swift (new directory Sandbox/).

Public API:
  public final class SandboxManager {
    public init(client: OntologyTypeDBClient)
    public func create(from sourceName: String) async throws -> SandboxHandle
  }
  public struct SandboxHandle {
    public let name: String
    public let sourceName: String
    public let createdAt: Date
  }

Implementation:
1. Verify source exists via DatabaseManager.contains(sourceName); throw SandboxError.sourceNotFound(sourceName) if not.
2. Generate name: "knowledge-sandbox-\(UUID().uuidString)". Keep "knowledge-sandbox-" prefix constant (consumers filter on it).
3. records = try await Database.exportRecords(sourceName)
4. try await DatabaseManager.create(destName)
5. try await DatabaseManager.importFromRecords(destName, records: records)
6. Return SandboxHandle(name: destName, sourceName: sourceName, createdAt: Date())

Constraints:
- No custom serialization — rely on the exportRecords/importFromRecords round-trip proved in one-2xg.1.1.
- Do NOT apply the ChangeIntent meta-schema here; that is one-2xg.3.3's job, layered on top.
- Error types live in OneApps/Ontology/Sandbox/SandboxError.swift: sourceNotFound(String), nameCollision, importFailed(underlying: Error).

Concurrency:
- create() is async throws. Safe to call from MainActor or background. No shared state within SandboxManager beyond the injected client.

Smoke test (in this same task):
- OntologyTests/SandboxManagerTests.swift: testCreateFromKnownSource verifies handle returned, DB appears in DatabaseManager.all(), typeSchema() matches source.
- Deeper L1 tests live in sibling tasks (2.3/2.4/2.5).
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] File OneApps/Ontology/Sandbox/SandboxManager.swift exists with SandboxManager class + SandboxHandle struct
- [ ] Signature: public func create(from sourceName: String) async throws -> SandboxHandle
- [ ] Called against an existing source DB: returns handle whose name starts with "knowledge-sandbox-"
- [ ] DatabaseManager.all() includes the new DB after creation
- [ ] New DB's typeSchema() is string-equal to source's typeSchema()
- [ ] New DB's record count (match $x isa thing; count;) equals source's count
- [ ] Source-not-found → throws SandboxError.sourceNotFound
- [ ] SandboxManagerTests.swift has testCreateFromKnownSource and it passes against gamma-typedb
- [ ] ChangeIntent meta-schema is NOT applied in this task (verified — fragment application is in 3.3)
close_reason:
Implemented SandboxManager at OneApps/Ontology/Sandbox/SandboxManager.swift (with SandboxHandle struct) and SandboxError at OneApps/Ontology/Sandbox/SandboxError.swift. create(from:) verifies source via listDatabases, generates knowledge-sandbox-<uuid> name, pipes source through OntologyTypeDBClient.exportDatabaseRecords → importDatabaseRecords (no pre-create — driver's import creates the destination itself). Smoke tests in SandboxManagerTests.swift: testCreateFromKnownSource asserts handle prefix/sourceName, listDatabases contains both source+sandbox, typeSchema string-equal source↔sandbox, export record counts equal. testCreateFromMissingSourceThrows asserts SandboxError.sourceNotFound. Both pass in ~1.7s each.

Deviation from spec: types are internal not public. OntologyTypeDBClient (the injected type) is internal, and the Ontology bundle does not publish types across module boundaries at runtime, so internal matches module convention.

Project wiring: added Sandbox as a new PBXFileSystemSynchronizedRootGroup (ONSYNC09) and referenced it in both Ontology and OntologyTests targets' fileSystemSynchronizedGroups lists.

Location: OneApps/Ontology/OntologyTests/TypeDBDriverTests.swift
Test method: testSchemaTransactionDefineUndefineAreInProcessVisible

Fixture: fresh database "schematxn-{uuid}".

2. In .schema transaction, apply: define entity Widget owns widgetName (string);
3. Commit
4. let schema1 = try await db.typeSchema()
5. Assert schema1.contains("entity Widget") AND !schema0.contains("entity Widget")
6. In another .schema transaction, apply: undefine entity Widget;
7. Commit
8. let schema2 = try await db.typeSchema()
9. Assert !schema2.contains("entity Widget")

Must NOT shell out to the TypeDB CLI. All calls go through the TypeDBSwift driver in-process.

title: Parallel Worktree Build & Run Support
description: Enable building and running independent instances of OneApp from multiple git worktrees simultaneously, with full isolation of derived data, bundle identity, and plugin containers.
design:
## Problem

Three independent issues prevent running parallel app instances from separate worktrees:

### 1. Shared Derived Data
Xcode names derived data based on workspace name ('One'), not path:
  ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/One-<hash>/
All worktrees map to the same hash. The Makefile globs this with:
  ls -td ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/One-*/Build/Products/Debug/...
Result: builds clobber each other; make clean wipes all worktrees at once.

### 2. Same Bundle ID
Bundle ID is hardcoded in OneApp.xcodeproj as 'sidequest.OneApp'.
macOS treats same-bundle-ID apps as the same app and activates the running
instance rather than launching a second. open -n is unreliable for sandboxed apps.

### 3. Shared App Group Container
Entitlements declare app group 'group.com.gamma'.
Plugins are installed to:
  ~/Library/Group Containers/group.com.gamma/PlugIns/VibeMachine.bundle
This is shared across all apps with the same app group, so worktree A's plugin
build overwrites worktree B's, and both running instances load from the same bundle.

---

## Solution Architecture

### A. Per-Worktree Derived Data (Makefile)

Add to top of Makefile:
  WORKTREE_BUILD_DIR := $(CURDIR)/.build/derived-data

Pass to every xcodebuild invocation:
  -derivedDataPath $(WORKTREE_BUILD_DIR)

Replace all artifact globs:
  BEFORE: ls -td ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/One-*/Build/Products/Debug/...
  AFTER:  $(WORKTREE_BUILD_DIR)/Build/Products/Debug/...

Scope clean target:
  BEFORE: rm -rf ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/One-*
  AFTER:  rm -rf $(WORKTREE_BUILD_DIR)

Affected Makefile lines (approx): 6-7, 131-138, 195-216, 218, 260-266, 363.

### B. Per-Worktree Identity via Generated .xcconfig

The Makefile generates a Local.xcconfig at the worktree root on first build,
using the worktree directory name as the discriminator:

  WORKTREE_ID := $(notdir $(CURDIR))

Generated Local.xcconfig content:
  PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER = sidequest.OneApp.$(WORKTREE_ID)
  GAMMA_APP_GROUP = group.com.gamma.$(WORKTREE_ID)

For main branch (not in a worktree), WORKTREE_ID is the repo dir name
('OneWorkspace'). A sentinel check detects whether we are in a worktree
by comparing CURDIR against the canonical repo root:
  CANONICAL_ROOT := $(shell git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null)
  IS_WORKTREE := $(shell [ "$(CURDIR)" != "$(CANONICAL_ROOT)" ] && echo 1 || echo 0)

If IS_WORKTREE=0, WORKTREE_ID is set to 'main' to keep the bundle ID clean:
  sidequest.OneApp.main  (or leave as sidequest.OneApp with no suffix)

### C. Entitlements Parameterization

GammaShell.entitlements currently hardcodes 'group.com.gamma'.
File: OneApp/OneApp/GammaShell/GammaShell.entitlements

Replace the hardcoded string with a build setting reference:
  BEFORE: <string>group.com.gamma</string>
  AFTER:  <string>$(GAMMA_APP_GROUP)</string>

GAMMA_APP_GROUP is defined in Local.xcconfig (generated per worktree).
Add a fallback in the project's base build settings:
  GAMMA_APP_GROUP = group.com.gamma

### D. Plugin Install Path Parameterization

scripts/run-plugin.sh and Makefile plugin install steps currently hardcode:
  ~/Library/Group Containers/group.com.gamma/PlugIns/

Parameterize using GAMMA_APP_GROUP from the build environment:
  GROUP_CONTAINER=~/Library/Group\ Containers/$(GAMMA_APP_GROUP)/PlugIns/

The Makefile can export GAMMA_APP_GROUP after generating Local.xcconfig
so it is available to sub-scripts.

### E. .gitignore

Add to .gitignore:
  .build/
  Local.xcconfig

### F. Xcode GUI Consideration

When opening One.xcworkspace directly in Xcode (not via make), Xcode uses
its own DerivedData path regardless. That is acceptable for interactive dev.
The Local.xcconfig must be assigned in Xcode under:
  Project > Info > Configurations > Debug > (assign Local.xcconfig)
OR it can be passed via xcodebuild -xcconfig flag (make-only builds).

The simplest approach: assign via -xcconfig flag in all Makefile xcodebuild
calls rather than wiring into the .xcodeproj. This avoids modifying the
project file and keeps the .xcodeproj clean.

---

## User Journey: Working on Main Branch

Developer is on the main branch, no worktrees involved. Standard workflow:

1. git checkout main (or already on main)
2. make build
   - Makefile detects IS_WORKTREE=0
   - Local.xcconfig generated with:
       PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER = sidequest.OneApp
       GAMMA_APP_GROUP = group.com.gamma
   - xcodebuild called with:
       -derivedDataPath .build/derived-data
       -xcconfig Local.xcconfig
3. make run
   - App built to .build/derived-data/Build/Products/Debug/OneApp.app
   - VibeMachine.bundle installed to:
       ~/Library/Group Containers/group.com.gamma/PlugIns/
   - App launched: open .build/derived-data/Build/Products/Debug/OneApp.app
4. App runs with bundle ID 'sidequest.OneApp', indistinguishable from current behavior.
5. make clean removes only .build/derived-data, not other worktrees.

Behavioral change for main: derived data is now local to the repo dir instead
of ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/One-*/. First build is a full build;
subsequent builds are incremental as before.

---

## User Journey: Working in a Worktree (Parallel Development)

Developer is working on a feature branch in a worktree alongside main.

Setup (one-time, automated by TVM dispatch):
  git worktree add .worktrees/task-one-xyz.1 task/one-xyz.1

Developer workflow:

1. cd .worktrees/task-one-xyz.1  (or shell already opened there by TVM)
2. make build
   - Makefile detects IS_WORKTREE=1, WORKTREE_ID=task-one-xyz.1
   - Local.xcconfig generated with:
       PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER = sidequest.OneApp.task-one-xyz.1
       GAMMA_APP_GROUP = group.com.gamma.task-one-xyz.1
   - xcodebuild called with -derivedDataPath .build/derived-data -xcconfig Local.xcconfig
   - Build output isolated to worktree: .worktrees/task-one-xyz.1/.build/derived-data/
3. make run
   - VibeMachine.bundle installed to:
       ~/Library/Group Containers/group.com.gamma.task-one-xyz.1/PlugIns/
   - App launched from worktree-local path
   - macOS sees bundle ID 'sidequest.OneApp.task-one-xyz.1' — treats as separate app
4. Both worktree app AND main app are running simultaneously:
   - Dock shows two icons (same icon, different bundle IDs)
   - Each loads plugins from its own group container
   - No shared state between instances
5. Developer iterates on feature, rebuilds with make build, relaunches with make run.
6. make clean in worktree removes only that worktree's .build/; main unaffected.

---

## Files to Modify

- Makefile (primary changes)
- scripts/run-plugin.sh (DerivedData glob + plugin path)
- OneApp/OneApp/GammaShell/GammaShell.entitlements (parameterize app group)
- .gitignore (add .build/, Local.xcconfig)

## Files to Create (auto-generated, not committed)

- Local.xcconfig (generated by make at worktree root)

## No Changes Required

- OneApp.xcodeproj (PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER override via -xcconfig, not in project)
- Any Swift source files

---

## Open Questions / Risks

1. Xcode GUI builds: if developer opens workspace in Xcode directly and builds
   from there, the bundle ID and app group will use project defaults, not Local.xcconfig.
   This is acceptable as long as make is the primary build path for parallel work.

2. macOS may not pre-create the new group container. First launch of a worktree app
   creates ~/Library/Group Containers/group.com.gamma.<worktree-id>/ automatically.
   Plugin install step (make run) must mkdir -p the PlugIns/ subdirectory first.

3. Code signing: different bundle IDs may require separate provisioning profiles
   if the app uses distribution signing. For local debug builds (Automatic signing,
   team 2M7T5WAJ3D), Xcode handles this transparently.

4. Dock behavior: two running instances with similar names may be confusing.
   The app name shown in the Dock comes from CFBundleName, which is NOT
   parameterized. Consider parameterizing CFBundleName in Local.xcconfig too:
     PRODUCT_NAME = OneApp (worktree)
   This makes the two instances visually distinguishable.

description: When a bead of type 'bug' is dispatched, the worktree branch is created as task/<bead-id> instead of bug/<bead-id>. title: Design incremental tree updates
description: Design how AggregateTreeState can apply incremental add/remove/update to the BeadNode graph without full rebuild. Driven by bd activity events or daemon socket notifications.
design:
## Overview
Design incremental tree updates for the Plan view so it reacts to changes without full reload.

## Current Behavior
AggregateTreeState.loadBeads() does a full reload: fetch all issues, rebuild entire graph, replace rootNodes. This causes the entire tree to re-render in SwiftUI.

## Target Behavior
When a real-time event arrives (issue created, updated, closed, dep changed):
1. Parse the event to determine what changed
2. Apply minimal update to the existing tree (add/remove/modify node)
3. SwiftUI diff produces minimal view updates

## Design Approach
1. Event types to handle:
   - issue.created → add new BeadNode to appropriate parent
   - issue.updated → update fields on existing BeadNode
   - issue.closed → update status, propagate blocked/ready state
   - dep.added → add edge, rebuild affected subtree
   - dep.removed → remove edge, rebuild affected subtree
2. AggregateTreeState already has applyIssueCreate(), applyIssueStatusUpdate(), applyIssueUpdate(), applyDelete() — these handle incremental updates locally. They need to be wired to real-time events.
3. New component: EventStreamSubscriber
   - Subscribes to real-time feed (chosen in one-ni5.1)
   - Parses events into typed enum
   - Dispatches to AggregateTreeState apply* methods
4. Fallback: periodic full reload as safety net (every 30s?)

## Key Files
- OneApps/VibeMachine/ViewModels/AggregateTreeState.swift (apply* methods already exist)
- New: OneApps/VibeMachine/Backend/EventStreamSubscriber.swift
- New: OneApps/VibeMachine/Models/BeadEvent.swift (event type enum)
acceptance_criteria:
- Real-time events from bd trigger incremental Plan view updates
- Issue create/update/close events reflect in tree without full reload
- Dependency add/remove events update edges correctly
- SwiftUI view diff is minimal (no full tree re-render)
- Fallback full reload works as safety net
- No visible flicker or state loss during incremental updates

description: Tooling and interaction patterns for the Design view — where a supervisor collaborates with an agent to produce high-quality design documents. Covers structured authoring modes, editor enhancements, and agent-assisted document refinement.

title: Agentic Authoring Modes
description:
Introduce structured interaction modes to the agent chat panel in the Design view. Rather than a single undifferentiated conversation, the agent operates in one of five distinct modes — each shaping how it responds, what tools it reaches for, and what kind of output it produces. The user can switch modes freely at any time.

The insight: unstructured chat with an agent produces mediocre documents. By giving the conversation explicit modes, the agent knows whether to diverge (Brainstorm), gather evidence (Research, Investigate), converge into prose (Author), or just listen (Talk). This structured dialog produces better design documents because each phase of thinking gets the right kind of AI assistance.
design:
## Overview
The agent chat panel (sidebar alongside the Design Editor) gains a mode selector. Each mode adjusts the agent's system prompt, available tools, and response style. The user switches modes freely — there is no enforced sequence, though a natural flow exists.

## Modes

### Brainstorm
- **Purpose:** Divergent thinking. Generate ideas, explore possibilities, challenge assumptions.
- **Agent behavior:** Generative and expansive. Offers alternatives, asks "what if" questions, builds on ideas. Does not prematurely converge.
- **Output style:** Bullet lists, mind-map-style expansions, provocative questions. Short bursts, not essays.
- **Tools:** None special — pure conversation.

### Research
- **Purpose:** Gather external knowledge relevant to the design.
- **Agent behavior:** Searches documentation, APIs, prior art, industry patterns, and best practices. Cites sources. Presents findings as evidence to inform decisions.
- **Output style:** Structured findings with references. "Here's what I found about X..."
- **Tools:** Web search, documentation lookup, API reference retrieval.

### Investigate
- **Purpose:** Analyze the actual codebase and repository.
- **Agent behavior:** Reads code, traces dependencies, examines existing patterns, identifies constraints and integration points. Grounds the design in reality.
- **Output style:** Code references with file paths, dependency diagrams, constraint summaries. "The current implementation does X in file Y..."
- **Tools:** Code search (ast-grep, grep, glob), file reading, dependency analysis.

### Author
- **Purpose:** Converge into written prose. Produce or refine the design document.
- **Agent behavior:** Writes structured, publishable content. Synthesizes prior Brainstorm/Research/Investigate context into coherent design sections. Edits for clarity and completeness.
- **Output style:** Markdown prose ready to insert into the Design Editor. Structured with headers, rationale, trade-offs, and decisions.
- **Tools:** Editor integration — can propose edits to the design document directly.

### Talk
- **Purpose:** Freeform, unstructured conversation.
- **Agent behavior:** No particular agenda. Responds naturally. Useful for ad-hoc questions, rubber-ducking, or exploring tangents that don't fit neatly into other modes.
- **Output style:** Conversational. No structured output expected.
- **Tools:** Whatever is contextually relevant.

## UX
- Mode selector lives at the top of the chat panel (segmented control or dropdown)
- Current mode is always visible
- Switching modes does NOT clear conversation history — context carries across
- The agent acknowledges mode switches naturally ("Switching to Research — what should I look into?")
- Each mode may have a subtle visual tint or icon to reinforce which mode is active

## Why This Matters
Most AI-assisted writing fails because the user and agent are in different cognitive phases. The user wants to brainstorm but the agent writes a final draft. The user wants code analysis but the agent speculates. Modes align the agent's behavior to the user's current intent, producing better documents through better collaboration.
acceptance_criteria:
- Chat panel displays a mode selector with all five modes: Brainstorm, Research, Investigate, Author, Talk
- Switching modes changes the agent's behavior and response style as described
- Mode switches preserve conversation history and context
- Research mode can search external sources and cite findings
- Investigate mode can read codebase files and reference specific code paths
- Author mode produces structured markdown suitable for the Design Editor
- Talk mode allows freeform conversation without structured output
- Current mode is always visually indicated in the chat panel
- User can switch modes freely in any order at any time

title: Feature-Scoped Ready Dispatch
description: Dispatch all ready tasks within a feature's subtree by selecting any bead in that feature and invoking Dispatch Ready.
design:
## Overview
Add a "Dispatch Ready" toolbar action that resolves the feature scope of the selected bead and dispatches all ready tasks within that subtree.

## Core Algorithm
1. User selects any bead (task, feature, or epic)
2. Clicks "Dispatch Ready" in the toolbar
3. System resolves dispatch scope:
   - If selected bead is a task → walk up to its parent feature (or epic if no feature)
   - If selected bead is a feature → use it directly as scope
   - If selected bead is an epic → use it directly as scope
4. Collect all ready tasks (no open blockers) within the resolved scope's subtree
5. Display confirmation: "Dispatch N ready tasks under [Feature Name]?"
6. On confirm, dispatch each ready task via tvm:dispatch

## Visual Design
- Ready tasks rendered as gold-colored rows in the tree view
- Selecting any gold row enables "Dispatch Ready" in toolbar
- Confirmation dialog shows the list of tasks that will be dispatched
- Progress indicator as tasks are dispatched sequentially

## Example
```
Epic: Authentication System
  Feature: OAuth Integration        ← resolved scope
    Task: Setup OAuth Provider       ✓ ready (gold)  → dispatched
    Task: Implement Token Refresh    ✓ ready (gold)  → dispatched
    Task: Add Error Handling         ✗ blocked        → skipped
    Task: Write Integration Tests    ✗ blocked        → skipped
```
Selecting either ready task and invoking "Dispatch Ready" dispatches both.

## Edge Cases
- If resolved scope has no ready tasks → show "No ready tasks" message
- If only one ready task → still use feature-scoped flow (consistent UX)
- Multiple features under an epic → only dispatch within the one feature the selected bead belongs to
- If user selects an epic directly → dispatch all ready tasks across all its children
acceptance_criteria:
- Toolbar shows "Dispatch Ready" button when any bead is selected
- System correctly resolves feature scope by walking up ancestry
- All ready tasks (no open blockers) within the feature subtree are collected
- Confirmation dialog shows task list and count before dispatching
- Each ready task is dispatched via tvm:dispatch
- Tasks not ready (blocked) are excluded
- Selecting different tasks within the same feature produces the same dispatch set
- Selecting an epic dispatches all ready tasks across its entire subtree
- Visual feedback shows dispatch progress
- Gold-colored rows visually distinguish ready tasks in the tree view

title: Experience Supervisor
description: Tooling for dispatching and overseeing ready work from the planning view. Enables a supervisor to identify ready work visually and dispatch agents toward specific goals (features or epics) rather than globally — controlling the blast radius of concurrent agent work.
design:
## Overview
The Supervisor Experience adds dispatch capabilities to the planning view toolbar, allowing a supervisor to launch agent work in a controlled, goal-scoped manner.

## Core Concept: Feature-Scoped Ready Dispatch
When a user selects any bead and invokes "Dispatch Ready," the system:
1. Resolves the dispatch scope — walks up the selected bead's ancestry to find its containing feature (or epic if no feature exists)
2. Collects all ready tasks within that feature's subtree (tasks with no open blockers)
3. Dispatches all of them as a batch

This prevents uncontrolled sprawl (dispatching all globally ready work could spawn hundreds of agents) while ensuring meaningful progress toward a specific goal.

## Dispatch Modes
1. **Individual Dispatch** — Select a single bead, dispatch just that bead
2. **Feature-Scoped Ready Dispatch** — Select any bead within a feature, dispatch all ready tasks in that feature's subtree

## Visual Design
- Ready tasks rendered as gold-colored rows in the tree view
- Selection of any gold row + "Dispatch Ready" dispatches all gold siblings under the same feature ancestor
- Toolbar actions: "Dispatch" (individual) and "Dispatch Ready" (feature-scoped)

## Key Interactions
- Selecting Task 1 or Task 3 under the same feature produces the same "Dispatch Ready" result — all ready siblings dispatched
- Visual feedback during dispatch (progress, agent status)
- Integration with existing tvm:dispatch workflow
acceptance_criteria:
- Toolbar shows dispatch actions in planning view
- "Dispatch" sends a single selected bead to an agent
- "Dispatch Ready" resolves the feature scope and dispatches all ready tasks within it
- Ready tasks are visually distinct (gold rows) in the tree view
- Dispatching provides visual feedback (progress/status)
- Feature-scoped dispatch works correctly across epic→feature→task hierarchy

description:
# Planning Experience

## Problem
Progressive planning requires transforming vague feature requests into actionable specifications through distinct phases.
Currently this process is manual and disconnected - users must context-switch between tools, invoke agents manually, and
track state across sessions.

## Vision
A native, wizard-style planning experience integrated into the Beads plugin that guides users through collaborative Epic
refinement with AI assistance, producing structured architectural proposals and work breakdowns.

## Agent Framework
**Selected:** [christopherkarani/SwiftAgents](https://github.com/christopherkarani/SwiftAgents)
- Full orchestration framework (Swift 6.2)
- ReAct/PlanAndExecute patterns
- @Tool macro for function calling
- Supervisor routing
- MCP (Model Context Protocol) support
- Memory systems for state

## User Journeys

### Journey 1: Plan a New Feature
1. User creates a sparse Epic: "Add dark mode support"
2. Right-clicks Epic row → "Plan It"
3. Planning view opens (new nav item below Dashboard)
4. New tab created for this Epic
5. Wizard Step 1 (Define): User collaborates with agent panel to:
- Refine Epic description (rich markdown)
- Brainstorm user journeys
- Define acceptance criteria
6. Wizard Step 2 (Analyze): Agent examines target repo codebase
7. Wizard Step 3 (Propose): Agent presents structured proposal:
- Technology choices & alternatives explored
- Component/architecture view
- Security considerations
- Testing approach
- Work breakdown (Features/Tasks)
8. Wizard Step 4 (Approve): User reviews, edits, approves
9. Child beads created, Epic updated, tab closes

### Journey 2: Resume Interrupted Planning
1. User was mid-planning, closes app
2. Reopens app → Planning nav shows persisted tab
3. Wizard resumes at exact step with full state
4. User continues where they left off

### Journey 3: Parallel Planning Across Repos
1. User planning Epic A in repo-one
2. Opens "Plan It" on Epic B in repo-two → new tab
3. Switches between tabs, each has independent state

## Key Constraints
- One Epic per tab (tabs can span different repos)
- State persists via bead K/V pairs
- No offline/fallback mode - agent is core to experience
- Epics only (Features/Tasks planned via this flow, not directly)

## MVP Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] User can complete full wizard flow (Define → Analyze → Propose → Approve)
- [ ] Child beads created on approval
- [ ] Tab state persists across app restart

title: Persistent disclosure state for nested relationship groups
description: Remember expanded/collapsed state of nested disclosure groups (Part Of, Subtasks, etc.) within the Relationships section
design:
## Overview
The Relationships section uses `@AppStorage` to persist its expanded state, but the nested `RelationshipGroup` components use `@State` which resets on view recreation. Make nested disclosures persistent.

## Current Implementation
File: `OneApps/Beads/Components/RelationshipsSection.swift`

```swift
// Line 15 - Parent disclosure (ALREADY PERSISTENT)
@AppStorage("beads.detail.relationships.expanded") private var isExpanded = false

// Line 129 - Nested groups (NOT PERSISTENT - uses @State)
@State private var isExpanded = false
```

## Solution

### Modify `RelationshipGroup` to accept storage key:

```swift
struct RelationshipGroup: View {
    let title: String
    let icon: String
    let nodes: [BeadNode]
    let kind: RelationshipKind
    let storageKey: String  // NEW: unique key for AppStorage
    var onRemove: ((RelationshipKind, BeadNode) -> Void)?
    var tint: Color = .secondary
    
    // Change from @State to @AppStorage
    @AppStorage private var isExpanded: Bool
    
    init(..., storageKey: String, ...) {
        self.storageKey = storageKey
        _isExpanded = AppStorage(wrappedValue: false, storageKey)
    }
}
```

### Update RelationshipsSection to pass unique keys:

```swift
// Part Of
RelationshipGroup(
    title: "Part Of",
    icon: "arrow.up.circle",
    nodes: node.parents,
    kind: .parent,
    storageKey: "beads.detail.relationships.partOf.expanded",  // NEW
    onRemove: onRemove
)

// Subtasks
RelationshipGroup(
    title: "Subtasks",
    icon: "arrow.down.circle",
    nodes: node.children,
    kind: .child,
    storageKey: "beads.detail.relationships.subtasks.expanded",  // NEW
    onRemove: onRemove
)

// Must Complete First (blockedBy)
storageKey: "beads.detail.relationships.blockedBy.expanded"

// Will Unblock (blocks)
storageKey: "beads.detail.relationships.blocks.expanded"

// Related
storageKey: "beads.detail.relationships.related.expanded"

// Discovered From
storageKey: "beads.detail.relationships.discoveredFrom.expanded"
```

## Storage Key Convention
Pattern: `beads.detail.relationships.<groupName>.expanded`
- `beads.detail.relationships.partOf.expanded`
- `beads.detail.relationships.subtasks.expanded`
- `beads.detail.relationships.blockedBy.expanded`
- `beads.detail.relationships.blocks.expanded`
- `beads.detail.relationships.related.expanded`
- `beads.detail.relationships.discoveredFrom.expanded`
acceptance_criteria:

- [ ] "Subtasks" disclosure state persists across view changes

- [ ] "Related" disclosure state persists across view changes
- [ ] "Discovered From" disclosure state persists across view changes
- [ ] Each group remembers its state independently
- [ ] States persist across app restarts

1. `feature-<bead-id>` (e.g., `feature-one-nr1`)
2. `task-<bead-id>` (e.g., `task-one-nr1`)
3. Direct bead ID match (e.g., `one-nr1`)

title: Lingo schema apply policy enforcement
description: Retarget Accept Edits enforcement away from VibeMachine file edits. In Lingo, the edit/apply policy controls schema proposal application safety: whether schema deltas require explicit user confirmation before being applied to the active sandbox/live database.
design:
## Scope
The Lingo composer already exposes an edit-policy picker. This bead makes that control honest for ontology schema application. It is not about file edits, Commander provider commands, or VibeMachine AgentService.

## Policy Meaning
- Ask First: schema deltas require explicit user confirmation before application.
- Accept/apply for session, if enabled: eligible schema deltas may apply to the active sandbox only after deterministic validation and within the session's safety bounds.
- No policy authorizes shell commands or arbitrary filesystem writes.

## Boundaries
Work belongs in Ontology Lingo view-model/agent/apply paths. The policy must be visible in the composer and enforced where `apply_schema_delta` or equivalent schema application occurs.
acceptance_criteria: Lingo edit policy state is owned outside local picker UI. Schema apply paths consult the policy before applying proposal deltas. Ask First requires explicit confirmation. Any automatic mode is session-scoped, clearly labeled, and never grants command execution approval. Manual explicit Apply remains explicit user intent. Focused Ontology tests cover policy branches.

title: Drift indicator and no-sandbox fallback
description: UX polish for the version-pinning feature. (1) When on-disk Resources/Packages version differs from sandbox-installed version, show a small badge on that package's section header. (2) When there's no active sandbox, fall back to the loaded packages with a clear banner explaining the fallback.
design:
Drift detection: compare on-disk version (from PackageManager.OntologyPackage.manifest.version) vs sandbox-pinned version (from SandboxInstalledPackages). For each live section:
- Same version: no badge.
- Different version: small amber pill on section header: 'on-disk vN, sandbox vM'. Tooltip explains.
- Sandbox version not on-disk: amber pill 'pinned to vM (not on-disk)'.

No-sandbox fallback: when activeSandbox is nil, the Lingo Explorer's live sections render from PackageManager.parsedEntities (V1 source) and a banner appears at the top of the sidebar (below the proposal banner): '⚠ No active sandbox. Showing on-disk package contents — may not match a deployed schema.' with a 'Select sandbox' button.

UX detail: when fallback is active, edit affordances and apply [Apply] still work (they target the sandbox you'd select before applying — actually the apply path has its own sandbox check; verify).

No-package-data fallback: if neither sandbox nor PackageManager has any package data, show an empty state: 'No live ontology data available. Load packages from Resources/Packages or select a sandbox.'

Edge cases:
- Pinned version fails to resolve (git ref missing): show error badge on section header; that section has no contents in the tree.
- Sandbox reports installed but git resolver can't find it: show drift badge with 'version not in repo' tooltip.
acceptance_criteria:
- On-disk and sandbox versions matching → no badge.
- Versions differing → amber badge with version pair shown.
- No active sandbox → banner appears, fallback data renders.
- No data at all → empty-state message guides user.
- Failed resolution → error badge, no crash.
- Banner 'Select sandbox' button opens the sandbox picker (existing UI).
